synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Elara Lin is a final-year medical student who talks all the time, practises stitches on bananas, and on her first morning on the surgical ward tells the chief resident he's missed a leak. She's right. By the end of the day Wang Xing Yue has handed her logbook to someone else, so that he can ask her to dinner. He's been in love with her for fifteen months. The only person he's told is his brother, who sent him a paper about voles.

She's also the Lins' surgeon. When the family's people bleed somewhere a hospital can't see them, she goes, with whatever she can steal. In a supply room at three in the morning she begs him not to ask, and he promises he won't. He keeps that promise for three and a half years: through a knife at her father's door that cuts through her right wrist, a winter when she stops talking, and the year she gets her hands back in secret on a machine in a garage and goes back to work in a cellar, in a mask, as Doctor Ghost.

He's known since she mended his pillowcase at two in the morning. He never asks her to stop. He restocks her bag instead, and when she finally calls him, he comes with blood.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Elara has been in the corner of every Lin book so far: late, in scrubs, with her hair falling out of its clip, crying at weddings, stapling somebody's head on a kitchen table. I wanted to know what all that cost her, and who looks after the person who looks after everyone.

Xing Yue isn't a nice man to anyone but her. He makes residents sick on his ward rounds, he checks her location, he goes through her bag, and he lies to his own professor without blinking. I didn't want the book to tell him off for any of it. The one thing he never does is ask her to be someone else, and that felt like the most romantic thing I could give her.

There's blood, because it's a book about surgeons, but the medicine stays at story level. The love scenes are slow and mostly come after night shifts, in early light, which is how she likes them. Nobody has a baby. They get a house with a long kitchen, two pagers, a phone in a drawer that rings at half past eleven, and each other.

21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This is a 21+ medical romance, warm and funny for most of its length, but it has some hard moments:

• Love scenes throughout, heated and detailed but not explicit, from She Narrates Everything on

• An infected knife wound treated over the phone at night (Three in the Morning, on Speaker)

• A gunshot wound, sepsis and surgery on a kitchen table, with stolen hospital supplies (Zhao Zhendong Is Bleeding Out, Fifteen Days of Drips)

• A shooting in a noodle shop and a head wound closed at home (Staples on a Kitchen Table)

• A people-smuggling boat and cold, frightened survivors at a border bridge (The Seventh Guest)

• Burns after a workshop fire (Again?)

• A knife attack, heavy bleeding and a serious hand injury (The Knife at the Red Door)

• Nerve pain, withdrawal into silence, and a father's confession to a crime that killed her birth parents in a fire (The House Is Too Quiet, A Name in a Ledger, Elara Before the Lins)

• A prison visit (Her Mother's Window)

• Secret surgery outside hospitals, falsified records and lies to police and employers (A Surgeon Who Doesn't Exist, The Cellar Under the Rope Store, Doctor Ghost)

• A girl's face cut with a bottle by her father, mentioned (The Cellar Under the Rope Store)

• A gunshot to the thigh and life-threatening bleeding (Two Surgeons, One Table)

• A workplace inquiry and suspension (I Know)

• A footbridge collapse with many casualties (A Mass Casualty Night)

• A partner who tracks her phone and goes through her bag, shown without judgement (from Three in the Morning, on Speaker)

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
City Hospital — the teaching hospital at the foot of the hill. Ward 9B, general surgery, is on the ninth floor of the tower; the old 1930s block stands behind it.
Harbourside General — the big hospital by the harbour, where Elara does her intern year and goes back to training in 2027.
The Crestview — the private hospital on the hill above the old racecourse, where Dr. Meng repairs her hand and Ms. Cui makes her cry.
The hospital garden — behind the old block: a camphor tree older than the hospital, a koi pond, and the fourth window along on the first floor, which was her mother's ward.
14 Banyan Terrace — his flat, the top two floors and roof of a white 1950s building ten minutes downhill from City Hospital.
2 Camphor Hill — the old doctor's house above the hospital, with a long kitchen and a back room for the rig. Bought in both their names, without asking.
The Walled City — the old district where the Lins live, behind a red door with a brass fish knocker and eleven chairs that don't match.
The cellar under the rope store — the room Raiden builds next to the garage near the Docks, behind a steel door painted to look like wood.
Doctor Ghost — the name the docks give the masked surgeon who never speaks and always hums.
The rig — Jinx's steel training machine for Elara's hand: springs, a pinch gauge, pins and a wire that buzzes. Every knob turns a quarter.
The ghost phone — the line that rings only from her father's or Uncle Mok's numbers. From July 2027 it lives in the kitchen drawer.
The dot — her phone location, shared with him ‘for night shifts’ from 2023, and his with her from 2026.
The rules — what they wrote on the back of his suspension letter. Rule one: nobody does this alone.
Qu Xiaoyue — her birth name, ‘little moon’. Elara is a moon of Jupiter, so she kept a piece of it.
Qu Lighterage — her father's firm: four lighter boats between the ships and the old Walled City piers.
Plum Steps — the children's home at the top of a long flight of stone steps, closed in 2011.
Loupes — magnifying glasses surgeons wear to operate. Hers are dark red, made for her eyes, with E.L. inside the arm.
Registrar, consultant — a registrar is a mid-level surgeon in training; a consultant is the senior surgeon in charge.

chapters.title: The Student Who Told the Chief Resident He Was Wrong
chapters.desc: On her first morning in surgery, a final-year student tells the chief resident he’s missed a leak. She’s right, and he has seen her face before.
chapters.epigraph: “I’d rather be wrong about this one.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
“Read it to me.”

Dr. Weng read the drug chart. An antibiotic, twice a day, normal dose.

“His kidneys work at a third of yours. It’s on the front page of his notes. Again.”

Weng read it again. Faster. He stopped in the same place.

“Again. Slower. You’re not tying your shoes.”

The old man in bed nine had put his spoon down to watch. Best thing on the ward all week, by his face. Weng went red from the collar up, read it a third time, and saw it.

“Oh.”

“Change it before lunch. Then look up what that drug does to kidneys. Tell me tomorrow. No notes.”

Monday. Ward 9B. Professor Liao was at a conference across the water until Thursday, so the round was Wang Xing Yue’s. Chief surgical resident, two months in. Thirty years old and already the thing the interns warned each other about.

His team trailed behind him. Dr. Rao, junior resident, neat notes he never reread. Dr. Weng, three weeks into his first job, jumping every time his bleep went. And four final-year students on their first day, in white coats with the packet creases still in them. Notebooks hugged to their chests. Shields.

Sister Shao was still on the floor, handing over after her night. Grey cardigan, pager clipped to the pocket, nothing she didn’t know. She looked the students over.

“Fresh ones,” she said, and went home to bed.

Three of the students were studying the floor. The fourth wasn’t. She was small, at the back, with her hair escaping a plastic clip. She had her head on one side. She was looking at him like he was weather coming in over the harbour. Interested. Not scared at all. Strange.

He had a ward to get round.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bed fourteen was Mr. Yin Shoucheng. Seventy-one. Retired bus driver. Day four after a cancer had been cut out of his bowel and the two ends joined.

Bad night. Fever in the small hours. Heart rate a hundred and twelve. He’d kept trying to climb out of bed, the nurses said. At the bottom of his right lung there were crackles.

“Chest,” Xing Yue said. “He’s seventy-one, he’s had an anaesthetic, it hurts to breathe deep. Sputum, chest film, antibiotics. Physio up before ten. Sit him out after.”

Rao wrote it down.

“Sorry. Um. Can I say something?”

She didn’t wait for a yes.

“His heart rate went up first. Before the fever. It was ninety yesterday lunchtime. A hundred and four by teatime. The temperature didn’t climb till night. It’s on the obs chart!”

She took a breath. She needed one.

“And he says his tummy’s worse today. Not better. I came in early to see my patients and he was awake, so I said good morning, and I sort of… pressed on his belly while I said it.”

Mr. Yin raised a hand off the sheet.

“She did.”

“He didn’t like it. On the right. Near where the join would be.”

Nobody on the team breathed. Rao looked like a man at his own funeral.

Did she know who she was talking to? Nobody corrected Wang Xing Yue. Not because he shouted. He never shouted. He was just almost never wrong. And if you told him he was, he took your argument apart in front of the patient while you stood there in your new coat and watched.

“Chest is the commonest cause of a fever on day four.”

“I know.”

Her face had gone pink. Her voice hadn’t moved at all.

“I’d still want the scan. If it’s his chest and we scan him, we’ve lost an hour and some money. If it’s a leak and we wait, Mr. Yin pays for it.” She swallowed. “I’d rather be wrong about this one.”

From the bed, through his false teeth:

“So would I, young lady.”

Xing Yue put the notes down. He rubbed his hands together to warm them. He laid one flat on the old man’s belly and pressed. Left side. Middle. Low on the right.

On the right the muscle went hard before he’d gone a centimetre. Mr. Yin sucked air through his teeth and grabbed the sheet.

“Sorry, Mr. Yin.”

He straightened. He looked at the student.

“You’re right. Book the scan.”

Then he turned to Rao.

“You saw this chart at six. Why did a student find it?”

Rao went white. His mouth opened.

“Don’t answer that. CT with contrast. Ring theatres and tell the coordinator I may need a slot today. Then read every chart on this ward again. Read the numbers this time. Don’t copy them.”

Rao went. Fast. Xing Yue picked up the chart and wrote. Out of the corner of his eye, the student. She’d gone from pink to white. She looked like she might be sick. She also looked like it was the best day of her life. Both, at once, on one small face.

He looked at her properly. Round face. Quick dark eyes. So much hair. A cardigan under the white coat, the pocket stuffed with pens and something that crinkled.

He knew that face. June, last year. The sixth floor, early on a Saturday, at the end of a call. A young man hit by a van. Three ribs cracked on the left, a clean scan, nothing for a surgeon. He’d been heading for the lift when a girl in a T-shirt cut him off. Hair coming out of a clip. All in one breath. Had anyone checked her brother’s spleen? Because it was the left ribs. The spleen sat right under them. She’d read it could bleed slowly and look like nothing for hours—

“We checked,” he’d said. “The scan’s clear.”

“Oh, good! Thank you. Sorry!”

Then she was past him and into the room. Talking already.

He’d gone home and not slept. He’d blamed the night. He’d been blaming the night for fifteen months. Was that still the night?

He signed the chart and moved on to bed fifteen.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of the round she slipped Weng something from her cardigan pocket. A boiled sweet in a twist of wrapper.

Weng held it like a medal.

✦ ✦ ✦

The students caught her by the sluice. He was coming the other way with a chart. They didn’t see him.

“Are you INSANE?”

“He’s going to fail you. He’s going to fail you so hard they’ll fail your parents.”

“He doesn’t fail people.” That was the tall one with the expensive haircut. “He just… makes them stop existing.”

“I don’t care!”

She did care. Her voice had gone right up.

“It was a leak. Probably. It was, wasn’t it? Oh my god. What if it’s his chest?”

“Then you’re dead, Lin.”

“Then I’m dead. Fine. Mr. Yin won’t be.”

Xing Yue walked past. Four mouths shut at once.

He was nearly at the lifts before he caught himself smiling. He stopped that.

✦ ✦ ✦

The radiologist scrolled through the scan in the dark. Stopped.

“There. Small leak at the join. And that collection’s new since Friday.”

“Theatre at one.”

“Want me to ring them?”

“Rao’s ringing them.”

“Rao? God help them.”

He found her in the corridor outside the doctors’ room. She was eating a cereal bar standing up and reading Mr. Yin’s notes over somebody’s shoulder.

“You found it. You’ll want to see it. Go and scrub.”

She stared at him with her mouth full. Swallowed.

“Yes! Yes. Sorry. Yes.”

She went. She came back. Wrong way.

✦ ✦ ✦

She talked while she scrubbed. Not to him. To herself.

“Soap. Where’s the—oh. There. Okay.”

“Is this hot? This is very hot. Fine. It’s fine.”

“Last time I did this it was for a toe. An ingrown toenail. Very glamorous.”

He stood at the next sink with his arms under the water. She glanced over and caught him watching her hands, and talked faster.

“Sorry. I’ll stop.”

“Don’t.”

Good hands. Small, quick, sure. Every finger, every side of every finger, the backs, the wrists. Everyone was taught that. Nobody still did it after first year.

The badge clipped to her scrubs said LIN ELARA, FINAL YEAR.

Lin. Well. Obviously. The van, the private room on six, the grey-haired man in the corridor with a face like the side of a building and two men behind him. Everyone in this city knew that family. And his name was at the top of her rotation sheet. Six weeks. Her logbook. The line at the bottom that said whether she was fit to be a doctor.

He held his hands up. Water ran off his elbows. She held hers up beside him, looked across, and went pink above the mask she hadn’t tied.

He decided. Right there at the sink, dripping. Then he decided what had to go first.

✦ ✦ ✦

In theatre she held the retractor where he put her. Two hours. It didn’t move a millimetre.

He took the join apart and washed Mr. Yin out until the fluid ran clear. He brought the bowel out onto the skin for a few months, till the old man was strong enough to have it put back. Ordinary work.

She murmured the whole way through.

“Okay, okay. There. Okay.”

Suyin, his scrub nurse, looked at her over her mask. Then at him.

“Does she always do that?”

“Apparently.”

“Do you want me to—”

“No.”

Suyin’s eyebrows went up and stayed up. He didn’t care. If the student had stopped, he’d have been annoyed. That was new.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dr. Fei Ran was eating noodles out of a plastic tub in the registrars’ office with her feet on the bin. Senior registrar. Four years older than him and in no hurry to be anything else.

“Take one of my students,” he said. “Assessments, logbook, all of it. Lin Elara.”

Fei put her chopsticks down.

“The one who found Yin’s leak? The whole floor’s heard.” She squinted at him. “Why?”

He didn’t answer.

“Because she was right?”

“No.”

“Because she’s a Lin?”

“No.”

“Oh.” Fei’s eyebrows went up and stayed there. “A student you met this morning.”

“Yes.”

Fei looked at him. He looked back. She picked up the rotation sheet, crossed out his name on one line, wrote hers, initialled it. Back to the noodles.

“I’m not going to ask,” she said, with her mouth full. “I’m going to tell everyone at Christmas.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Recovery, early evening. Mr. Yin was awake, more or less, with a mask on his face. Puzzled. Calm. Still full of anaesthetic.

“Doctor.”

“It went well, Mr. Yin. You’ll be sore. You’ll be all right.”

The old man nodded slowly. Then he turned his head on the pillow and looked past him, down the ward. Searching.

“Where’s the little doctor? The one who talks.”

Gone. Fei had sent her home after watching her eat a second cereal bar standing up.

“Tomorrow. She’s in at six.”

Mr. Yin squinted at him over the mask.

“How do you know that?”

He’d read the student rota on the way down. Twice.

“Go to sleep, Mr. Yin.”

chapters.title: Love at First Sight Is a Sleep-Deprivation Symptom
chapters.desc: Elara finds her logbook handed to someone else and marches into the chief resident’s office to apologise for being right. He tells her why, and it isn’t a question.
chapters.epigraph: “I can’t take you to dinner and sign your logbook. I picked dinner.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
On Tuesday he didn’t look at her once. Elara knew, because she spent the whole round standing where he’d have to. End of the bed. By the drug trolley. At bed six she got so close to his elbow she could smell him. Hospital soap, the cheap kind from the dispensers. And tea.

He turned a page.

“Potassium, Dr. Rao.”

Like she was a coat stand. Wonderful. Rao got the potassium. Then Rao got everything else.

“Why does a man on a drip have no fluid chart?”

“I—it’s in the—”

“It isn’t. Why has nobody told the woman in bed eight her drain’s stopped?”

“I was going to—”

“What does ‘patient comfortable’ mean? You wrote it at four in the morning. He’d had morphine twice.”

Rao answered the first one. After that he gave up and just stood there going red. By bed twelve his ears were a dark, painful colour. The patient in twelve, a big woman with a gallstone, reached out and patted his hand once Wang had moved on.

“There, there, son.”

“Thank you, auntie.”

At the end of the round Elara dug in her cardigan pocket and gave Rao a boiled sweet. He took it without looking. Then he looked at it.

“Thanks.” He sounded like he’d been punched. “Seriously. Thanks.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to see Mr. Yin after. He was sitting up with the bag under his gown. Grey, cross, alive.

“The jelly in this place tastes of shampoo.”

“I’ll tell the kitchen.”

“Don’t. They’ll make it worse.” He sniffed. “The tall one came at six. Looked at my bag. Didn’t say good morning.”

“He doesn’t say good morning.”

“You do.” He looked her up and down. “Are you married?”

“I’m a student!”

“That’s not an answer.”

He went to sleep. Just like that, mid-glare.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday Dr. Fei stopped her outside the sluice with a tub of noodles.

“I’m doing your logbook now, by the way. I’ve got your sheet. Find me Friday and we’ll go through it.”

“Oh! Okay. Sure. Thank you.” A beat. “Um. Why?”

Fei was already walking.

“Ask him.”

The lift doors shut on her. Elara stood outside the sluice and felt her whole face go hot.

She knew why. Of course she knew why. First morning, first round, and she’d told the chief resident he was wrong. In front of his team. In front of the patient! She’d said tummy. Twice. She’d eaten a cereal bar at him in a corridor with her mouth open. And now he’d given her logbook away because he couldn’t stand the sight of her. Six weeks of being invisible. Then someone would write fine in the box at the end. Fine was what you wrote about a student you’d forgotten.

She thought about it through a clinic. On the bus. In the shower. At the long table in the Walled City, pushing rice round her bowl.

Ah Sim stood over her with the ladle.

“Little sparrow. You’re eating like a bird.”

“I am a bird. You named me.”

“Eat, bird.”

Raiden had come for dinner, which meant nobody else got to talk. Tonight he stopped halfway through a story about a crane and pointed his chopsticks at her.

“What’s wrong with her?”

“Nothing’s wrong with me.”

“Something’s wrong with you. You’ve said nine words. You usually say nine words a second.” He leaned in. “Who do I have to fight?”

“Nobody!”

“I’ll fight anyone. I’ve been hit by a van. I’m basically armoured now.”

“It’s not a person. It’s a surgeon.”

From the head of the table, their father put his bowl down.

“Which surgeon?”

Oh no.

“No surgeon. A hypothetical surgeon. A… general surgeon. In general.” She shoved rice in her mouth. “I’m eating, Baba. Look. Bird’s eating.”

Lin Jian looked at her the way he read the small print on a contract. Then he picked his bowl up again.

Raiden mouthed hypothetical at her across the table. She kicked him.

✦ ✦ ✦

At midnight the light was on under Eliana’s door. It was always on. Her little sister was nineteen and slept from four in the morning till noon, like a bat. She lived in a nest of hoodies with three screens on the desk and a fourth on her knees. Elara sat on the end of the bed and told her everything. The round. Mr. Yin. The leak, the scan, the sink. The logbook. Fei and the noodles.

“And I said tummy, Eli. TUMMY. To him.”

Eliana didn’t turn round.

“He’s thirty. From the north. No girlfriend. Nothing online. He eats beef noodles at eleven every night he’s on call. The place across from the ambulance bay.”

Elara stared at the back of her sister’s head. How? No. Nobody in this family asked Eliana how. You only got a look.

“I didn’t ask for that.”

“No.”

Eliana kept typing.

Elara lasted about four seconds.

“Is he nice?”

“He made a registrar cry in July.”

“That’s not NICE.”

“It was a good cry. The registrar was wrong.”

“How do you even—no. Don’t tell me.”

“Wasn’t going to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday she went to apologise.

She’d written it out on the bus, in her head, in three parts. She did that with patient histories so she wouldn’t lose anything. One: sorry for contradicting him in front of Mr. Yin. You didn’t do that. Two: sorry about the corridor. Three was the important one. Three had fallen out of her head somewhere near the fish market. It would come back. It always came back.

His office was at the end of the surgical corridor on nine. A cupboard with a window. Desk, two chairs, a computer older than her, a shelf of journals. The door was half open. He was writing in a set of notes. From the doorway his handwriting looked like an earthquake. She knocked on the frame. He looked up. He put the pen down.

“Dr. Wang. Sorry! Have you got a minute? It’ll be one minute. Maybe two. I wanted to say sorry. I’ve got three things.”

He said nothing. He took his glasses off and started cleaning them on a folded handkerchief. Was that a yes? She decided it was a yes.

“One. I’m sorry I contradicted you in front of Mr. Yin. You don’t do that. You don’t correct a senior doctor in front of a patient, it undermines—well, you know what it undermines, you’re the senior doctor.”

He went on cleaning the glasses.

“Except I’d do it again. Because of Mr. Yin. So I’m not sure that’s an apology. It’s more of a… report.”

She could hear herself not apologising. She kept going. Brilliant.

“And two. The cereal bar. I’m normally quite tidy.”

That was a lie. She felt it land on her face.

“I’m normally very tidy,” she said, to make it more convincing.

Then she stopped. Three hadn’t come back.

“And three… Mr. Yin’s eating jelly. He says it’s terrible. I don’t think that’s three. But I thought you’d want to know about the jelly.”

She ran out. A trolley with a bad wheel went past in the corridor. He put his glasses back on.

“You didn’t do anything wrong. Not on the round. Not in the corridor. You were right. You’ll be right again, and you should say so again. Don’t come and apologise for it.”

“Oh.” She blinked. “Then why did Dr. Fei—”

“I asked her to take your logbook because I’m taking you to dinner.”

Same voice. Exactly the voice he’d used for the potassium.

“I can’t take you to dinner and sign your logbook. I picked dinner.”

Elara stood in the doorway. He looked back at her. Nothing on his face moved. Serious face, older than thirty. Dark glasses. Short neat hair. Tired round the eyes, like the tired lived there and paid rent. Was he joking? Did he even know how?

“That wasn’t a question.”

“No.”

“You’re meant to ask! People ask. Would you like to have dinner? Then I say yes or no.”

“You can say no.”

That was it. He sat with his hands flat on the notes and waited. Oh. Oh no. If she said no, he’d say all right. He’d pick up his pen. He’d never mention it again, and tomorrow on the ward he’d be exactly the same. She could see it so clearly her stomach turned over. She didn’t say no.

“Oh.”

That was all she had. Oh.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then, because she was her, she kept going.

“Is it allowed? It can’t be allowed. You’re the chief resident and I’m a student on your unit. There’s a rule. There has to be a rule. There’s a rule about how long you can leave a cannula in.”

She got her phone out. She found the student handbook. The university had hidden it inside another document inside a folder called General.

“Who calls a folder General? General what? They moved the anatomy exam once and told us by FAX.”

He waited.

“Found it.”

She read it out. Students should not enter into a personal relationship with any member of staff who has a role in their teaching assessment or supervision. Where such a relationship exists or begins, the staff member must declare it and withdraw from that role.

She read it twice. She looked up.

“You’ve withdrawn.”

“On Monday.”

“That’s before you asked me!”

“I still haven’t asked you.”

She opened her mouth. Shut it. He was right, which was annoying.

“Friday. After your skills session.”

“I can’t Friday. It’s banana night. In the skills lab. We suture bananas, all the final years. It’s sort of a competition. It’s not really a competition. It’s practice. But everyone treats it like one, and I won last year, so if I don’t go Shu Kai will say I was scared.”

“Then after the bananas.”

“Okay,” she heard herself say.

“I’ll wait outside the lab.”

“You don’t know when it finishes.”

“Half past eight.”

“How do you—” She stopped. “Oh. You used to teach it.”

“Three years.”

“Of course you did.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked her to the lifts. She noticed things. Noticing was the one doctor thing she’d been good at before she knew anything. He cleaned his glasses when he wanted time to think. He’d done it when she knocked. Again when she read the handbook, slowly, every corner. His watch was plain steel with a second hand. For pulses. His phone had buzzed on the desk three times and he hadn’t looked at it once. And he walked beside her. Not in front. His legs were twice as long as hers and he’d shortened his steps without seeming to notice.

She talked. Mr. Yin and the jelly.

“He asked if I was married. I said I’m a student. He said that’s not an answer. Is that an answer? I think it’s an answer.”

“It’s not an answer.”

“Whose side are you on?”

“Mr. Yin’s.”

She laughed, too loud for a corridor, and told him about her brother. In this hospital, once, on the sixth floor, after a van.

“Baba stood in the corridor all morning. Every nurse on the floor was terrified. One of them dropped a tray!”

He didn’t say anything to that. Bored? She looked up. He was listening. Like she was a history he’d have to present on the round. Every word.

They reached the lifts. He pressed the button. The doors opened and his hand went to the small of her back to steer her in. Light. Through her cardigan. One step’s worth. Then he took it away fast, like he’d touched a hot pan, and put it in his pocket.

She turned round in the lift. He was standing in the corridor in his white shirt and dark tie with his hand in his pocket. Same serious face. And his ears had gone pink.

She didn’t think. She reached out of the lift and took hold of his tie. She didn’t pull. She just held it in her fist. Dark blue silk, warm from him. He went completely still.

The doors started to close. She looked down at her own hand on his tie like a stranger had put it there. She let go. The doors shut between them. She rode down nine floors with her hands over her face.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, in the corridor, he was still standing there. He looked at the lift doors. He looked down at his tie. It was creased where she’d held it. He didn’t straighten it.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the taxi she worked it out. She’d gone in there with three things to apologise for. She’d done two, lost the third, talked for a quarter of an hour about a folder called General, and come out with a date she hadn’t been asked on. Except she’d said yes. Hadn’t she? Somewhere between then I say yes or no and after the bananas. She hadn’t decided. It just came out. Like grabbing something that’s falling. She’d held his TIE.

She put her forehead on the cold window and laughed out loud. The driver looked at her in the mirror.

“Good day?”

“I don’t know. I think so?” She wiped her eyes. “Ask me on Friday.”

“What’s Friday?”

“Bananas.”

The driver decided not to ask anything else.

✦ ✦ ✦

The light was still on under Eliana’s door. Elara went past it into her own room and lay down on the bed with her shoes on.

Her phone buzzed on her chest.

Eliana: the noodle place shuts at 1. fyi

She hadn’t told her. She hadn’t told anyone! She stared at the ceiling. The phone buzzed again.

Eliana: you’re welcome

Elara: HOW

Eliana: night

Three came back in the middle of the night, when she was nearly asleep. It had never been an apology at all.

She’d been thinking about him since the sink.

chapters.title: Suturing Practice on a Banana
chapters.desc: She beats every student in the skills lab with a needle and a banana. At dinner she talks for three hours, and on the steps outside he stops her in the middle of a story.
chapters.epigraph: “Finish the story later.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
On Friday nights in September the skills lab smelled of bananas. Xing Yue wasn’t teaching. He’d taught it for three years and handed it to a registrar this autumn. He had no reason at all to be in the old medical building. He’d driven up the hill anyway, parked, walked down the corridor and stopped at the glass panel in the door.

Thirty students at long benches. A banana each, taped to a board, with a cut down the skin. Needle holder, forceps, scissors, a packet of suture. Close the cut so neatly you couldn’t get a fingernail into the line. That was the point. The registrar at the front had a stopwatch. That was not the point. There had always been a stopwatch. They were students.

She was on the second bench by the window. Talking. Obviously. Her head kept turning to the boy beside her, the tall one with the expensive haircut, who looked like he’d pay money for her to stop. Her hands didn’t care. Down the cut. In, out. The needle turning in the holder, a knot, a snip, the next one. No hurry. Not one wasted move. Like watching someone knit while telling you about their holiday.

She put her instruments down and stuck her hand up. The registrar checked the stopwatch. Checked the banana. Ran a fingernail down the line.

“Lin. AGAIN. Unbelievable!”

The room groaned. The boy with the haircut put his head on his arms. Xing Yue stayed at the glass with his hands in his pockets. He didn’t go in.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came out with her bag on her shoulder, her cardigan buttoned wrong, eating the banana. She saw him and stopped dead.

“You’re faster than me,” he said.

She swallowed a mouthful of banana.

“You were watching?”

“From the start.”

“Oh no.” She looked at the banana. She’d eaten down to the stitches. “Everyone says I talk too much to be a surgeon. Dr. Mao said it in second year in front of the whole class. Miss Lin, theatre is a quiet place. I said fine, then I’ll be quiet in it. I wasn’t! I’m still not.”

“You can talk and sew at the same time. Most people can’t do either.”

The door banged behind her. The boy with the haircut, board under his arm. He saw who she was talking to and his whole face rearranged itself.

“Dr. Wang. Sorry. Would you mind looking at my knots? I’m never sure about the tension.”

Xing Yue looked at the banana. He didn’t take it.

“Your third and fifth knots will slip by morning. In a person that’s a bleed. You’re pulling the second throw up before the first is down, because you’re watching her and not your hands. Do fifty tonight. Not here.”

The boy went the colour of the banana.

“Thank you, Dr. Wang.”

He went down the corridor fast.

Elara watched him go. Then she looked up with her eyebrows somewhere near her hair.

“That was Shu Kai. His father’s on the hospital board.”

“Then he’ll want his knots to hold.”

She laughed. One short, startled laugh that went all the way up the corridor. Then she dropped the banana skin in the bin by the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Old Bian’s was up a steep flight of stairs above a tailor’s. Eight tables. A kitchen you could see into. A calendar from a flour company on the wall and the same plastic tablecloths it had had when he first came south. Old Bian came out in his vest. He looked at Xing Yue. He looked at her. He looked at Xing Yue again. He said nothing. From Old Bian, that was a speech.

Elara stood at the top of the stairs and looked down at herself.

“I’m in my cardigan.”

“Yes.”

“There’s banana on it! You said dinner and I thought canteen. Noodles from a cart. So I didn’t change. And you’re in a coat!”

“It’s the coat I wear on the ward.”

“It’s a nice coat.”

“Sit down, Elara.”

She sat.

The menu was in chalk on the wall. She read it the way she’d read Mr. Yin’s obs chart. Everything, top to bottom. Then she went back to some of it. The lamb dumplings. The cold cucumber. The noodles in chilli oil. The braised pork with the eggs. Old Bian came. Xing Yue ordered all four. Then soup, flatbreads, and a pot of tea.

“That’s too much!”

“You looked at them twice.”

She went pink. Then she forgot to be pink, because the food came, and she ate like someone who’d been on a ward since six in the morning. Which she had. Then she started talking.

“Mr. Yin asked for me twice today. He says the jelly tastes of shampoo. He’s not wrong, I tried it.”

“You tried his jelly.”

“For science! And for the bananas, right, bananas are the closest thing to skin you can get for the price. The peel holds a stitch. If you’re rough it tears, same as skin. In first year we used pigs’ feet from the market and the whole lab stank for a week. Shu Kai was sick in a bin.”

He poured her tea.

“Oh! And in second year I split my jeans down the back seam at a bus stop on the way to an exam, so I went into the station toilets with my sewing kit and—” She stopped. “Wait. No. Not that one yet. That’s a long one. Later.”

“Later.”

“You’re not going to forget? People forget. I’ve told that story to the start eleven times.”

“I won’t forget.”

“You say that now.”

So she told him the Walled City instead. In pieces.

“Big family. Tall old house. Too many stairs. My father’s in logistics.” She made a face. She knew exactly what he’d think of logistics. “My big sister has a flower shop. My brother draws buildings. My other sister doesn’t talk. And my little sister has three screens and knows everything about everyone. She knew you eat beef noodles at eleven on call nights.”

He put his cup down.

“She’s right.”

“Of course she’s right! She’s always right. It’s HORRIBLE!”

He listened to all of it. The brother. The bus stop. The pigs’ feet. He wanted every piece, and not to use. Just to have. He’d sat through hours of talk. Consultants. Professors. His father’s board, in the north, saying the same six things in a long room. He’d felt the time go past like water on his hands. He didn’t feel it now. When he checked his watch it was nearly eleven.

She caught him. She stopped with a dumpling halfway to her mouth.

“You’re doing it.”

“Doing what?”

“Listening. Like it’s a history. Like you have to present me on the round tomorrow.” She put the dumpling down. “Nobody listens to me like that. My family love me, but they stopped listening when I was about four. I never stop, so I’m sort of… the radio.”

“I’m not going to stop.”

“Everyone says that. Then about an hour in, their eyes go—” She did a face. Glazed. Dead fish.

“It’s been three hours.”

“…It has?”

“Nearly.”

She looked at him across the plastic tablecloth for a good few seconds. Then she ate the dumpling.

✦ ✦ ✦

Late, she remembered names.

“I’m named after a moon. Did you know? Elara. It’s one of Jupiter’s. A small one. There are about eighty and nobody can name more than four, and I’m one of the ones nobody can name.” She was delighted about it. “My mother chose it. Baba says she liked the sound.”

He drank his tea. He watched her get there. She’d seen his name on the rota a hundred times. Wang Xing Yue. She looked at the ceiling. At the flour calendar. Back at him. Her face went red from the neck up. Slowly. All the way.

“Star.”

He said nothing.

“And moon. Your name is star and moon.”

“Yes.”

“Oh no.” Both hands over her face. “Oh NO. Don’t tell anyone. If my brother finds out he’ll put it on a cake.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He paid while she was in the toilet. Old Bian counted out the change. He looked at the door she’d gone through. Then at Xing Yue.

“She talks.”

“Yes.”

“Good. You don’t. Five years you’ve been coming up my stairs and I’ve had nine words out of you.”

“That’s not true.”

“Thirteen.”

Old Bian nodded, like that settled something, and went back to his kitchen.

✦ ✦ ✦

The stairs down were steep and narrow. A bulb at the top, a bulb at the bottom, nothing in between. She went first. On the last step but one she stopped under the bottom light and turned round. Story time.

“So I’m in the station toilets. In my underwear. Jeans across my knees. The sewing kit’s one of those tiny hotel ones, three colours of thread and none of them blue—”

He was on the pavement. One step down. On the step she was nearly as tall as him. Her face was level with his. He took his glasses off. Folded them. Put them in the pocket of her cardigan. She glanced down at the pocket. Kept going.

“—and I’ve got eleven minutes till the exam, which is ANATOMY, and I’ve been up all night for it, so my hands are shaking, and I’m doing a running stitch down the whole back seam—”

He put two fingers on the side of her throat. Under the angle of the jaw. Where the pulse was. She stopped. He felt it. Quick, light, hard. A bird’s, if you held one. He took his time with it. Like he was going to write it down.

“Fast,” he said, and kissed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started careful. His fingers were still on her throat. Checking she was all right. Was she all right? No. Absolutely not.

It didn’t stay careful. She made a sound against his mouth and grabbed his shirt in both fists. Right at the front, a great handful each side. And pulled. Hard. Up the step, into her. He had to put his other hand on the wall by her head. He forgot her pulse. The step. The street. Old Bian, who was absolutely listening at the top of the stairs.

She kissed him back like she’d been waiting for him to stop wasting time. She tasted of tea and chilli. When he pulled her closer she went up on her toes and her clip gave up. It fell. He caught it without looking.

When they stopped she didn’t let go of his shirt. She stood on the step with her forehead nearly on his and her breath going fast. Hair everywhere, all of it down now. She was laughing with no sound. Little breaths.

“Finish the story later,” she said.

She didn’t finish it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He had to get the spare glasses out of the glovebox before he could drive. She watched him do it. Her hand went to her cardigan pocket and stayed there. She wouldn’t let him drive into the Walled City. She made him stop at the mouth of the alley, by the noodle stall, under the one streetlight.

“I’ll walk you to the door.”

“No.”

“Elara.”

“Not yet. If Baba sees a car he doesn’t know at the door after midnight, he’ll have the plate run before you’re home. He runs checks on the postman. I’m not joking! Same postman for nine years and Baba still has him looked at every New Year.”

He didn’t like it. He kept that to himself.

“All right.”

She got out. She walked three steps up the alley. Then she came back. Running. She bent to his open window with one hand on the roof of the car and her hair blowing across her face.

“I’ve got your glasses. In my pocket.”

“I’ve got another pair.”

“I know. I saw. But those are yours.”

“Keep them till Monday.”

She looked at him through the window. Then she leaned in and kissed him again, fast, on the corner of his mouth.

She hadn’t come back for the glasses at all. He knew it. She knew he knew it. She straightened up and ran. Up the alley, round the corner, past a red door he couldn’t quite see. Gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana was sitting on the stairs inside the red door in a hoodie, eating cereal out of the box.

“You’re missing a clip.”

“It fell.”

“Your hair’s down.”

“It’s WINDY.”

“Your cardigan’s buttoned wrong.”

“It was like that before!”

Eliana ate another handful of cereal. She didn’t look up from her phone.

“His car’s still at the end of the alley.”

Elara stopped on the third stair.

“How do you know that?”

“He’s waiting for your light.”

Her light. Four flights up, at the top of the house, with the window onto the alley. Elara took the stairs two at a time. All four flights. She burst into her room, slapped the switch, and pressed her face to the glass.

Down at the mouth of the alley, under the one streetlight, a pair of headlights came on. They sat there a second. Then they pulled away. She stood at the window with her hand on her cardigan pocket. Was that normal? Did people do that? Nobody had ever waited for her light. Downstairs, Eliana’s voice came up the stairwell.

“Gross.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d waited for the window. The top floor, the one that lit last. Four flights. Of course she lived at the top. At the first red light on the hill road he found his hand still closed round something. Her hair clip.

He opened the glovebox and put it in, next to the empty glasses case. He looked at it there for longer than a grown man should look at a plastic clip. Was this a symptom? Of what?

He didn’t give it back on Monday.

chapters.title: She Narrates Everything
chapters.desc: A month of noodles at eleven and slow walks to the taxi rank. Then she turns up at his flat with breakfast after his night on call, and doesn’t go home.
chapters.epigraph: “I thought it was sleep deprivation. I gave it fifteen months.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
“You’ve had that drain on your list since eight.”

The registrar on the phone was explaining. High and fast. Something about a blockage.

“It’s eleven. Don’t ring me to tell me it’s blocked. Ring me when you’ve been to look at it.”

He put the phone face down on the table. He turned back to her.

“More chilli?”

Elara stared at him over her noodles.

“That was HORRIBLE.”

“He’ll go and look at it.” He pushed the chilli oil across. “You were telling me about the man with the fish hook.”

She was. She went back to it. What else could she do?

The noodle place across from the ambulance bay had four tables, a fridge full of beer nobody was allowed to drink, and a television on a bracket that only showed horse racing. On call nights he came down at eleven in his scrubs with his pager on his waistband. From the second week of September, she was there first. She’d moved to Dr. Fei’s team on the seventh floor by then. Colorectal. They never saw each other on the wards, and that was the point. So she saw him here instead. And on the walk from here to the taxi rank at the main doors. That walk took four minutes if you were normal. Twenty if you were her.

Tonight, outside, she took his hand. She’d never done that before. He looked down at it. He didn’t say a word. He held on the whole way, all twenty minutes, and when the taxi came he was the one who let go last.

✦ ✦ ✦

He kissed her in doorways. At the taxi rank, against the pillar by the main doors, while the security guard studied the sky. In the porch of the old granite block, under the verandah, where nobody went at night. Once in the rain at the bottom of the hill, when a taxi drove straight past them.

“Oh, you absolute—”

“Elara.”

“He SAW us! He had his light on!”

He laughed and pulled her in under his coat. They got soaked anyway.

But never more than that on a call night. He’d told her on the first one.

“I don’t start anything I might have to walk away from in the middle.”

“That sounds very grand. Like a ship’s captain.”

“It isn’t grand. It’s true.”

Then his pager went. He walked away in the middle. She found it maddening. She also found it sweet, which was worse. At one in the morning she told Eliana so.

Eliana didn’t look round.

“Ew.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first Friday in October he was on call all night. She knew his rota better than her own. Off at seven on Saturday morning. He’d walk home down the hill, because he walked to work and only drove at night. She knew where home was, too. He’d given her the address in the second week, plainly, in case she ever needed it. She’d pretended not to write it down. She’d written it down.

At dawn on Saturday she bought breakfast from the bakery by the hospital, the one that opened first. Two pork buns. Two egg tarts. A soy milk. A hot tea.

The woman at the counter winked.

“Second bun for the boyfriend?”

“Yes.”

Then she stood in the queue going hot. Boyfriend? Since when? Since right now, apparently.

14 Banyan Terrace was a white building from the fifties, four floors, curved balconies, a frangipani tree by the gate. His name was on the top buzzer. She stood there with the bag and her heart going.

This was a terrible idea. Nobody had asked her. He’d been up all night. He was going to open the door and look at her like a blocked drain. She pressed the buzzer.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, he was standing in the kitchen with his keys still in his hand. He’d come in four minutes ago. He hadn’t managed to take his shoes off. The buzzer went. He looked at the screen. Her. Small and grainy, holding a paper bag up to the camera like a hostage note.

He stood there a second longer than he needed to. Just looking. Then he let her in.

✦ ✦ ✦

He opened the flat door in his scrubs and socks with his glasses pushed up on his forehead. Grey all the way through. The colour of the hospital walls. He looked at her. He looked at the bag.

“You shouldn’t have come. I’m no use to anyone. I’ve been in theatre since three.”

“I know! That’s why I came. I brought pork buns.” She held up the bag. “You can tell me to go away. I’ll go away. But I’m leaving the buns.”

He stood in the doorway. Then he stepped back. She went in and looked. The whole top of the building. Two floors, and a staircase up to a roof she could see light coming down from. One wall of books, floor to ceiling, medical and not, in no order at all. Round flat cakes of tea stacked on a shelf by the kitchen. A long grey sofa. A low table. A good lamp. That was it. No photos. No plants. Her footsteps echoed.

“You live like a monk.”

“I live at work.”

She put the bag on the counter and turned round. He was holding onto the back of the sofa.

“Shower. Go on. You smell of theatre. I’ll make the tea. Then you’re eating, and I don’t want to hear you’re not hungry, because you’re a surgeon who’s been up all night. You’re always hungry. You just don’t notice.”

He looked at her like she’d spoken Portuguese. Then he went upstairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came down in a grey T-shirt and soft trousers with his hair wet. She sat him on the sofa and put a pork bun in his hand. He ate it. She watched him. It was weirdly satisfying.

“The bakery lady asked if the second bun was for my boyfriend.”

He stopped chewing.

“I said yes. Before I thought. So. That’s happened.”

He started chewing again. Slower.

She told him the jeans story at last. All of it. The station toilets, the hotel sewing kit, the pink thread, the exam.

“Pink?”

“There was no blue! I walked into anatomy with a pink seam down my bum and I PASSED.”

He’d finished both buns and an egg tart. He was leaning back against the arm of the sofa with his tea and his eyes half shut. He hadn’t looked away from her once.

“I saw you before,” he said. “Before the ward round.”

She stopped.

“Last June. The sixth floor. Your brother had been hit by a van. I was called down to look at his ribs. Your family came up the corridor, and you stopped me by the lift and asked if anyone had checked his spleen.”

Elara stared at him. She tried. She really tried. The phone at dawn. Baba’s face. The car. The corridor on six. Raiden in the bed with one eye swollen shut, telling everyone he was fine in his stupid voice. The spleen, yes. She’d asked everyone about the spleen. Him? Nothing. Not his face. Not his glasses. Not even tall.

“Oh no. Oh no, no. I don’t remember you! I’m so sorry. That’s AWFUL. You were there, and you were tall, and you were a doctor, and you told me about my brother, and I don’t remember one single thing about you.”

“I’d have worried if you did. You’d been up all night with your brother in a bed.”

“But you remembered me.”

“Yes.”

He drank his tea.

“I thought it was sleep deprivation. I gave it fifteen months.”

She sat there with her hands round her cup and her face on fire. She opened her mouth. Nothing came out. Nothing came out of Elara Lin. When did that ever happen? He started to smile. Which was even rarer.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him about the Lins then. Because she was embarrassed, and when she was embarrassed she talked. He’d only had the funny parts so far.

“Baba’s in logistics the way the tide’s in water. Anyone in the Walled City over fifty still goes a bit quiet when he walks down the street. Even now he’s old and grey and scared of his daughters.”

“Scared of you?”

“Scared of Elowen. Everyone’s scared of Elowen.” She turned her cup round. “I’m the fourth of five. And I’m not really any of their blood.”

He waited.

“I’m adopted. Baba brought me home from a children’s home when I was three. That’s all I know. I asked once, when I was about seven. He said I came from a children’s home and he’d wanted me, and that was all there was. And he looked so sad I never asked again.”

His jaw went tight. He was angry. For her. At something he couldn’t see or cut out. She could tell he hated that more than anything in the world.

“My mother died a few months after I came. Having my little sister.” She kept her eyes on the cup. “The house went quiet after. Not for long. A month, maybe. But I remember it. All the doors shut. Nobody talking at dinner. Baba sitting in the kitchen at night. I was three and I didn’t like it.”

She shrugged.

“So I talked. Somebody had to. I think I just… never stopped.”

She looked up. Too much? Was that too much for eight in the morning?

“Keep talking,” he said.

She laughed, a bit wet, and kept talking. Ah Sim, who’d been with the family since before any of them were born and called her little sparrow. The noodle stall at the end of the alley. Her room at the top of the house, with posters she was far too old for and refused to take down.

“There’s this band on the second one. They were huge when I was twelve. The lead singer had this hair that went—”

He put his tea down. He leaned across. He took her chin in his fingers and tipped her face up to the window. Like turning a patient to the light to check their pupils. She kept going. Of course she kept going.

“—it went up at the front, sort of like a wave, and their name was—”

He looked at her face in the morning light. Her eyes. Checking something. Finding it fine. Then he kissed her in the middle of the band’s name.

She laughed into his mouth. He’d done it again! On purpose! He didn’t stop. After a while she stopped laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’ve got a rule.”

She said it a while later, with her hands in his wet hair. He was lying back along the sofa. She was more or less on top of him. The tea had gone cold. The sun had moved round onto the books.

“About call nights.”

“That was last night. Now I’m off.”

“That’s cheating!”

“It’s the rule.”

His glasses were on the table. His eyes were dark. Wrecked and wide awake at the same time. He didn’t ask her anything. He put his hand flat on her back, under her cardigan, warm through her shirt.

“Don’t go home.”

She was already taking the cardigan off.

✦ ✦ ✦

His bedroom was under the slope of the roof. A window onto the hill, the hospital tower, the harbour. Blinds that cut the morning into stripes. She talked. She’d known she would.

“You’re doing my buttons like you’re taking out stitches.”

He didn’t answer. He kept going. One at a time. Slow.

“You are, though. Like you don’t want to mark the skin. I can tell. I’ve watched you.”

His mouth went to her throat. The exact place his fingers had been on the steps. He stayed there.

“My pulse is probably a hundred and forty. You should write it down.”

“Elara.”

“What?”

“Be quiet.”

“Make me.”

So he did. For a bit. His glasses were long gone. His hands were warm on her ribs, her waist. Careful. Exact. Learning her like a map he’d be tested on. She pulled the T-shirt over his head and stopped with it in her hands.

“Oh. You’re… huh.”

“What.”

“Stronger than I thought. You’ve been hiding that under a white coat this whole time? That’s fraud.”

He laughed against her shoulder. Low and startled, like it had been surprised out of him.

He was careful. So careful she started to laugh again.

“I’m not going to break.”

“I know.”

“I’ve watched you close an abdomen. I know you can go faster than this.”

He stopped, above her. His breath went once, hard, against her neck.

“You’re sure.”

“Xing Yue.”

Then he wasn’t careful any more. Somewhere after that she stopped narrating.

She didn’t notice when. Only after. The stripes of light sliding up the ceiling. His breath at her ear, ragged. Her hands on his back, holding on. Her own voice, saying his name. All of it, every syllable, like it was the only word she had left and she was going to make it last. And his voice saying hers. All of it. Every time. Not once did he shorten it. So this was what all the talking was for. So you’d know what it meant when you stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

After, he tucked her in. She was lying in the middle of his bed in the striped light with her hair everywhere. He got up. Bathroom? No. He pulled the sheet and blanket up over her shoulders and tucked them in, down both sides, firm. Like the nurses on the ward. She was a spring roll.

“What are you DOING?”

“You’ve been up since dawn.”

He fished her phone off the floor, where it had fallen out of her cardigan. He held it to her face to unlock it, and set an alarm.

“Three o’clock. You’ll want to eat.”

“You’re the one who’s been up all night!”

“Yes.”

He lay down beside her, on top of the blanket, and went out like a light. Before he went he found her hand under the covers. He turned her wrist over. His thumb settled on the inside of it, on the pulse. She felt his hand go heavy as he fell asleep. It didn’t move.

She lay awake in the striped light looking at his face. Younger, asleep. Less sure of itself. She thought about telling him. No. She’d keep that one.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke at three to her alarm and an empty bed. A glass of water on the table. And on the pillow, a note on a sheet torn from a prescription pad.

She picked it up. It looked like a heart monitor having a bad day. Pharmacists at City Hospital rang him to ask what he’d written. Nurses held his drug charts up to the window. She read it anyway. It didn’t take long.

Gone to buy food. Back by half three. You don’t snore. You talk in your sleep. Don’t go home.

What had she SAID?

She lay back in his bed with the note on her chest and laughed until she had to put the pillow over her face.

✦ ✦ ✦

The door went downstairs. Bags. Footsteps on the stairs.

He came in with two carrier bags and stopped in the bedroom doorway.

“What did I say?”

“When?”

“In my SLEEP!”

He put the bags down.

“Something about Mr. Yin’s jelly.”

“I did not.”

“And my name.”

“…How many times?”

“I wasn’t counting.”

She threw the pillow at him. He caught it, put it back under her head, and went to cut up a mango.

chapters.title: The Lins Are Not Told
chapters.desc: For her twenty-third birthday he gives her surgical loupes made for her eyes. She goes to the family dinner without him, and climbs into his car at midnight still in her dress.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re the one part of my life nobody’s ever bled on.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
“It’s my birthday. And you’ve bought me a pencil case.”

“Open it.”

He’d given it to her at breakfast. He couldn’t wait till the evening, and the evening wasn’t his. She was at his kitchen counter in his T-shirt and her own socks, eating rice porridge straight out of the pan. She stayed most nights now that weren’t call nights. Some that were, too. She’d sleep in his bed while he was at the hospital and leave it looking like a crime scene.

A hard black case. Pencil-case size. A clasp. She put the spoon in the pan and opened it.

Grey foam, cut to fit. Inside, a pair of surgical loupes. Glasses with little magnifying barrels set into the lenses, angled down, for fine work. The frames were dark red.

She’d said once, at Old Bian’s, that every pair she’d ever borrowed in the skills lab was black and made her look like a beetle. She didn’t touch them.

“These are through-the-lens. These are made for someone. For a person’s eyes. You can’t just buy these, you have to be measured, you have to—”

She stopped. He watched her get there.

“The eye test.”

“Yes.”

“September! The staff eye test! The email from occupational health!”

“Yes.”

“I went to the optician on four in the old block, and a woman measured how far apart my eyes were. She made me hold a needle holder over a bit of foam. At working height!”

“Yes.”

“I thought it was the university being weird. They once made us do a hearing test in a CUPBOARD—”

“I booked it.”

“You…”

“I booked it.”

She took them out of the foam. Turned them over. Inside the left arm, tiny, in plain capitals: E.L. She put them on.

He’d known they’d fit. He’d still been worried. They sat right on her small nose, the barrels exactly at the angle of her eyes. She looked down through them at the porridge pan. At her own hands. Then, without meaning to, at his. On the counter. She started to cry.

“They cost more than my year. My whole year. Fees and books and food.”

“They’re for twenty years of work. That isn’t expensive.”

“That’s not how money WORKS.”

“It’s how mine works.”

She took them off and held them in both hands and cried on them a bit. She wiped them on his T-shirt. She laid them back in the foam like they were made of sugar, and shut the case. Then she wrapped her arms round his neck from the stool and held on.

“You got me measured without telling me.” Muffled, into his collar. “You lied to me with an EMAIL.”

“Yes.”

“That’s not normal.”

“No.”

He didn’t say sorry. She wouldn’t have wanted it. She held on tighter.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the door, putting her shoes on, she asked him not to come to dinner. He’d known since the box that she would.

“Not yet. It’s not you! It’s them. It’s Baba. You know what he’s like about the postman.”

“I know about the postman.”

“If I bring a man to dinner, he’ll have you looked into before the soup. City Hospital, chief resident, from the north. Then everything else. Your school. Your grandmother. What you had for breakfast in nineteen ninety-eight. Then he’ll sit at the end of the table and say nothing at you for three hours.”

“I can sit through three hours.”

“I can’t! I want to do it properly. When it’s a good time.”

“When’s a good time?”

“I don’t know yet.” She did her laces. “Soon.”

He nodded. He kept the rest to himself.

She went up on her toes and kissed him on the chin. As high as she could reach without the step. Then she went off down the stairs with her bag on her shoulder and the black case hugged to her chest like a hymn book.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Stop. Take your hands out.”

The registrar took his hands out.

Perforated ulcer. All afternoon. A registrar who’d been told twice already where the duodenum was.

“What’s that?”

“The—”

“Don’t guess. You’ve guessed twice. Look at it. When you know, tell me. Until you know, keep your hands where they are.”

Suyin looked at the ceiling. The registrar stared at the duodenum for a full half minute, sweating into his mask. Then he named it. Correctly.

“Good. Now you can put your hands back.”

They finished without another word.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fei caught him at the lifts.

“It’s your student’s birthday. Ex-student. Lin Elara.” She was watching his face hard. “The whole of the seventh floor sang to her at handover. The nurses made a card. Mr. Yin sent mooncakes in with his daughter. A month late. With a note.”

“What did it say?”

“For the little doctor who talks.” Fei tilted her head. “Thought you’d want to know.”

“Thank you.”

The lift came. Fei got in. She kept looking at him until the doors shut.

✦ ✦ ✦

The dinner was in the Walled City. A house he’d never seen, behind a red door he’d seen the edge of once in the dark. He sat at his desk all evening with a paper on bile leaks. He read the first page four times. Then he gave up and got the car keys.

The dark blue saloon. He only drove it at night. He drove across the city with the windows down and parked at the mouth of the alley, by the noodle stall with its shutters down, under the one streetlight. Engine off. Waiting. Was this what men did now? Sat in cars in alleys? Apparently this one did. Just after midnight the passenger door opened and she got in.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was in a dress. He’d never seen her in a dress. Dark green, plain, knee length, short sleeves. A coat over it. Her hair was up. Properly up, with pins, for once, and some of it was already escaping. On her lap: a bakery box, a bag of oranges, and a paper crown from a cracker. She saw him looking and pulled the crown off her head.

“Raiden. He makes everyone wear them. Drive. No! Don’t drive. Wait. Let me tell you first or I’ll forget.”

She told him the dinner. In no order whatsoever.

“Ah Sim made the long noodles and stood over me till I’d eaten the whole bowl without biting through one. For long life. If you bite through, it’s bad luck. I nearly CHOKED.”

“Did you bite through?”

“No! Because I nearly choked instead.”

“Good.”

“Raiden did a toast. Six minutes. Mostly about a crane he’s drawing. Elowen brought a chestnut cake from the good bakery on Harbour Road. Her husband stood behind her the whole time with his hands in his pockets like a wall.”

“Like a wall?”

“A nice wall. A scary wall. Then Eliana gave me a USB stick and said don’t plug it into anything at the hospital. She won’t say what’s on it.”

“Don’t plug it into anything at the hospital.”

“I KNOW.”

Then she stopped.

“And Ev wasn’t there.”

He waited.

“My sister. The one who doesn’t talk. Something happened to her in October.”

She pressed her lips together.

“She won’t say what. Nobody will tell me. She’s staying in the room over Elowen’s shop and she won’t come to the house. So I took her cake on the way. I sat with her half an hour.”

“Did she talk?”

“Ev? No. So I talked for both of us. Mr. Yin. The jelly. The loupes.”

She turned the box a quarter turn on her knees.

“I told her about you.”

He didn’t move.

“Not your name. Just that there was a you. And she looked at me.” Her voice went odd. “She doesn’t look at people much. She looked at me and I think she was pleased. I think. You can’t always tell with Ev.”

He didn’t ask what had happened to her sister. He could see she didn’t know.

“And Baba asked if I was happy. At the end, when everyone was finding their coats. He doesn’t ask things. He’s learning. Elowen’s making him.”

She smoothed the dress over her knees.

“He came and stood next to me by the fire and asked if I was happy at the hospital. I said yes. He gave me his small-print look and said, good.” She swallowed. “I didn’t say why.”

Then she went quiet.

Quiet. Her. He turned in his seat to look.

“I’d like to be the why,” he said. “Out loud. In front of them.”

“I know.”

She was looking out through the windscreen. The alley. The lamp on the wall. The red door round the corner she wouldn’t let him see.

“Soon. I promise. I just…” The box turned again. “Everything in that house is everybody’s. Everybody knows everything. Everybody’s had their hands in everything. Things come home in the middle of the night that you can’t talk about. You help. You don’t ask. You wash it off in the sink.”

She looked at him then.

“You’re the one part of my life nobody’s ever bled on. I want to keep it like that for a bit.”

He heard it twice. The first time, it was the best thing she could think of to say about him. She meant it. He believed her. The second time, under it, he heard a door being eased shut. With him on the far side. She couldn’t hear that at all. Fine. He let it go. For tonight.

She’d started again already. Baba at her school play when she was nine, in the front row in his coat, and the whole hall going silent, and the boy playing the king forgetting every line—

He reached over and took her hand off the bakery box. He turned it palm up in the light from the streetlamp. Small wrist. Blue lines under the skin. He found the pulse with his thumb. It jumped when she felt him do it. The king story stopped.

He bent his head and kissed the inside of her wrist, right on the pulse. Then he kissed her mouth. Hard. Halfway through a word about the king.

She made a noise and grabbed his collar with her free hand. The bakery box slid off her knees. The oranges went everywhere. She came across the car at him as far as her seatbelt allowed, which wasn’t far.

“Stupid—belt—”

He felt her laugh into his mouth. Then not laugh. Her hand moved from his collar to the back of his neck and pulled him down.

Her elbow hit the horn. It went off down the alley like a ship. They broke apart. A shutter flew up somewhere above the noodle stall.

“DO YOU KNOW WHAT TIME IT IS?”

She clapped both hands over her mouth. She was shaking with laughter, hair coming down, crown on the floor. Somewhere up the alley a dog started.

“Drive.” Through her fingers. “Drive, drive, drive, before Baba comes out in his dressing gown!”

He drove.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t let go of him all the way home. Her hand was on his knee. Then higher. She talked fast about nothing. The oranges rolling round the footwell. The woman over the noodle stall who’d been shouting at Raiden for twenty years. He took every bend on the hill road slower than he wanted to.

“You’re driving like a grandad.”

“Yes.”

“On purpose?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He didn’t answer. Her hand went higher. He took the next bend even slower.

The green dress came off in the hall in the end. He’d meant to get her upstairs. She had other plans. The zip was at the back, and she turned round on the stairs and stood with her back to him, one step up. Hair falling out of its pins.

“Please. It’s been driving me mad all night.”

He took the zip down slowly. One tooth at a time. He kissed every bit of her back as it came out.

“Xing Yue. That’s not—you’re meant to—”

“I’m doing it.”

“You’re doing it SLOWLY—”

“Yes.”

After that she gave up on the dress as a topic. He took her up the rest of the stairs.

He was slow with her. The first time he’d been slow because he didn’t want to get anything wrong. Now he was slow because he knew how. Because it was her birthday. And because she’d shut a door on him in the car, and he wanted, without saying a word about it, to be let back in by another one.

He took her hair down. Every pin. He lined the pins up on the bedside table. In a row. Neatly.

“Are you counting my hairpins?”

“No.”

“You are. You’ve put them in a line. Oh my god.”

He kissed the inside of her wrist again. Then the other wrist. The inside of her elbow. The hollow of her throat. He went on and on. Her talking slowed. It broke. It came back in a lower voice with no stories in it.

“Don’t stop. Don’t you dare—”

“I won’t.”

Then it wasn’t talking. Only his name, into the dark, again and again. Like she was calling him back from somewhere.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay on her front across the bed with her chin on her hands, in the light from the landing. He lay on his back and watched her think. Then she got up without a word. She went downstairs, naked. She came back with the black case. She got back into bed. She opened the case. She put on the loupes.

She turned and looked at him through them, close up. Two little barrels pointed straight at his face. Enormous eyes. A beetle in red glasses.

“Dr. Wang.” Her best ward-round voice. “I’m going to need to examine you more closely.”

He laughed.

Not the short sound she sometimes got out of him, half swallowed, into her shoulder. He lay on his back in his own bed and laughed out loud with his hand over his eyes. Helpless. Until his ribs hurt.

She sat beside him in her loupes and nothing else and stared down at him through the barrels.

“I’ve never heard you do that!”

He couldn’t answer.

She took the loupes off and put them away. Slowly. She put the case on the table, next to the row of hairpins. Then she lay down on top of him and put her ear flat on his chest.

“Do it again. I want to hear it from the inside.”

chapters.title: Three in the Morning, on Speaker
chapters.desc: Her silent sister rings from a strange phone about a man with an infected knife wound who can’t go to a hospital. For three weeks Elara calls back at three every morning, and Xing Yue writes it all down and never asks who.
chapters.epigraph: “Go back to sleep. I’ve written it down.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
In February she was on her student internship at Harbourside General, across the harbour. A junior doctor in everything except the pay.

She clerked. She took blood. She put in drips and wrote up drug charts for a registrar to sign. She did nights, with her list in biro on the back of her hand. The patients adored her because she talked to them. She knew every grandchild on the surgical floor by name. She knew which old man wanted the window open and which one had been a dancer and would show you his arms if you asked.

She ate standing up at the nurses’ station. She gave her egg tarts to whoever looked like they needed one more. And she slept wherever she was when she stopped. Mostly his bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The third Thursday in February. Five in the afternoon. Asleep. She’d come off a night that morning. He’d come off call at noon and got in beside her without waking her. Grey light through the blinds. Both of them out cold. Her phone went on the floor.

She found it by feel. Unknown number. Fourth ring. Eyes shut.

“Ev?”

She knew. Before anyone spoke. How did she know?

“Ev, it’s—what is it? Where are you? Whose phone is this?”

“I need you to tell me what to do.”

Elara sat up. Something in her changed. It happened on the wards, at night, when a nurse called her name in a certain voice. It happened now, in his bed, with the sheet round her waist. The sleep went. The warmth went. What was left was clear. Cold. Very still.

“Tell me what you see.”

The mattress moved beside her. The lamp came on. He was sitting up against the headboard, looking at her face. When had he woken? She hadn’t even felt it. She put the phone on speaker and laid it on the duvet between them. Hands free.

Ev’s voice came out of it. Low. Flat. Saying more words in a row than Elara had heard from her in a year. A fever. Shaking, all over, so the bed rattled. A wound on the left side, low, under the ribs. A knife. He’d stitched it himself. Red all round, hot, swollen in a ridge. Something yellow at the bottom end. A smell. A red line running out from the cut towards the hip.

“He’s talking. But not to me. He doesn’t know me.”

A pen landed in Elara’s hand. Where had that come from? Then the back cover of a journal, torn off, blank side up. She was writing on her knee before she’d thought about it.

“How long since the injury?”

“Six days. I think.”

“Is he breathing fast? Is his heart going fast?”

A pause.

“Yes.”

“Is he confused? Does he know where he is?”

“No. He’s talking to someone who isn’t there.”

Elara breathed out.

“Ev. He needs a hospital. That’s an infected wound and it’s spreading.”

“I know it’s—”

“That red line is the infection going up the lymph channels. He’s got a fever, his heart’s racing, he’s confused. That’s how sepsis starts. People die of this, Ev. Young, strong people.”

“He can’t.”

“Ev—”

“He can’t. If he goes to a hospital, they’ll ask. Then they’ll find out.”

The line went quiet. A radio somewhere at Ev’s end. Something that might have been a cat.

“Who is he?”

Nothing. Elara looked up. Xing Yue wasn’t looking at the phone. He was looking at her. His face was completely calm. He didn’t say a word. He picked his own phone up off the table and started searching, fast, with his thumb.

“Okay.” Her voice went level. “Okay. Listen to me. I’m going to tell you exactly what to do, and you’re going to do all of it, and if any of the things I tell you to watch for happen, you put him in a car and take him to a hospital whether he can or not, and you call me from the car. Do you promise?”

“Yes.”

“Do you have something to write on?”

Paper moving.

“Go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Stitches out. Every one.”

“All of them?”

“All of them. It’s full of infection with nowhere to go. It has to drain. Then you wash it out. Boiled water, cooled, with salt. Lots. More than you think. Until what comes out is clean.”

“Then stitch it?”

“NO. Leave it open. Pack it loosely. Change it twice a day.”

Then the antibiotics. She named two. The two she’d have wanted for him if he’d been on her ward. Xing Yue turned his phone round and held it up so she could see. He’d found the same two. Under them, the things to watch for. She nodded at him without stopping.

He took the journal cover off her knee. Under her notes he wrote the names of both drugs. Square careful block capitals. Each letter separate, like a child’s, so anyone on earth could read them. Elara could read his scrawl. Nobody else alive could. He did it anyway. For Ev.

“Mark where the red line is now. With a pen. Then you’ll know.”

“Yes.”

“If he gets more confused. If he can’t stay awake. If his skin goes blotchy. If he stops passing water. If the line keeps climbing.”

“Yes.”

“Any one of those, and you go. Promise me again.”

“I promise.”

Elara looked down at the phone on the duvet. She had to ask. She didn’t want to. She had to.

“Ev.” Her voice wobbled. Once. She hated that. “Ev, do you love him?”

The radio. The cat. Nothing else.

“Call me at three.”

Click.

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat on the edge of the bed with the phone in her lap and shook. Not crying. Just shaking, all over, from the shoulders down. Like after running for a bus. Her teeth were going.

He sat up behind her. He put his hand flat on her back, between her shoulder blades. He left it there. He didn’t say anything. She waited for it.

Twenty minutes in his bed, on speaker, telling her sister how to treat a stab wound on someone who couldn’t see a doctor. He was a surgeon. He’d heard every word. He’d looked it up on his phone. Any second now. Who is he? What is this? Elara, you can’t do this.

“Will she do it right?”

She turned round and stared at him.

“Ev?!” Her laugh came out cracked. “She’ll do it exactly. More exactly than anyone at Harbourside. She’ll write it down in tiny letters and do it to the minute.”

“Then he’s got a chance.”

“I don’t know who he is!”

“No.”

He put the journal cover with the block capitals on the table on her side of the bed. Squared up with the edge. Where she’d see it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He set an alarm. She didn’t know until it went off just before three. Low. On his side. He turned it off. His hand found her shoulder in the dark.

She sat up and rang the number. Ev answered before the second ring. Had she been standing next to it all night?

“Better, I think. Yes. The line hasn’t moved. Yes. I promise.”

Elara lay back down with the phone on her chest.

“It hasn’t moved.”

“Good.” From the other pillow. “Go back to sleep. I’ve written it down.”

Written what down? In the morning she found out. A sheet off the prescription pad, on the kitchen counter, under the teapot. The night’s date. Line hasn’t moved. And under that, in his own hopeless scrawl, the list of things to watch for. A chart. He was keeping a chart on a patient he’d never seen.

✦ ✦ ✦

She called at three every night for three weeks. Mostly from his flat. Twice from a night shift at Harbourside, in the doctors’ room with the door shut, while the nurses wondered who she was talking to in that voice. Once from her old room at the top of the tall house, whispering, with her father asleep two floors down. The line went back. A centimetre. Three. Then there was no line at all. He was awake. He was difficult.

“He’s eating…”

That was Ev’s whole report. Two words. From Ev. About food. That was basically a parade. And every morning there was tea on the counter.

He made it before she woke. The dark Pu’er he drank, in the small brown pot, under a folded cloth to keep it hot. Then he was gone to the hospital, or asleep, or at the table with a journal. He never mentioned it. Not once.

On the morning the line was gone, she came downstairs in his shirt and found him reading at the counter. She climbed onto the rung of the stool beside him to be tall enough. She took his face in both hands and kissed him until he put the journal down.

“What was that for?”

“The tea. Every day. You think I don’t notice!”

His glasses had gone crooked.

“I know you notice.”

He pulled her off the stool.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the second week he asked to have her location. At breakfast. Plainly. While she was hunting for her other shoe.

“For night shifts. You cross the harbour at two in the morning in taxis. You walk from the ferry. If something happens, I want to know where.”

She laughed. She found the shoe under the sofa. She got her phone out and did it right there. She held the screen up so he could watch her name appear on his. A little blue dot. In his kitchen.

“There. Now you’ll know every time I go to the bakery.”

He put his phone in his pocket.

✦ ✦ ✦

He looked at it more than he’d ever have admitted. Before a list. Between cases. In the lift. Four times before lunch on a Tuesday. Was that a lot? It didn’t feel like a lot. It felt like checking a pulse. You didn’t stop checking a pulse because it was fine. He knew when she’d been to the bakery before she said so. He knew when her taxi went the long way round the harbour.

“Roadworks?”

She stopped with her key in the door.

“How did you—oh my god. The dot.”

“The dot.”

“You’re terrible.”

“Were there roadworks?”

“…Yes.”

“Good.”

“It’s NOT good! You’re supposed to pretend you don’t look!”

“Why?”

She opened her mouth. She couldn’t think of a single reason.

✦ ✦ ✦

Once, on a night shift, she went down to the hospital car park at four in the morning for some air. She stood by the ambulance bay for ten minutes in the cold. Her phone buzzed.

Xing Yue: Car park?

Elara: AIR. go to sleep

Xing Yue: I’m on call.

She read it twice by the ambulance bay. Then she put the phone away and went back up to the ward. Smiling. Why was she smiling? Somebody was watching her stand in a car park at four in the morning. She didn’t turn it off.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Thursday in March, at three, Ev asked if he could have a shower.

“Yes. Fine. A quick one. Don’t scrub it, pat it dry, and if he’s an idiot about it I’ll know.”

She hung up and lay back in the dark. He was awake. He was always awake for the calls. His pager had gone earlier and he’d taken it in the kitchen. She’d heard him through the floor. Low. Flat. Terrible.

“If you ring me about a potassium of four point one again, I’ll come in and give it to you intravenously myself.”

Then he’d come back up, got into bed, put his warm hand on her hip, and waited with her for three.

“She’s got a man.”

“Mm.”

“Ev! My sister who says about ten words a month. She’s got a man, and he’s alive, and he wants a SHOWER.”

“Good for her.”

“He was dying in February! On a floor somewhere. And all he had was HER.”
