Faster now. She’d been frightened and she wasn’t any more, and it all wanted to come out.

“And I don’t know who he is. I don’t know his name. I don’t know what he does that means he can’t walk into a hospital with a stab wound—”

“Elara.”

“—and Ev’s never had anyone. She’s never even let anyone sit next to her on the bus! And now she’s in a room with a man who’s been knifed and she rang ME—”

“Back to sleep.”

“I’m in bed.”

“Sleeping, then. It’s three in the morning. You’ve got a ward round at eight.”

He brushed the hair off her face and tucked it behind her ear. She let him. She kept talking anyway.

“When she was little she used to sit under the kitchen table with a book while everyone shouted. She grew orchids on the windowsill and checked the roots without touching them. I always thought she’d end up alone in some tall room full of plants and be perfectly happy. I never once thought she might want—”

He leaned over her in the dark and stopped her mouth with his. She squeaked. Then she stopped being surprised.

She got her arms round his neck and pulled him down on top of her. The duvet slid half off the bed. She felt him laugh against her mouth.

“You said sleep.”

“I changed my mind.”

They didn’t sleep till it was light.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay with her head on his chest and watched the blinds go grey. Three weeks of calls at three in the morning. A man with a knife wound and no name. Her sister in a room somewhere. Two drugs in block capitals. He hadn’t asked once. Not who. Not where. Not why. He’d set alarms. He’d made tea. He’d sat up in the dark every night and kept a chart.

She had a world that rang in the middle of the night. She’d always gone towards it when it did. Always. Without thinking. She’d always thought that was the part of her nobody would put up with. That one day someone would sit her down and say: them or me.

She lifted her head. He was asleep. His thumb was on the inside of her wrist. Would he ever say it? She looked at his face. Then she put her head back down. She’d stopped wondering.

chapters.title: Zhao Zhendong Is Bleeding Out
chapters.desc: Her sister’s husband crawls home with a bullet in his side, and Elara steals what she needs from the hospital. Xing Yue walks into the supply room and catches her, and she begs him not to ask.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t ask me. If you ask, I’ll tell you.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
The emergency department at City Hospital on a Saturday night sounded like a market on fire. She loved it. Six weeks as a student on it, her last rotation before finals, and she loved it more than anything except the bananas. A drunk man in cubicle four was singing. Badly. A girl in cubicle six had put her hand through a window. She was very brave about it in front of her boyfriend and not brave at all once he went for coffee.

“He’s an idiot.”

“He’s not an idiot!”

“He went for coffee. While you’re bleeding.”

“…Okay, he’s a bit of an idiot.”

The girl laughed and forgot to watch the needle. Job done. At three in the morning Elara was eating a biscuit at the nurses’ station. Upstairs, Xing Yue was in theatre with an appendix. He’d texted earlier.

Xing Yue: Appendix. Then possibly another. Eat something.

She’d sent him a photo of the biscuit. Just after three her phone rang again. A number she didn’t know.

“Miss Lin? Miss Elara?”

A young man. High. Shaking.

“It’s Peng. From the gatehouse. At your sister’s. The house on the hill.”

She put the biscuit down.

“It’s Mr. Zhao. He came back. He—he crawled. From the sea road.”

“Is he breathing?”

“Yes! Yes. Miss Lin said to tell you. Gunshot, left side, three days, fever, he’s lost a lot of blood, he’s been in the sea.”

“She said bring everything. She said steal it if you have to.”

“Peng—”

“She said no hospital. She said come.”

“I’m coming.”

She was already walking.

✦ ✦ ✦

The surgical supply room was off the corridor between the ED and the lifts. Keypad on the door. Every student knew the code because the nurses said it out loud. She went in. Shut the door. Stood with her back against it. Then she started.

Two big blue bags from the stack by the door, the ones the porters used for linen. Open on the floor. Bags of fluid off the shelf. Four. Six. Three days and a fever. Eight. Giving sets. Cannulas, two sizes, a handful each. Tape. Saline for washing, the big bottles, as many as she could lift. Gauze, a box. Another box. Gloves. A green drape in its paper. Local anaesthetic. Syringes. Needles. A suture pack. She wouldn’t close it. You didn’t close a wound like that after three days in the sea. She took it anyway. On the shelf by the window, the instrument cases from theatre, sterile, sealed in blue wrap. She grabbed the top one. Into the bag.

Antibiotics. The shelf where they should be was empty. The emergency drug cupboard. Two doors down. In front of the nurses’ station. Fine. She’d smile at Sister Kuai. I’ve been sent. Sister Kuai would believe her, because everybody always believed her. She was already planning the smile. The exact words. Her hands were steady and fast. Her heart was going so hard she could feel it in her teeth. The door opened behind her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She spun round with a bag of fluid in each hand. Him. Theatre scrubs, cap, mask pulled down round his neck, glasses on. He’d come down for a drain, for a man in resus with an abscess. He came in fast, the way he did everything. And stopped.

He looked at the blue bags on the floor. The fluid. The cannulas. The saline. The instrument case in its wrap. Her, in her scrubs, at half three in the morning, holding a bag of fluid in each hand. The two bags touched. Clink. She watched him understand. She was stealing. A lot. Everything you’d need to keep someone alive on a table that wasn’t in a hospital. His mouth opened.

“Don’t.”

It came out of her like a sob.

“Don’t ask me. Please. If you ask, I’ll tell you. I’ll tell you everything, I won’t be able not to, and then it’s yours too. Then you know. Then it’s yours as well as mine and you’ll have to do something about it, because you’re the chief resident, and I can’t—”

Her voice cracked right down the middle.

“Please. Please don’t ask me.”

He didn’t say anything. He stood in the doorway and looked at her. Outside in the corridor somebody laughed. A trolley went past. The drunk man in cubicle four started a new song. How long? Five seconds? A year? Then he came in and shut the door behind him.

He crouched by the bag on the floor. He took out the instrument case. He turned it over and read the label on the wrap, the typed list from sterile services. He put it back on the shelf.

“Take the other one. That one’s missing a needle holder.”

He took the next case down. Read its label. Put it in her bag. She stared at him.

“I won’t ask.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He picked up both bags. She grabbed for one. He didn’t let go.

“I need antibiotics. They’re in the drug cupboard. I have to go past the station.”

“Which?”

She told him. He put the bags down by the door and went out. She stood alone in the supply room with both hands over her mouth. What was he doing? What had she DONE?

He came back with two boxes. He put them in the top of the second bag, under the gauze, without a word. She found out later he’d signed them out to the man with the abscess.

He carried both bags down the corridor, past the ambulance bay, out to the taxi rank at the main doors. In his theatre scrubs. At nearly four in the morning. Like he did it every night. One taxi. He opened the back door. He put the bags in. They clinked. The driver looked round and then looked very hard at the windscreen. He didn’t ask where she was going.

He took his phone charger out of his scrubs pocket, cable and plug, and pushed it into the outside pocket of her bag. Why? She didn’t know why. She’d find out a little after six.

Then he turned round and put his hand on the back of her head, under her hair, and kissed her against the side of the taxi. Hard. Short. Nothing like the slow kisses at the rank in the autumn. The kind you do with your hands when there’s nothing else they can do. The car was cold through her scrubs. She grabbed his arms. He let her go.

“Go. Ring me when you can.”

She got in. The taxi pulled away. When she twisted round to look out of the back window, he was standing on the kerb under the lights of the main doors with his hands at his sides. Then the taxi turned onto the hill road and he was gone. “Where to, miss?”

“The hill road. Past the sea road, all the way up. Please hurry.”

“Hospital’s behind you, miss.”

“I KNOW where the hospital is.”

He looked at her in the mirror. Then he drove like he meant it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went back up to theatre. The second appendix was waiting. He scrubbed. He opened. His hands did what they always did.

“Dr. Wang? Is everything—”

“Suction.”

“You came back from resus without the drain.”

“Yes.”

“Do you want me to go and—”

“I want you to watch the bleeder at your left hand. You’ve missed it twice.”

The registrar watched the bleeder.

Between that case and the next he stood in the theatre corridor with his phone. A blue dot, moving fast along the sea road. Then the hill. Then it stopped, up there, near the top. He stared at it. Whose house? He didn’t know. He wasn’t going to look.

Suyin came out of the changing room with her cap in her hand.

“You’ve been staring at that phone for five minutes.”

“Yes.”

“Is it bad news?”

“I don’t know yet.”

She looked at him. He put the phone away and went to scrub again. He took it out four more times before dawn.

✦ ✦ ✦

The gate was open. The guard at the gatehouse waved the taxi straight through and then ran up the drive after it. Gravel. Front steps. Eight minutes to four.

“Miss Lin! Kitchen! Go, GO!”

That was Peng, gasping, behind her. She went in with a bag over each shoulder. Every light in the kitchen was on. She came through the doorway at a run and stopped. He was on the kitchen table.

Zhao Zhendong. Her sister’s husband. The wall who stood behind Elowen. Grey. Blue at the lips. Naked to the waist, with something filthy knotted round his middle and a towel pressed over his side. Elowen at the head of the table in her nightdress, bare feet cut and bleeding from the gravel, holding his hand. Elara felt her face go white. Then still. Then it turned into somebody else’s.

“Elara.” Elowen’s voice. Calm. Too calm.

“I’m here. I’m here, Jie.”

“Okay. Okay. Okay.”

She dropped the bags on the counter and ripped them open.

“I stole all of this. From the hospital. From the supply room. If anyone ever finds out, I will never be a doctor, and I’ll go to prison, and I don’t care, Jie, I don’t care, move his arm, I need a vein.”

Second try, inside the elbow. The first would’ve been fine if her hands had been warm. Tape. Somewhere to hang the bag? Nowhere. She grabbed a coat hanger off the back of the hall door and hung the fluid from the cupboard above the table. A second line in the other arm. Then the two boxes from the drug cupboard. The ones he’d signed out to a stranger.

“Antibiotics. The strongest I could find. Into the drip. He needs fluids, he needs these, and he needs—”

She stopped. She looked at the towel.

“Show me.”

Elowen lifted the towel. Elara looked at the wound and didn’t say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

Two hours. Afterwards she couldn’t put any of it in order. The light. Long and bright over the table. Elowen chose this for cooking, and now look. The black strips of shirt he’d packed into himself, stiff, coming out one at a time. The noise he made. She didn’t stop. Saline running off the table onto the floor, the guards on their knees with towels. Pink. Red. Pink. Cutting away what was dead, grey and black, in tiny snips, with the case he’d chosen for her.

The needle holder was in it. Right where it should be. She thought of him for one second. Then she put him away. She didn’t talk. Everyone remembered that afterwards. Elara Lin, silent for two hours. She didn’t know she was doing it. Only the small words, under her breath.

“Okay. Okay. There. Okay.”

Elowen talked. Elowen held his face between her hands and talked for two hours straight. The flower market. The soy milk man. A lemon tree. When he screamed she put her forehead on his and kept going.

“The soy milk man’s son passed his exams. Did I tell you? He brought a cake to the shop.”

“Granny Su counted every bunch again on Tuesday. Every single one.”

“Zhendong. Seven lemons. You have to come and see.”

“Look at me. Don’t look at her. Look at me…”

“Elowen.” Zhao’s eyes were open. “Go upstairs.”

“No.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At six the kitchen window went grey. Elara stripped her gloves. Red to the wrist. She dropped them on the floor and stood with her hands braced on the counter and her head down, breathing.

“That’s all I can do. It’s clean. It’s open. The antibiotics are going in. Now it’s his body. If the fever breaks in the next two days, he lives. If it doesn’t—”

She stopped.

“If it doesn’t, we take him to a hospital, Jie, Red Notice or no Red Notice. I won’t let him die on a kitchen table because of a piece of paper.”

“Neither will I.”

Elara lifted her head. The blood on her sister’s hands. Her nightdress. Her bare cut feet. Her face, perfectly calm.

“You held him for two hours. You didn’t look away once. You didn’t even cry.”

“I’ll cry later.”

Chen Si was standing in the kitchen doorway. Soaked to the knees. A ruined camel coat. Elara had no idea when he’d come in.

“Is he—”

“Alive. For now.”

Chen Si looked at his brother on the table. Then he turned and walked out into the hall.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her phone was dead. She found out in the hall. Screen black. She stood by the lemon tree in her bloody scrubs and stared at it. Then she remembered the outside pocket of her bag. His charger. His cable. His plug.

She plugged it into the wall by the stairs, sat down on the bottom step, and put her face in her hands. He’d known. Somehow he’d known her phone would die. How did he always KNOW?

✦ ✦ ✦

They carried Zhao upstairs at seven on a door Raiden had taken off its hinges.

When had Raiden come? She had no idea. He was just there, in a coat over his pyjamas, white as paper, with a screwdriver. He had the door off the cupboard under the stairs in about a minute.

“Where?”

“Big room. End of the corridor.”

“Can he feel this?”

“Not much. Lift on three.”

“Okay.”

He didn’t make a single joke. That frightened her more than anything.

She hung the drips from the curtain rail in the big room at the end of the corridor. She checked the lines. The dressing. His breathing, his pulse, his colour. She wrote them on the back of an envelope off the dressing table, with the time. Like Xing Yue would have.

Elowen sat on the floor by the bed and took his hand.

“Go and sleep, Elara.”

“In a minute.”

“Now.”

“In a MINUTE, Jie.”

Elara went out.

✦ ✦ ✦

She locked herself in the guest bathroom at the other end of the corridor and texted him.

Elara: Alive. For now.

The reply came before she’d even put the phone down. So fast. He’d been holding it. He’d been watching her little blue dot on the hill all night. Between the appendix and the next one. In the corridor. Wherever.

Xing Yue: Good. Eat.

She turned on the tap. Full. So it roared. She slid down onto the floor with her back against the bath and her knees up and his charger in her fist, and cried with her other hand over her mouth, so nobody in the house would hear her over the water.

Good. Eat. Who said that to someone who’d just done this? Him. Only him. She cried harder.

chapters.title: Fifteen Days of Drips
chapters.desc: For two weeks she changes drips and dressings on the hill, and he drives her there in the dark and waits at the bottom of the road. On the last night he asks one question.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not asking who. I only want to know if he’s alive.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
“How did you know the times?”

She was blinking at him from his sofa. Shoes still on. She’d come down the hill for two hours to shower and sleep, and slept for forty minutes, and now her alarm was going and so was his.

He turned her wrist over and showed her. The list was on her own skin, in blue biro. Drips every four hours, round the clock. Dressings, morning and evening. He’d copied the whole thing into his phone while she slept. Then into hers, with a different sound. If one didn’t wake her, the other would wake him.

She looked at her wrist. She looked at him. Then she laughed. The first time since Saturday. Short, tired, cracked. She put her face against his arm.

“You’re a witch.”

“I can read.”

“Nobody can read. I wrote that in the dark with my left hand.”

“You write better with your left hand than I do with my right.”

“That’s not hard,” she mumbled into his sleeve.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove her back. He stopped at the bottom of the hill road, where it left the sea road and started to climb. Two kilometres below the gate. A bus shelter, a streetlight, nothing else. A car came down out of the dark to meet her. One of the cars from the house, with the young guard from the gatehouse at the wheel. She had her hand on the door.

“You could take me to the top.”

“No.”

“It’s only two kilometres—”

“No.”

She looked at him. No explanation came. She let it go. She’d asked him not to ask, and he’d said he wouldn’t. If he drove up to that gate, he’d see. Whatever he said afterwards, he’d have seen. He wasn’t going to see. He’d decided that in the supply room. It was very simple.

She got out. The car took her up into the dark. He turned his engine off and sat there.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday she rang him in clinic. He was between patients. Small room on the third floor, couch, sink, a window onto the car park. He picked up on the first ring because the phone was already in his hand, under the desk. She didn’t say anything at first. A corridor. Breathing. Someone crying with a hand over their mouth so a house full of people wouldn’t hear.

“Elara. Breathe first. Then tell me.”

She breathed. Twice. Exactly how she’d have told a patient to.

“It hasn’t broken. The fever. It’s the second day. It should be coming down by now.” Her voice went thin. “It’s thirty-nine eight.”

No who. No where. No with what. He asked what he’d have asked a registrar at two in the morning.

“Last dose?”

She told him.

“Heart rate?”

“A hundred and twenty. Bit less.”

“Passing water?”

“Yes. Not much.”

“The wound. Redder than this morning?”

“No. Same. Maybe less.”

“Then this is what I’d watch for in the next six hours.”

He told her. Then he told her what would make him stop watching and put the patient in a hospital, whatever anybody said.

“That’s what I said!” Her voice came back up. “That’s EXACTLY what I said to them!”

“Then you were right. Eat something. Ring me at six.”

He put the phone face down on the desk. He sat with his hand flat on it. Then he called in the next patient. A woman with a hernia. He was completely polite to her for fifteen minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

The phone buzzed on his pillow in the small hours of Tuesday.

Elara: It broke

Elara: it broke!! he’s sweating through everything. heart rate down to 96

He’d been awake since one. Lying on his back in the dark, watching the little blue dot of her on the hill. It hadn’t moved since evening. He’d watched it not move. Was that sleep? No. It wasn’t anything.

Xing Yue: Sleep now. I’ll get you at four.

✦ ✦ ✦

After that he drove her every morning. She’d gone back to the ED in the daytime. Finals were in seven weeks. She couldn’t not. So she went up the hill twice a day. Evening, by taxi, after her shift, to change the packing. And just before dawn, with him, to change it again before she was due on the floor.

He picked her up outside the main doors in the dark. He drove across the city with the windows down so she wouldn’t fall asleep. Bus shelter. Streetlight. The car from the house. Up into the dark. Engine off. He waited.

Sometimes he slept in the driver’s seat with the seat back and his glasses on the dashboard. You learned to sleep anywhere as a resident. He woke every time a car came down the hill. It was never hers. He went back to sleep. Then the car from the house brought her down, turned, and went back up. She walked over in the grey light with her bag on one shoulder and a black bin bag in her other hand, knotted at the top. The first morning he got out and held his hand out for it.

“It’s clinical waste. You can’t just—”

“I know what it is.”

He took it off her.

“The hospital has a whole room for it.”

“And if someone finds bloody dressings in your boot?”

“Nobody looks in my boot.”

“Somebody might!”

“Who?”

She opened her mouth. Nobody. Nobody would dare.

He put it in the boot. When he went in for his day, he carried it down to the basement, to the waste room behind the boiler house, and dropped it in the yellow bin. With everyone else’s. Nobody would ever look at it again. He did that every morning for two weeks.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday he went down to the theatre office and asked for the stock book. It was an old ledger. The computer kept losing things, so they still kept a book. On Saturday night’s page, against the appendix he’d done, he wrote: one instrument set opened, contaminated, returned for reprocessing. Then the fluids. The dressings. The gauze. It came out close enough to what had gone out of the supply room in two blue bags. He initialled it.

The theatre manager, who’d known him six years, looked over his shoulder.

“Busy night.”

“Yes.”

“All that for one appendix?”

“It was a difficult appendix.”

“…Must have been.”

He put the book back on the shelf. He’d never written anything untrue in a hospital book. Not once. He looked at his initials a second longer than he needed to. Then he went to his ward round.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday Dr. Geng caught him at the lifts. The ED’s student lead. A good doctor. A kind man. He actually wanted to know.

“Your Miss Lin. She’s missing shifts. Leaving early. She looks like she hasn’t slept since Christmas. Is there something I should know?”

“It’s a family emergency. It’s real. She’ll make up the hours.”

Dr. Geng waited for more. There wasn’t any more.

“All right. Tell her if she needs anything, she can come to me.”

“I’ll tell her.”

He meant it. Geng meant it too. The lift came.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday it was Dr. Nie. Nie was an ED registrar. Two years ahead of him in training and two years behind in everything else. He liked to stand at the nurses’ station and talk loud enough for the patients. Xing Yue was down for a gallbladder referral. Nie leaned on the station beside him with a coffee.

“Your little student friend’s gone walkabout again. Third time this week. Rolled in yesterday at ten. Some of us were here at eight.”

The nurses at the station went quiet.

Xing Yue finished writing in the gallbladder man’s notes. He signed them. He put his pen in his pocket.

“Would you like to talk about your absences instead?”

Nie’s coffee stopped halfway to his mouth.

“The two Fridays in February when you were at a course. The course has no record of you. The afternoon in January you left your list to a first-year and went to the races. I know which race. I can tell you which horse.”

Nobody at the station breathed.

“Which horse?” a nurse whispered, before she could stop herself.

“It came fourth.”

“Or would you like to go and see the man in bay three? He’s been waiting an hour and a half with a broken wrist.”

Nie put his coffee down on the station and went to bay three. Nobody in the ED asked about Miss Lin again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He fed her. She didn’t eat otherwise, so he put food in her hand. Rice balls in seaweed from the shop by the ferry. Soy milk with the straw already in. Pork buns from the bakery by the hospital, which opened at six, which was when he went, and he was back before she was out of the shower. A box on the passenger seat every morning. She ate it on the way across the city without noticing she was eating. Talking with her mouth full. He watched the box empty out of the corner of his eye.

“Is this egg?”

“Yes.”

“I hate egg.”

“You’ve eaten two.”

“…I hate egg less at five in the morning.”

Between the dawn dressing and her shift she slept in his bed. Between her shift and the evening dressing she slept in his bed. He came home at lunch twice that week. He never came home at lunch. Both times she was face down on the duvet in her scrubs with her shoes on. He took the shoes off. He put the blanket over her. She didn’t wake. He put the shoes by his front door. Facing out. Toes to the door, side by side. So when the alarm went in the dark she could step straight into them without bending, without a light. On the third day she noticed. He heard her stop in the hall in the dark.

“…Did you turn my shoes round?”

“Yes.”

“They look like two little dogs waiting for a walk.”

She laughed. Then she stepped into them. She kept them that way afterwards. She never said why.

✦ ✦ ✦

One morning, halfway across the city, she fell asleep mid-sentence. A man in the department with a fish bone stuck in his throat. He’d insisted on keeping the bone.

“—and he wanted it in a little bag, like a—”

Nothing. He looked across. Her head had gone against the window. Her mouth was open a little. She was breathing slowly for the first time in a week. The clock on the dashboard. She was due at the bus shelter in a quarter of an hour. He drove past the turning for the hill road.

He drove on along the sea road to the roundabout at the end, and round it, and back. Past the turning. On to the roundabout at the other end. Round. Back. Slowly. Sea on one side, hill on the other, in the dark. Twice. It came to twenty minutes.

When he stopped at the bus shelter she woke up and saw the clock.

“Oh God. I’m late. I’m LATE—” Then she looked at him. “Did you drive round?”

“Twice.”

“You can’t just—”

“It’s a dressing. It’s not a drip. It’ll keep twenty minutes. You won’t.”

She stared at him. Then she got out with her bag and went up the hill. He didn’t regret it at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the tenth morning she came down grey. He got out and took the bin bag. Then he took her chin and turned her face to the streetlight and pulled her lower eyelid down with his thumb. Gently. Like in clinic, checking for anaemia.

“You’re pale.”

“I’m not anaemic! I’m just tired. I’ve had about nine hours’ sleep in four days. You don’t need to examine me in a bus shelter—”

He kissed her. Thumb still on her cheekbone. Against the side of the car, in the grey light. Slow.

She stopped arguing. She put her arms inside his coat, round his waist, and leaned on him with her whole weight. Her legs had just been told they could stop. He held her up. A car came down the hill road. Its lights went over them and away.

“Fine,” she said into his mouth. “I’m pale.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The fifteenth day was a Sunday. She texted at four.

Elara: Last one tonight I think. Come and get me?

He was at the bus shelter early. She came down when it was nearly dark. The car from the house left her and went back up. She walked over slowly with her bag on her shoulder. No bin bag. He got out and stood by the car and watched her come. She stopped in front of him.

“That’s the last one. He’s on tablets. He can do his own dressings, or my sister can. I showed her. He walked to the bathroom on his own this morning and hated every step.” She was looking at his chest. “I’m not going back up.”

He’d promised. Fifteen days. He’d driven her to the bottom of a hill in the dark every morning for two weeks. He’d carried a stranger’s blood to a bin. He’d written a lie in a book. He’d gone after a registrar in front of a whole station. And not one question. He asked one now.

“I’m not asking who. I only want to know if he’s alive.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She looked up at him. Her eyes filled.

“It was my sister’s husband. Elowen’s. Zhao. He’d been shot. Three days before. He crawled up from the sea.” She swallowed. “You didn’t ask. So I’m telling you. I wanted to.”

He put his hand on the side of her face.

“I’m glad it was you up there.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She got in the car. She didn’t put her seatbelt on. He was reaching for the key when she climbed over the gearstick into his lap. It was not graceful. Her knee hit the steering wheel. Her bag fell in the footwell. Her elbow knocked his glasses sideways.

“Ow—sorry—ow—”

“Elara—”

“Shut up. Shut UP.”

She took his face in both hands and kissed him like she’d been starving for two weeks and he was the first food she’d seen. He shoved the seat back, blind, one-handed, to make room. She followed him down with it. Her hands were in his hair. His mouth, his jaw, his mouth again. Hard. A desperate little sound at the back of her throat. Fifteen days, all coming out at once. He held her. He let her.

Then, slowly, she slowed. The kisses got softer. Further apart. Her forehead came down against his and stayed. Her hands went loose in his hair. Her whole weight settled on him, warm and heavy.

“Sorry,” she said. Slurred. “I’m so tired. I’ve got to tell you about the gauze. Evangeline’s got this way of folding it. In thirds. She says it’s how our mother folded towels. And I love you. And it’s so much neater than mine. I’m going to start doing it on the ward—”

She was asleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat in the driver’s seat at the bottom of the hill road, under the streetlight, in the dark. Her face in his neck. Her breath on his skin. His glasses crooked on his nose. He left them.

She’d never know she’d said it. She wouldn’t remember. Did it count, if she was asleep?

Yes. He decided it counted.

He sat there an hour without moving. He’d keep it, like something a person drops without noticing. He’d give it back when she knew she’d lost it.

chapters.title: Every Wrong Answer
chapters.desc: Finals, flashcards in bed and a dare he cheats on. She graduates with her family in the hall, and on the back stairs afterwards he hands her a form already filled in, and she says yes in the middle of a sentence.
chapters.epigraph: “Get it wrong and I’ll kiss you anyway.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
“Leave her, leave her! It’s beautiful. It’s like a statue.”

Elara opened her eyes. Sunday lunch. The long table in the Walled City. A dumpling in her chopsticks, an inch from her mouth. Her arm was aching. How long had she been holding it there?

“The dumpling’s going cold, sparrow.”

“I’m awake, Ah Sim! I’m awake.”

She’d come straight from a night in the ED, scrubs under her coat, because Sunday lunch was Sunday lunch. You didn’t miss it for less than a death. Even then Ah Sim would want a note. Everyone was looking at her. Nobody was laughing except Raiden. Baba was looking at her like a ship that was late.

“Night shift. Sorry. I’m fine.”

She ate the dumpling. Cold.

Halfway down the table Evangeline passed the vinegar to Elowen. Elara watched her hand cross the cloth, half asleep. And saw it. A ring. Plain silver. Fourth finger, left hand. She looked at it. She looked at Ev’s face, which was doing nothing at all. As usual. She looked at her own bowl.

Ev had never once asked about the phone calls. Elara could manage not asking about a ring.

✦ ✦ ✦

Finals started in the middle of May. She revised at his flat. The tall house had too many stairs, too many people on them, and a brother who kept coming in to explain drainage. His flat had a study nobody used. A desk, a lamp, nothing. In a week she’d spread over the whole thing. Textbooks. Flashcards in rubber bands. Highlighters with the lids off. A skeleton hand on loan from anatomy, due back by the end of term.

He’d come in at night and find her asleep across the desk with her cheek on the brachial plexus and a highlighter in her fist. He’d take the highlighter. Put the lid on. Carry her upstairs.

Sometimes, before he carried her, he stood in the doorway a while with a tape measure. She never knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Be horrible.”

Midnight. Second week. She was in his bed in one of his shirts, cross-legged, with a stack of flashcards in her lap.

“Be like you are on the round. Be like you are with Rao. If I get it wrong I want to feel like I’ve been run over.”

He took the cards. He read the first one.

“Signs of a tension pneumothorax.”

She got most of it. She forgot one.

“Nearly.”

“Nearly? NEARLY? That’s what you’d say to a dog! Do the voice. The you’re-not-tying-your-shoes voice.”

He looked at her over the card. He opened his mouth. She watched him try. He got as far as the first word of something cutting. Then he looked at her, cross-legged in his shirt with her hair everywhere. And gave up.

“I can’t.”

“Why not?”

“Because it’s you.”

She went pink. She snatched the card and hit him on the arm with it.

“That’s not helpful! That’s lovely, and it’s NOT helpful.”

She put her chin on her hand. He could see her plotting.

“Fine. Dare. Every one I get right, you kiss me. Every one I get wrong, you tell me something about you. Something real. Because you never tell me anything. You just listen. I’ve told you everything I’ve thought since I was three, and I know about four things about you, and one of them’s your shoe size.”

He thought about it. Exactly long enough for her to start regretting it.

“All right.”

She got the first one right. Causes of a raised calcium. He leaned over and kissed the corner of her mouth. Light. Like ticking a box. The second, right. Longer. His hand on her knee. The third—

She knew it was wrong while it was coming out. Two nerves in the hand, mixed up. She never mixed those up. She’d done hands for a week.

“Wrong. Go on. Something real.”

He kissed her.

“That’s cheating! That’s a wrong one! You don’t get to—”

“Get it wrong and I’ll kiss you anyway. I’ll pay later.”

He kissed her again. She forgot which nerve. They did about a dozen cards. She got most right. He kissed her for all of them. By the last one the cards were all over the floor, his shirt was half off her shoulder, and his glasses were on the bedside table.

“You owe me three. You owe me THREE—”

“I know.”

He didn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

He paid on Thursday. She was on the sofa with her feet in his lap and a textbook on her chest. He was reading a journal. He didn’t look up.

“My father wanted me to run his hospitals.”

The textbook went down.

“In the north. A group of them. Private. My grandfather built them. My father’s the chairman. I was supposed to train there, then go on the board, then take it over.”

He turned a page.

“I wanted to cut people open. Not sit in a room and talk about them. So I came south. As far as I could get. That’s one.”

She froze. Like with a cat. Don’t frighten it.

“Two. I have a brother. An Yu. Three years younger. He started a company at twenty-two and earns more before breakfast than I will in my life. He rings every Sunday to tell me I work too hard.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

“What’s three?”

He put the journal on his knee. He looked at her socks. They didn’t match.

“Three is that I’ve never told anyone the first two. Not like that. Not because they wanted to know.”

She climbed along the sofa and put her arms round his neck. His hand went to her back. The textbook slid off the cushion onto the floor. Nobody picked it up. How many hospitals? A few, probably. Some clinics. A family business, like hers.

She’d find out in November how wrong she was.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the third week of finals her phone rang in the middle of the night. Baba’s number. It was never Baba.

“Little sister. Sorry. Sorry.” Uncle Mok. He’d driven her to school every day for twelve years. “It’s Ah Kuen, from the boats. He’s cut his hand on a cable. It’s deep. Your father says not the hospital. But only if you can. You’ve got exams. He said to say you’ve got exams.”

“I’m coming.”

She was already pulling her jeans on over his shirt. He was awake beside her.

“The Walled City. One of Baba’s men. A hand. It’s not a—it’s just a hand.” She grabbed her bag. She’d started keeping a few things in it since March. “I’ll get a taxi.”

He already had his car keys. He stopped at the mouth of the alley under the one streetlight. She still wouldn’t let him see the red door. He didn’t ask to.

In the kitchen Ah Kuen sat at the long table with his hand wrapped in a tea towel and his face grey. He used to give her sugar cane when she was six. Baba stood by the fire with his arms folded. Mok by the door. She unwrapped the towel. The cable had gone across the palm, deep. Tendons? She made him bend every finger. Every one moved.

“Good. Good. Okay.”

She washed it at the sink. Numbed it. Sat at her father’s table a week before her surgical paper and closed it, neat and fast, under the kitchen lamp. Saying nothing but the small words. Baba watched her the whole time. When she’d dressed it, she pointed at Ah Kuen.

“Come and see me in a week. Don’t get it wet. Don’t lift anything. Come to me. Not anybody else.”

“Yes, little sister.”

Baba unfolded his arms.

“You’ve got exams.”

“I know.”

“I said only if you could.”

“I could.”

He gave her the look. Small print. Then he nodded and went to put the kettle on. That was all. That was a lot, from Baba.

She went back down the alley. The car was under the streetlight with the engine running. He got out before she reached it. He took a folded handkerchief out of his pocket, ironed, and wiped a smear of Ah Kuen’s blood off the inside of her wrist. She hadn’t even seen it.

“Were you careful with your own hands?”

“Always.”

“Show me.”

She held them up under the streetlight. He turned them over. Palms. Backs. Fingers. Then he kissed her knuckles, both hands, and opened the car door for her.

“You’re very weird,” she told him, and got in.

✦ ✦ ✦

The results came out in the middle of June. A Thursday. She read them in his kitchen on her phone, three times. Distinction. And a separate email: the prize in clinical surgery for her year. She screamed. She didn’t mean to. The woman in the flat below banged on the ceiling with something. Elara didn’t care. She rang him at the hospital, mid ward round, and screamed down the phone.

“Give me one minute.” Not to her. To someone on the ward. Then: “Tell me again. Slowly.”

She told him again. Slowly.

“Good.” His voice had gone strange. “That’s—good. Elara. That’s what you are.”

In the background somebody on 9B said, “Dr. Wang? Are you all right?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Graduation was on the last Thursday in June, in the Great Hall at the top of the hill. Grey stone. Hammer-beam roof. Windows that let in more pigeons than light. Her whole family came.

Baba in the funeral suit, because it was his only suit, with Uncle Mok two steps behind. Elowen in green, with Zhao Zhendong beside her, walking carefully. Good. Raiden in a waistcoat he’d designed for the occasion, covered in tiny embroidered scalpels. Evangeline, at the end of the row, in pale blue, silent, with the silver ring on her hand. Eliana with her phone.

Fourth row. When she crossed the stage they cheered so loud the Vice-Chancellor stopped and looked at them over his glasses. Raiden whistled through his fingers. Elowen cried, and would later deny it. Baba didn’t move at all. When Elara looked down from the stage with her certificate, his face was wet.

Xing Yue was at the back. By the doors, in a dark grey suit, against the wall behind the last row with the photographers and the latecomers. No wave. No smile. Hands folded. Watching her come down the steps like nobody else was in the hall. Nobody in her family knew who he was.

Except Eliana. Eliana turned round in the fourth row and looked straight down the hall at him. One second. Then she lifted her phone, took a photo, and turned back. She said nothing to anyone.

✦ ✦ ✦

The back stairs ran from behind the stage to a side door by the porters’ lodge. Nobody used them but the porters and the pigeons. She took them at a run in her gown, skirt in one fist, cap in the other. He was on the landing. By the old wooden banister with the carved knob at the turn. Of course he knew which way she’d come.

She didn’t slow down. She came down the last steps and grabbed his tie, and this time she pulled. He came.

She kissed him against the banister with her cap in one hand and his tie in the other and the gown sliding off her shoulders. He got both arms round her and lifted her off the step and kissed her back, hard. Two hours at the back of that hall, waiting to be allowed. The carved knob dug into her spine. Did she care? Not even slightly.

“Dr. Lin,” she said against his mouth. She’d never said it before. She wanted to hear it.

“Dr. Lin.” Low, into her hair. Like signing it somewhere official.

She burst into tears.

“I’m a doctor. A real one. Oh my GOD.”

“You were one in September. Bed fourteen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He set her down on the landing. Overhead, the hall was emptying. Somewhere outside, Raiden was yelling her name.

“Elara. I’d like to meet them. Properly. I’ve been standing at the back of rooms for nine months.”

She put her forehead on his chest.

“Elowen’s getting married. Properly, this time. In September, in the shop. Everybody’s going. All of us, all the friends, half the Walled City.”

She looked up at him.

“Come to that. If I bring you to Sunday lunch it’s you and Baba at one end of a table for three hours. At the wedding they’ll all see you at once and nobody can make a scene, because it’s Elowen’s day and she’d kill them.”

“September.”

“I promise.”

“Then I’d like to come as your husband.”

She laughed.

“Ha. Very funny. Ha—”

She stopped. His face hadn’t moved. He took an envelope out of his inside pocket and gave it to her.

Inside was a form. Notice of intended marriage. The registry in the old town. Every box filled in. Square block capitals, each letter separate, so any clerk on earth could read them. WANG XING YUE. And under it: LIN ELARA. Her date of birth. Her address at the tall house. Her ID number.

“This is my ID number.”

“Yes.”

“How do you have my ID number?”

“It’s on your logbook.”

“Fei has my logbook!”

“Fei leaves her door open.”

“You—” She shook the form at him. “You filled in my FORM! You did it in capitals!”

“So the clerk can read it.”

“That’s not a question! AGAIN!”

“No.”

“People kneel! Or there’s a ring, or a—”

“You’re on the step. We’re level.” He didn’t blink. “The rings are at the jeweller’s. Two. Plain gold.”

“What size am I?”

He told her.

“How do you KNOW that?”

“You fell asleep on the brachial plexus.”

She stared at him. Her mouth was open. Her face was wet. Her cap was somewhere on the floor.

“We’ve known each other ten months. You’ve never met my father. My father has the postman checked. I start at Harbourside on Monday—”

“I know.”

“—I’m going to be doing fourteen-hour days, Elowen’s wedding is in September and I’m not stealing her year, my sisters are going to kill me, and—yes—and Raiden will put it on a cake, and you haven’t even—”

She stopped.

“Wait. Did I say yes?”

“In the middle.”

“…I did. I said yes.”

“You did.”

Something in her face changed. He watched it go. The tears stopped. The pink went. What was left was cold and clear. He’d seen it once before, in his bed, with her sister on speaker.

“Okay. Rules.”

He waited.

“One. Nobody in the family. Not yet. Not Baba. Not my sisters. If Baba hears before I tell him, you’ll be looked into before the ink’s dry, and he’ll sit at the end of a table and say nothing at you until you die.”

“Agreed.”

“Two. The old town’s good. Nobody in that office owes Baba a favour. Three. I pick the witnesses.”

“Fine.”

“Four.” She held up the form. There was one box he’d left empty. “The date’s blank.”

“You pick the date. I’ve picked everything else.”

“Yes. I’d noticed that.”

“Anything else?”

She folded the form in half. Then in half again. She tucked it down the front of her gown, under the collar, against her skin.

“Five. Nobody bleeds on it.”

He took his glasses off. He folded them. He put them in the pocket of her gown. Then he took her jaw and kissed her, slow this time, on the back stairs, with her family shouting for her through two stone walls.

“ELARA! ELARA, WHERE ARE YOU? BABA’S CRYING AGAIN!”

She pulled back. She took his glasses out of her pocket and put them on his face herself. Crooked.

“Don’t follow me up.”

She ran up the stairs holding her gown, with a marriage form against her heart, laughing so hard she missed a step.

chapters.title: The Flat on Banyan Terrace
chapters.desc: She starts as an intern across the harbour, living out of a bag, and he hands her the key to a room he’s already finished. She picks the date. On a Friday morning in the old town they marry in secret, with a retired bus driver and a night sister for witnesses.
chapters.epigraph: “Now that’s an answer.” — Mr. Yin
chapters.content:
On the first of July he became an associate consultant. New badge. Better office. A parking space he’d never use. His name on the board outside 9B in white letters instead of pencil.

On the third of July she started as an intern at Harbourside General, and he didn’t see her awake for nine days. Fourteen-hour days. Out before six, back after nine. Some nights to the Walled City, some to him, depending on where she fell over. She lived out of a canvas bag. Scrubs. Stethoscope. A banana. Three chargers. A rice ball squashed flat in the back of a textbook.

The form from the back stairs was in there too. Folded in four. Date still blank. He didn’t ask. He checked her rota instead. Twice a day. Was that a lot? It was her rota.

When he could, he picked her up from the ferry. Three nights running she fell asleep mid-sentence before they’d left the car park. On the third night he parked outside 14 Banyan Terrace and watched her breathe against the window for twenty minutes.

Then he went to see the architect.

✦ ✦ ✦

The same week, he made an intern cry. A man on the ward overnight, pressure falling, belly swelling. The intern had written repeat in the morning and gone to sleep, because the registrar hadn’t answered his bleep. Six hours of bleeding. Xing Yue found him on the round and had him in theatre within the hour. He lived. Just. At the lunchtime meeting, in front of the whole department, the man’s obs chart went up on the screen.

“Read them out. Every hour. From ten at night.”

The intern read them. Nobody moved. Around four in the morning his voice went. Xing Yue waited. The intern started again.

“What did you write at midnight?”

“Repeat in the morning.”

“Why?”

Nothing.

“When your registrar doesn’t answer, you ring again. Then the next one up. Then me. You ring until somebody comes. If I’m asleep, I’ll wake up. If I’m in theatre, someone will hold the phone to my ear.” He didn’t raise his voice once. “Nobody on my team writes repeat in the morning next to numbers like that. Do you understand?”

“Yes.”

The intern was crying by then. No sound. In front of forty people.

“Thank you for presenting. Next case.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Fei caught him in the corridor afterwards.

“That was brutal.”

“The man nearly died.”

“I know. I’m not saying it was wrong. I’m saying it was brutal.” She narrowed her eyes at him. “You were always bad. You’ve got worse since you’ve been happy. Like you’ve got more to lose.”

He didn’t answer that.

“Oh my god. You’ve got more to lose. What have you done?”

“Nothing yet.”

“YET?”

He went into the lift.

✦ ✦ ✦

He gave Elara the envelope on a Sunday at the end of July. Her first day off in three weeks. Inside: a key, freshly cut. And a floor plan. The architect’s, not an estate agent’s. The top two floors of 14 Banyan Terrace, every room drawn in. One of them, the small room off the big room, the one with the window over the frangipani, had a single letter on it in his handwriting.

E.

“What’s this?”

“A key. And a plan.”

“I can SEE it’s a key and a plan.” She turned the plan round. “You’ve drawn an E on the study.”

“Come and look.”

He opened the door. The old desk was gone. A new one. Wide, pale oak, lower than he’d ever have used. A lamp with a long arm. A suturing board, the good kind, with a skin pad that would take a hundred hours. Shelves she could reach without a chair, her textbooks already on them, and a row of empty ones waiting. An armchair by the window. Under it, the frangipani in flower. She didn’t go in.

“When did you do this?”

“The last three weeks.”

“The desk’s the wrong height. For you.”

“It’s the right height for you.”

“How do you know what height I—” She stopped. “May. Finals. I was asleep on the desk.”

“Your elbows. In pencil, on the wall. I’ve painted over it.”

“You MEASURED me in my SLEEP?”

“Yes.”

“And downstairs. The postbox. It says WANG, and under it, LIN. I thought it was a mistake!”

“It’s you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She was furious for an hour. She stomped round the big room with the plan in her fist.

“You decided for me! You put my name on a box like I’m a parcel. Then you showed it to me finished. Like an operation. Like I’d been under the whole time!”

He let her go.

“What if I hate oak? What if I don’t want to live here at all?”

“Do you?”

“That’s not the POINT.”

He waited until she ran down. Then he gave her the only thing he had.

“If you say no, I’ll take it all down. The desk goes back. The name comes off the box. You keep the key, for when you want to come. Nothing changes.”

She stopped walking. He’d have had the desk out that night with a screwdriver. He meant it. And she wasn’t going to say no. She’d known in the study doorway. She’d been shouting for an hour because he’d known first.

She went back into the study and hopped up onto the desk, legs dangling. It was exactly the right height for that, too. He hadn’t measured that. She held her hand out. He came.

She pulled him in by the front of his shirt until he was standing between her knees. Then she kissed him, hard, both hands on his face. Still angry. Quite a lot.

“It’s the right height,” she said, when she let him breathe. She didn’t sound pleased.

“I measured.”

“I KNOW you measured. That’s what I’m angry about.” She kissed him again. Slower. “I’ll pay rent.”

“It’s paid for.”

She’d known that, really. She’d seen the letters from the bank that weren’t asking for anything.

“Then I’ll buy the groceries. All of them. Every week. You’re not allowed to buy a single egg.”

She’d paid for her own books since eighteen, on a scholarship and pride.

“All right.”

Then she reached into her bag on the floor without getting off the desk. The form came out, soft from a month of being folded.

“I’m moving in on Saturday the twelfth. Uncle Mok can bring my boxes. Mok doesn’t talk.” She smoothed the form flat on the oak. “And I’m not moving in as your girlfriend.”

He stopped breathing for a second.

“Friday. The eleventh. I’m off till noon. If I’m moving in, I’m moving in married.”

She took a pen out of his shirt pocket and wrote the date in the empty box. Her own handwriting. Small and fast.

“Witnesses?”

“Mr. Yin.”

“Mr. Yin.”

“He asked me if I was married. A year ago. I owe him an answer.” She tapped the pen on his chest. “And you can pick one. One.”

“Sister Shao.”

“She’ll tell EVERYONE.”

“She’s known since September. She hasn’t told anyone.”

“How do you know she knows?”

“She told me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The registry in the old town smelled of floor polish and old paper. Mr. Yin got there first. On the steps in his bus driver’s jacket, dark blue, every brass button polished. He’d had his stoma put back in the spring and wanted everyone to know.

“All plumbed back in! Like new. Better than new.” He looked Elara up and down. “That dress is too nice for a registry.”

“It’s the only dress I’ve got!”

The dark green one. Her birthday. The alley. The horn. Did he remember? His face said he remembered.

Sister Shao came straight off nights. Grey cardigan, pager clipped to the pocket, a paper cup of coffee the size of a vase. She looked at the three of them on the steps.

“You have twenty minutes. Then I’m going to bed.”

Xing Yue was in the dark grey suit. He didn’t say anything. He looked at Elara in the green dress on the registry steps and forgot, briefly, how to do anything else.

“You’re staring,” she whispered.

“Yes.”

“Stop it. Mr. Yin’s watching.”

“Mr. Yin can watch.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine the doors opened. The clerk was a small round woman with reading glasses on a chain. She read their form with her nose nearly touching it.

“Oh, lovely. Lovely clear capitals. You would not believe what people hand me.”

Elara made a noise like a sneeze. He didn’t look at her. If he looked at her, she’d go.

“Mr. Wang Xing Yue?”

“Yes.”

“Miss Lin Elara?”

“Yes! Sorry. Yes.”

The clerk turned the book round. A pen on a chain. Two lines. Elara picked up the pen. Her hand was shaking. She’d cleaned out a gunshot wound on a kitchen table without a wobble, and now look at her.

She signed. LIN ELARA. Small and fast. The pen skidded on the last letter. He signed under her. One stroke. Nobody alive could have read it.

“Witnesses, dear.”

Mr. Yin signed like he was filling in a bus timesheet. Slow. Proud as anything. Sister Shao signed without putting her coffee down.

“Rings?”

He took them out of his inside pocket. Two plain gold bands, in no box at all. Warm from him. He took her left hand. He turned it over first. His thumb went to the inside of her wrist, to the pulse, and stayed there one second.

“You’re shaking.”

“I am NOT shaking—”

He put the ring on her finger. It went on smooth. Exactly the right size. Obviously. She took his hand. She pushed his ring on. It stuck at the knuckle. She shoved. It went.

“There.” She held on to his hand with both of hers. “Mine.”

The clerk stamped the book. Thunk.

“That’s you, dears. Congratulations.”

“Thank you! Thank you so much. And I’m sorry I sneezed, I didn’t sneeze, I laughed, it was the capitals, he did them so you could read them, he’s very—”

He took her jaw in his hand and turned her face up and stopped her mouth with his. Right there. In front of the clerk and the book and the stamp. She made a muffled sound. Then she grabbed his lapels with both fists and kissed him back. Up on her toes. Ring hand flat on his chest.

Behind them, Mr. Yin cleared his throat. Loudly.

“Now THAT’S an answer.”

Sister Shao took a photo and finished her coffee.

“Fourteen minutes. Congratulations. I’m telling nobody. I never do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the steps outside he took a thin gold chain out of his other pocket.

“You can’t wear it on the ward. Or in theatre.”

“I know.”

He slid the ring back off her finger, threaded it on the chain, and did the clasp up under her hair. It sat against her collarbone. Under scrubs, nobody would see.

“You bought a chain.”

“Yes.”

“Before I’d even picked a date?”

“The day after the stairs.”

She looked down at his left hand. His ring was still on it.

“Aren’t you going to hide yours?”

“No.”

“People will ASK!”

“Nobody asks me anything.”

He meant it. Wang Xing Yue was going to walk onto 9B with a wedding ring on, and the whole department would stare at it, and nobody would dare say a word. She laughed so hard Mr. Yin had to hold her elbow on the steps. By noon she was on the surgical floor at Harbourside in her scrubs, taking blood. Married.

Elara: my registrar just asked why I’m smiling

Xing Yue: What did you say.

Elara: constipation

Xing Yue: Good.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came home after ten. Their flat. She got as far as the sofa and lay down on top of him in her scrubs.

“Wedding night,” she announced, into his shirt.

“Yes.”

“I’m going to seduce you.”

“Yes.”

She was asleep in under a minute. One shoe still on. He took the shoe off. He put both of them by the door, facing out.

Then he went back and lay down under his wife, and didn’t move until morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven on Saturday an old black Mercedes stopped outside 14 Banyan Terrace. He watched from the top-floor window. A big grey-haired man got out and opened the boot. Boxes. ELARA — BOOKS. ELARA — WINTER. ELARA — DON’T ASK.

Elara ran down in her scrubs and met him at the street door. She took every box from him there. She didn’t let him in. He never tried.

When the last box was down, the big man stood on the pavement by the frangipani and looked up. Straight at Xing Yue in the window. At the hand on the frame. His left hand. No expression at all. Then he got back in the Mercedes and drove away.

Elara came up the stairs behind a box, out of breath.

“That was Uncle Mok. Baba’s driver. He’s driven me since I was six. He doesn’t talk.”

“He saw me.”

“Mok sees everything. He doesn’t talk.” She put the box down and kissed him on the chin and ran for the ferry. “He DOESN’T talk!”

✦ ✦ ✦

She worked fourteen hours. He unpacked nothing. He wasn’t stupid. He stacked the boxes in the study in the order she’d want them. Then he filled the fridge. He hadn’t meant to keep a list. He’d kept one anyway.

Peach yoghurt with the bits in. Not the smooth one. Sesame paste she ate off a spoon. The small mandarins with the loose skin. Old Bian’s hot sauce, which Old Bian didn’t sell, in a jam jar handed over with a look.

And the bad orange fizzy drink from the vending machine on the seventh floor. The one she drank when she was sad.

She came in after ten. Through the door that was hers now. Talking. A gallbladder. A man who’d tried to discharge himself in his gown. Shoes by the door, facing out. Bag on the floor. Lanyard on the counter. Stethoscope on the stairs. He followed her round and picked them up and lined them up on the counter. She walked past the counter and pushed them into a heap. Neither of them said anything about it.

She opened the fridge. She stopped talking. The peach yoghurt. The sesame paste. The bad orange drink, in a row on the bottom shelf.

“You said I’d buy the groceries.”

“There are no eggs.”

She looked. There were no eggs. There was everything else in the world and not one egg. She shut the fridge. She put her forehead on the door.

“You’re having a bath. Doctor’s orders.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He ran it while she sat on the closed toilet lid and talked about the gallbladder. Hotter than he liked. He tested it with his wrist. She sank in up to her chin. Still talking.

He knelt on the floor and took her clip out. He wet her hair with the shower head, one hand over her eyes. His shampoo. She complained it made her smell like him. She leaned her head back into his hands anyway. He took his time. Scalp to ends. Rinse. Again. His fingers slow and firm at the back of her neck, where she carried everything.

The gallbladder stopped. Small sounds instead. Then nothing at all. The gold chain was still round her neck. The ring sat in the hollow of her throat, under the water. He rinsed the last of it. He squeezed the ends out.

“I love you.”

Plain. On his knees on a wet floor, like giving her a result. He’d been carrying it since April.

She opened her eyes. She turned her head on the edge of the bath.

“You heard that? In the car? In April? I thought I DREAMED that. I was talking about gauze!”

“Yes.”

She sat up so fast the bath went over the side onto his knees. Both wet arms round his neck.

“I love you. I love you. I meant it. I was asleep but I meant it—”

He kissed her with his hands still in her hair. By the time he stopped there was nearly as much water on the floor as in the bath.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took her to bed with her hair still wet. He dried her first. All of her. Slowly, with the towel, like it was a job worth doing properly. She laughed at him. Then she stopped laughing, because he didn’t stop when she was dry.

“Xing Yue.”

“Mm.”

“Husband.”

He went still.

“Say it again.”

“Husband.” She pulled him down by the back of his neck. “Husband, husband, husband. You did my form in capitals. You measured my elbows. You’re the worst man I’ve ever met—”

He kissed the inside of her wrist. Where he always started. Then the chain at her throat, and the ring on it, and the skin under the ring.

“Wife.”

That was all he said, after that.

It was slow. Nowhere to be. Nobody who’d ring. No going home afterwards, for the first time, because this was home. Her wet hair cold on his arm. The rest of her warm. She held his face in both hands in the lamplight and looked at him. Checking. Like he always checked her. His control went somewhere in the middle. She felt it go, and laughed into his shoulder, and then she couldn’t laugh.

“Don’t you dare be careful,” she breathed. “I’m your WIFE.”

He wasn’t careful.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay across him with her damp head on his chest and her ring between them on its chain.

“We’re married.”

“Yes.”

“Nobody knows.”

“Sister Shao.”

“Sister Shao doesn’t count. She knows everything anyway.” She drew a circle on his chest with one finger. “Nobody in my family knows.”

“Uncle Mok looked at my hand.”

Her finger stopped.

“Mok doesn’t talk,” she said.

Less sure, this time.

chapters.title: The Cake
chapters.desc: Elara makes four tiers of cake for Elowen’s wedding, and the tall doctor in glasses stands beside it all night while nobody introduces him. At midnight her father asks his name, and he tells him: her husband.
chapters.epigraph: “Sunday. One o’clock. Bring him.” — Lin Jian
chapters.content:
“It’s relaxing.”

“It’s three in the morning.”

“Relaxing things can happen at three in the morning. Pass me the ball tool.”

He passed her the ball tool. She’d come in from Harbourside at ten, scrubbed her hands at his kitchen sink like she was going into theatre, and sat down at the counter with a tray of pink sugar paste and a pair of tweezers. That was five hours ago. One petal at a time, rolled so thin you could see the lamp through it. Four tiers of deep-pink camellias, for Elowen’s wedding on Saturday. She’d said yes to the cake in June. Before she knew about fourteen-hour days. Before she knew she’d be married.

Six weeks now. Her ring was on its chain under her T-shirt, knocking her collarbone every time she leaned over the tray. His was on his hand.

“Your ring’s gone pink.”

He looked at it. “It’ll wash.”

“Elowen’s cake has your ring dust on it. That’s practically a confession.”

“Then don’t tell her.”

“I’m not telling ANYONE. Rule one.”

He’d worked out on the first night that she was faster if somebody moved the light to wherever she was looking. So he stood at her shoulder and moved it. When she held her hand out without looking up, he put the next thing in it. Tweezers. Brush. The dish of water for the edges.

“You’d make a terrible scrub nurse.”

“Why?”

“You keep looking at my face. Not my hands.”

“Your hands don’t need watching.”

She went pink and dropped a petal.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second night he said, “You hum.”

“I do not hum.”

“You’ve been humming for an hour. The same tune. It goes up at the end.”

“I DON’T hum! I’d know if I hummed.”

“Would you?”

She opened her mouth. Shut it. Tried to catch herself at it for ten minutes, and couldn’t, because it only happened when she wasn’t listening.

“Again,” he said.

“Oh my god.”

“It goes up at the end. Like a question.”

“Probably because I never knew the answer.” She laughed. Then she frowned at the petal. “Where did I even get a tune? Ah Sim only sings to fish before she kills them.”

He didn’t know. She forgot about it. A minute later she was doing it again, and this time he didn’t tell her. He just listened.

At two she put the tweezers down. Sugar dust all over her fingers. A petal stuck to her thumb. She turned round on the stool, took his face in both pink hands and kissed him. Slowly. Like she’d been waiting all evening and had made herself finish the flower first.

When she let go there were fingerprints on his jaw. She started to laugh.

“Don’t wipe them.”

“Elara.”

“Leave them! You look like you’ve been attacked by a very small flamingo.”

He left them. In the morning one was still there, faint, under his ear. She saw it on her way out and laughed all the way down Banyan Terrace.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third night there were four tiers in his fridge, which he’d emptied for them. And one more camellia on its own, in a small box. Deep pink, on a wire stem.

“That’s Zhao’s. For his lapel.” She poked the box. “Mr. Wen says the real bush has given enough this year, so Elowen won’t cut it for a buttonhole. He gets mine. I’ve told him not to eat it.”

“Will he eat it?”

“He’ll probably eat it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden’s van came for the cake at nine on Saturday morning. Elara was already at Harbourside. Day shift. She’d tried to swap. Nobody would. She checked her phone in the sluice all day.

Raiden: in the van. alive

Raiden: on the counter. still alive

Raiden: under the arch. GORGEOUS

Raiden: it fell off

The last one was a photo of Raiden eating a petal.

Elara: I WILL END YOU

Raiden: worth it

She came to the shop at nearly eight, straight off the ferry, in a dress she’d changed into in the doctors’ toilets. Lanyard still round her neck. White roses down a four-metre aisle. An arch of dark shipyard timber. Thousands of tiny lights on the ceiling, all off. Two dogs in ribbons. Thirty people.

And her cake, by the cooler, every petal warm in the light from the street. She stood in front of it. She was so proud it hurt.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the cooler somebody was being introduced to everyone. A tall, quiet woman in a black leather jacket, grease under her nails, backed into the corner by the big glass fridge. Raiden was beside her, glowing like a lamp.

“Jinx. My wife. She built Xiao Pan’s bike. Don’t touch her tools.”

Raiden’s wife. Raiden had a WIFE?

Elara was next in the queue before she’d shut her mouth. She stuck her hand out. She saw the woman’s hands, the shiny pink marks on the backs of them, old and new, and her mouth went on without her.

“Elara. I’m a surgeon. Are those burns from an exhaust? You should use silicone gel.”

The woman looked at her own hands. Then at Elara. She opened her mouth to say something. Elara didn’t hear it.

Across the room a tall young man in glasses had just come in off the street. Dark suit. A little out of breath. He looked round once and found her. She forgot the woman at the cooler completely.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came straight across the shop. Past Aurelia Chen in gold. Past the tea-shop men. Past the dogs. He stopped beside her and the cake, very close, his sleeve against her arm, and looked at the cake.

“It’s the best thing in the room.”

Her ears went hot. Nobody introduced him, and everyone noticed.

Aunties she’d known since she was three looked at him over their paper cups. Aurelia looked at him for a full minute with her head on one side. Then her eyes dropped to Elara’s collar. To the thin gold chain just showing at the neckline.

Aurelia smiled and went back to bossing the caterer. Oh no. Aurelia sold rings for a living. Of course Aurelia saw.

Mrs. Chau from the fish stall came to admire the cake. Then she looked up. A long way up.

“And who’s this?”

“A colleague,” Elara said. Instantly. “From the hospital.”

Mrs. Chau’s eyes went to his left hand. To the plain gold band. Back to Elara. Her whole face said married colleague in capital letters.

“How nice.”

She took a photo of the cake and went straight to the other aunties.

Beside her, he went still. Only for a second. He didn’t move away. But she felt it, like a hand taken off her back.

“I didn’t mean—”

“I know.”

“It’s what I say at WORK.”

“I know.”

Four aunties had their heads together by the roses. They weren’t even trying.

“Did you see his hand?”

“Married.”

“Standing like THAT. Next to Lin Jian’s girl.”

“Shameless.”

Elara wanted the floor to open. They thought she was standing next to some poor woman’s husband. Which she was. Her own.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the shop a lanky boy with a medical textbook under his arm, beside Eliana, had seen him. His ears went pink. Xing Yue looked back at him over the roses. Nobody nodded. One second. Then they both looked away.

“Do you know him?”

“He’s my cousin. Yu Chen. He lives next door to your father.”

“Your COUSIN lives next door to my FATHER and you never—”

“You never asked if I had a cousin.”

She opened her mouth. Shut it. That was true. Infuriating, but true.

“Later. You’re telling me all of it later.”

“Yes.”

“All of it.”

He reached over and fixed her lipstick with his thumb. One quick stroke at the corner, where she’d smudged it on a paper cup. She froze. He didn’t even look round to see who’d seen. Four aunties had.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine o’clock Baba walked Elowen down the aisle. Funeral suit. His only suit. Four metres should have taken a few seconds, but his arm was shaking, and halfway down, past the second row of tulips, he stopped.

“Zhendong.”

The shop went quiet.

He asked Zhao something about a lemon tree. Elara didn’t understand it. Zhao did. Zhao, who’d crawled up a hill with a bullet through him and lain on a kitchen table under her hands without once asking her to stop. He stood under the arch in his black suit, and his face opened like a door.

“Nine lemons. The most it’s ever had.”

Baba’s eyes went wet. Then Elowen’s. Then Elara’s, obviously. She cried at weddings and graduations and dogs on the news. She stood by her cake and cried with her mouth open.

Without looking, he put something in her hand. A handkerchief. White cotton. Ironed into a square with a sharp crease.

“You iron your handkerchiefs?” she whispered. Wetly.

“Yes.”

“Every one?”

“Yes.”

She blew her nose on it during the vows. Loudly. He didn’t flinch.

Chen Si said exactly four sentences. Elowen said a thing about keeping. Zhao said a thing about doors, and Elara put the whole handkerchief over her face.

The lights came on at nine forty-one. All of them at once, gold and warm, like the sky had come into the shop. Everyone looked up except Eliana, who pressed one key on her laptop and shut it. Zhao took Elowen’s face in both hands and kissed her, not politely at all, until Aurelia started counting out loud.

Elara looked up at the lights. Then sideways at her husband. He wasn’t looking at the lights.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards Zhao came over for cake. He ate it off a paper plate with his fingers. Her camellia was still in his lapel. Uneaten! Then he looked up at the man beside her, and Elara knew that look. She’d seen men in the Walled City go grey under it.

Xing Yue looked back.

“How’s the side?”

Zhao didn’t answer. What did he know? What had he worked out from the bags she’d brought up the hill in March, the hospital labels, the instrument case with the needle holder in it? His eyes went down to Xing Yue’s left hand. Up again.

“Hm.”

He took another slice and went back to his wife. Elara breathed out so hard the handkerchief fluttered.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody else came near them all night. The whole family was busy with Raiden. Raiden himself swung past at eleven with a paper cup in each hand.

“Elara! Have you met my WIFE?”

“I’ve met your wife!”

“Isn’t she terrifying? Hello, tall person. Lovely suit. Can’t stop.” He was already going. “Two years next Saturday!”

“TWO YEARS?”

But he’d gone.

“Two years,” Elara hissed. “Since 2021! He hid a wife from all of us. Who does that?”

He looked down at her.

“…Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face did.”

“My face is always like this!”

Baba had gone out to stand on the step for ten minutes after the word wife. Elowen went over to Jinx with a face like a closed door and came back with a different face. Everyone was talking about Raiden. Raiden was talking about Raiden. Her brother’s secret was so big and so loud that hers slid by underneath it. She’d never loved Raiden more.

✦ ✦ ✦

At midnight he said he had to be on the ward at seven. They went out the front. Eliana had gone out the back lane with the boy from next door an hour ago and hadn’t come back, and Elara was absolutely not thinking about that. Taxi rank at the end of the street, under the awning of the old pharmacy. A bench. No taxis. The smell of rain coming.

She rubbed her arms. He took both her hands and put them in his coat pockets, with his own on top.

“I said colleague.”

He didn’t answer.

“And she looked at your ring. Now four aunties think I’m stealing some poor woman’s husband. I AM. I’m stealing mine—”

“I heard.”

“It’s not what you are.”

“What am I?”

He’d asked it plainly. Like a ward-round question. His face wasn’t plain at all.

He took his glasses off, folded them, and held them out. She took them. Then he took that hand by the wrist and pressed it flat against his chest, under his jacket, so she could feel his heart. It was going as fast as hers had on the restaurant steps a year ago.

“Oh,” she said.

He kissed her. Like he’d stood beside her all night without being allowed to touch her and had run out. Her back hit the pharmacy shutter and it rattled. She didn’t care. She got her arms round his neck with his glasses still in her fist and kissed him back until her knees went. Then a taxi came round the corner and the driver leaned on his horn.

They broke apart. The driver was grinning.

“Sunday,” Elara said, out of breath, hand flat on his chest. “I’m telling them. All of them. Baba first. Rule one’s finished. I’m never saying colleague again in my life.”

He put his glasses back on.

“Your bag. You left it on the counter.”

The driver threw his hands up and drove away.

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked back for her bag. Baba was in the doorway of the shop.

Alone. Hands in his pockets. The gold light behind him. Enormous and grey in his funeral suit. He’d seen them come up the street together, and from his face he’d seen a good deal more. The taxi rank was in plain view of the shop door. It always had been. Why hadn’t she thought?

He didn’t look at her. He looked at the man beside her.

“Who is he?”

She felt her mouth want to do it again. Colleague. A friend. Baba, this is— She didn’t let it.

“Ask him,” she said.

Baba looked at her for one second. Then up at Xing Yue, who was taller than him. Hardly any men were.

“What’s your name?”

“Wang Xing Yue.” He didn’t blink. “Her husband.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nothing happened. That was the worst part. Down the street the guitar went on. Somebody laughed. A moth hit the shop light, twice.

Baba’s eyes came round to her. Slowly. Like a ship turning.

She pulled the chain out from under her collar. Her fingers shook so badly she nearly broke the clasp. The ring came up out of her dress and swung in the light. He looked at it a long time.

“When?”

“August.” Tiny voice. “The registry in the old town.”

“Who stood for you?”

“Mr. Yin. He’s a patient. A bus driver. And Sister Shao from my husband’s ward. She came straight off nights.”

“A bus driver.”

“He polished all his buttons, Baba!”

Baba said nothing. He looked at the band on the man’s hand. At the man. Reading the small print. She’d seen him read men twice this size, and she’d seen those men leave the city.

Then his eyes went past them both, down the street, to the black car at the kerb. Uncle Mok was leaning on it, looking at the sky.

“Mok.”

Mok went on looking at the sky.

“Mok saw his hand,” Elara whispered. “In August. He didn’t say?”

Baba didn’t even turn his head. “Mok doesn’t talk.”

He made a sound. Not a laugh. Not not a laugh. Then he looked back at the man beside her.

“You didn’t come to me.”

“I wanted to. She had rules.”

“She has rules.”

“Five of them.”

Baba’s eyes went to her. She went red to the hair.

“Your brother. Tonight. And now you.”

“I’m sorry. Baba, I’m SO sorry, I was going to tell you on Sunday, I’d just decided, I swear, three minutes ago, ask him—”

“Elara.”

She stopped. Was his face wet? In that light she couldn’t tell. His voice wasn’t.

“Sunday. One o’clock. Bring him.”

He went back inside. He fetched her bag off the counter, came out, put it into her hands without another word, and shut the shop door on the light and the noise. Elara stood on the pavement holding her bag.

“…Did my father just invite my husband to lunch?”

“Yes.”

“Oh my GOD.”

chapters.title: Sunday Lunch in the Walled City
chapters.desc: The red door, eleven chairs and a father who has learned to ask things. Raiden asks his intentions, and Xing Yue tells the whole table he’s already married her.
chapters.epigraph: “Does she eat when she’s on nights?” — Lin Jian
chapters.content:
The week after the wedding, Elara’s phone didn’t stop. Elowen rang at seven on Sunday morning. Xing Yue could hear her from the kitchen. The phone was on the other side of the room.

“A REGISTRY?”

“I know.”

“On a FRIDAY?”

“I know!”

“With a BUS DRIVER?”

“He’s a very good bus driver! He’s driven the number nine for forty years!”

“Elara, I am going to come over there—”

“You can’t, you’ve got a husband and two dogs and it’s your honeymoon—”

Elara ended up face down in a cushion saying “I know, I know, I KNOW” for twenty minutes. Eliana sent one text.

Eliana: I know. Since the 11th. You were in green.

Elara: HOW

Eliana: spreadsheet

Evangeline sent nothing at all. Raiden sent a photo of two steel washers on a napkin with the caption TWINS. Elara threw her phone across the sofa.

The first Sunday, he was on call. Elara rang her father to say so. Xing Yue heard her side of it from the kitchen. The rota. The ward. The general unfairness of surgery. A silence. Then: “Yes, Baba. The next one. I’ll tell him.”

She came out with the phone in her hand and a strange look on her face.

“He said a surgeon on call is a surgeon on call. He said I don’t mind waiting.” She stared at the phone. “He’s never said that in his life. Elowen’s been teaching him things. It’s frightening.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Sunday they took the ferry over.

“Don’t mention the north.”

“All right.”

“Don’t mention money. Don’t mention the hospitals. Don’t sit in the carved chair, that’s Baba’s. Don’t sit in the high chair, nobody sits in the high chair.”

“What do I mention?”

“Nothing! I’ll talk.”

“I know you’ll talk.”

“Don’t say it like that.”

The red door was at the top of the alley. Past the noodle stall. Round the corner he’d never been allowed to turn. Deep lacquer red. A brass knocker shaped like a fish, rubbed gold in the middle by sixty years of hands. Elara didn’t knock. She opened it, because it was her house, and went in talking, and he followed her into a hall that went straight up into the dark. All stairs. Soup and woodsmoke.

“Don’t be nervous.”

“I’m not.”

“You’ve cleaned your glasses twice since the ferry.”

He put his handkerchief away.

The kitchen was long and low, a fire at one end. A table down the middle with eleven chairs round it, none of them matching. A carved one at the head. A bentwood one. A child’s high chair nobody had sat in for years and nobody had moved. The whole family looked up. An old woman the size of a child came out of the scullery with a ladle. She looked at him from his shoes to his hair and back.

“Too thin. Sit.”

He sat where the ladle pointed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He knew who they all were. Elara had told him a hundred times, and he’d listened every time. Lin Jian at the head in the carved chair. Grey. Enormous. A cardigan. Hands flat on the table either side of his bowl. Elowen on his right, cool and sharp, in green. Zhao beside her, in black, who looked at Xing Yue across the table and didn’t stop. Raiden opposite, a plaster on his thumb, chair tipped back, delighted with everything. Eliana halfway down with her laptop open beside her soup, not looking at him at all. He didn’t believe that for a second. Evangeline at the far end by the fire. Grey. Silent. A silver ring on her left hand. Not blinking much.

And Elara beside him, talking for both of them. She talked through the soup. The ward. The ferry. Mr. Yin, who’d sent a card to say his stoma had been reversed and he was back on his bus pass.

“He was at the registry! He polished his buttons. Did I say about the buttons? Baba, I said about the buttons.”

“You said.”

“And Xing Yue once made a registrar cry in three sentences, and the registrar sent him a THANK-YOU card at Christmas, which tells you—”

She was frightened. He could hear it. Did she even know? She was doing for him what she’d done for her sister in the room over the shop. Filling every gap before anything could get into it. He put his arm along the back of her chair. She went on talking. Her voice dropped half a tone.
