Lin Jian let her go on. He ate his soup and listened to his daughter with his eyes on her husband. When she stopped to breathe, he put his spoon down.

“Does she eat when she’s on nights?”

The table went quiet. Even Raiden’s chair came down onto four legs.

Not the question he’d prepared for. He’d prepared for the north. His family. His salary. You married my daughter in secret, at a registry, with a bus driver. He’d had answers ready for all of it.

He looked at Lin Jian and saw a man who’d brought a three-year-old home from a children’s home and listened to her talk for twenty years. Who’d watched her fall asleep over a dumpling at this table in April. Who wanted to know one thing.

“Not unless someone puts it in her hand.”

“Do you?”

“Every time.”

Lin Jian looked at him a few seconds more. Then he picked his spoon back up.

“Good.”

Beside him, Elara let out a breath she’d been holding since the alley.

✦ ✦ ✦

The fish came. Steamed, whole, ginger and spring onion. Ah Sim put the best piece of the belly in Elara’s bowl without asking anyone. Elara reached for it.

“Wait.”

He took her bowl. He picked the bones out of the belly with his chopsticks, every one, small and fast, and lined them up on the side of his own plate. Then he put the bowl back in front of her. Nobody said anything. Ah Sim had stopped with the ladle in the air.

“…He does that,” Elara whispered. Bright red. “At home. He does that at home.”

“Does he,” Elowen said.

“I choke on them otherwise! I’ve always choked on them, I choked on one at my sixth birthday, Baba had to—”

“I remember,” Lin Jian said.

Raiden was grinning so hard his face looked painful. Elowen hadn’t finished.

“A Friday.”

“You had a Tuesday!”

“I had Chen Si.”

“I had a bus driver. He’s better than Chen Si. He polished his BUTTONS.”

Zhao, beside his wife, said “Hm” into his fish. Elowen turned and looked at him. He went on eating.

To make up for it Elara picked up a dumpling and put it straight into her husband’s mouth with her own chopsticks, in front of everyone.

“Oh, I’m going to be sick.” Raiden clutched his chest.

“Good. Be sick. Ah Sim, he’s going to be sick.”

“Not at my table.” Ah Sim didn’t even turn round from the stove.

✦ ✦ ✦

Of course it was Raiden who asked. Over the fish, chopsticks waving.

“So. Dr. Wang.”

“Raiden.” Elowen didn’t even look up.

“No, I have to. I’m the only son. It’s in the rules. Baba, it’s in the rules, isn’t it?” He pointed his chopsticks across the table. “You married my little sister. In secret. Without asking anybody.”

“Raiden, you were married for TWO YEARS before—”

“I’m in no position. I know. I’m aware. I’m asking anyway.” He leaned in. “What are your intentions?”

Xing Yue put his chopsticks down.

“To have married her. In August.” He turned his head. Not to Raiden. To the head of the table. “I’d like your blessing for the rest of it.”

The table went silent.

Elara had just taken a mouthful of soup. She choked on it. She choked so badly she had to put the bowl down and put her head between her knees. He put his hand flat on her back without looking at her, and kept his eyes on Lin Jian. Lin Jian said nothing.

Raiden stared. Then he laughed. The whole of him went, tipped back in his chair, hands on his stomach. The laugh went up the stairwell and round the house until Ah Sim came out of the scullery to see what had died.

“The rest of it,” Raiden wheezed. “Baba. Baba, did you hear him? He wants a blessing for the REST OF IT—”

Lin Jian had heard him. He said nothing at all. But at the head of the table, his eyes had gone wet at the corners. At the far end, Evangeline looked at Elara bent double with her napkin over her face. The corner of her mouth moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch Zhao stood up, looked at him, and went out. He followed him through the red door into the alley. Grey afternoon. The noodle stall at the bottom had its shutters up and its steam going. Zhao stood by the wall with his hands in his pockets.

Big. Broad. A face that didn’t move. Xing Yue had stood beside the cake with him a fortnight ago. He’d thought about the scar since, every day, without ever seeing it. Two wounds left open to drain. Packed morning and evening for two weeks by a final-year student with stolen gauze.

“You saw her bags.”

“Yes.”

“You didn’t ask.”

“No.”

Zhao looked at him in the grey light. Down at the ring on his hand. Back up. A nod. Once. The smallest movement a head could make. Was that a yes? From Zhao it was practically a speech. Then Zhao went back in through the red door and left him in the alley on his own.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara caught him at the bottom of the stairs.

“Come and see my room. Quick. Before Raiden finds us. He’ll want to show you his drawings of the house. He’s got drawings of every house. Come ON.”

She pulled him up four flights, each narrower than the last. Past a landing window over the roofs of the Walled City with a cat asleep on the sill. To a room at the very top, under the roof. Sloping ceiling. A bed with a faded quilt. Posters. She hadn’t been joking. Five boys with a great deal of hair. A film. A heart cut out of a magazine with arrows she’d added in pen. A map of the moons of Jupiter.

“That’s the band, I liked the one with the fringe, don’t judge me, and that’s the film, I saw it four times in one weekend when I was fourteen, I cried every time at the same bit, the dog bit, and that’s the heart, and there’s a mistake in one of the arrows, look, there, I never fixed it, I was going to fix it when I got into medicine and then I got into medicine and I thought it was funnier to leave it—”

Too fast. Much too fast. She was nervous of him in her old bedroom in a way she’d never once been in his. He shut the door.

“Elara.”

She stopped. She turned round and looked at him, standing against her bedroom door with his hand still on the handle. He crossed the little room in two steps. He took her chin and tipped her face to the window, to the light, like he was checking her pupils. She opened her mouth to say what—

He kissed her against the door. She went up on her toes into it at once. Her back hit the wood. Her hands went into his hair. Five boys watched from the wall. The whole house came up the stairwell, Ah Sim’s voice, dishes, Raiden laughing at something. He kissed her until they were both breathing like they’d run the four flights. Until she was pulling at the back of his shirt and her hands found the skin of his back.

He stopped first. Forehead on hers. Eyes shut. Hands flat on the door either side of her head.

“Not in your father’s house.”

She opened her eyes. Flushed to the collar. Hair everywhere.

“That’s a rule?”

“It is now.”

“We’re MARRIED. It’s allowed. It’s practically compulsory!”

“Not in your father’s house.”

She looked so outraged and so pink and so pleased at once that he nearly broke it inside a minute. He stepped back and straightened his glasses.

“Ask me again at home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They left at five. Ah Sim gave him a bag of leftover dumplings and a look. Raiden shook his hand and said, “The rest of it,” and started laughing all over again, and Elowen steered him away by the arm. Lin Jian stood at the bottom of the stairs and nodded to him once, the way Zhao had in the alley.

“Next Sunday.”

That was all. He went back into the kitchen. Elara grabbed Xing Yue’s sleeve so hard she nearly tore it.

“That’s it. That’s yes. That’s the blessing. He’s never said next Sunday to ANYONE—”

Evangeline was at the red door. She was holding it open for them, in grey, with her silver ring. She looked at him as he went past. Steady. Her face doing nothing.

“Good.”

Elara burst into tears on the step.

✦ ✦ ✦

She cried in the car for ten minutes and talked for twenty. Her father’s eyes. Raiden’s laugh. Zhao in the alley, which she’d watched from the landing window. And Ev. Ev, Ev, Ev.

“She said GOOD. She says about ten words a year, and one of them was to YOU—”

When they got home she put her shoes by the door, facing out. Then she stood in the hall in her coat and looked at him.

“I’m asking you again. We’re home.”

He’d been waiting since the top of her father’s house. She took the lapels of his coat and walked backwards up the stairs, pulling him with her, one step at a time. She kissed him on every third step. Halfway up she took his glasses off herself and put them in her own coat pocket. He heard himself laugh. At the top she dropped her coat on the landing, then his. Then she took his hand, turned it over, and kissed the inside of his wrist. Watching him. Doing his move back at him.

“I pay attention,” she said against his pulse.

He forgot about rules. It wasn’t careful. She’d been nervous all day, and now it came out of her a different shape. Eager. Laughing. Greedy. She pushed him down onto the bed and took her time, and talked the whole way through. What she’d wanted to do in the room at the top of the house. All of it. In detail.

“—and then the poster, I’d have taken the poster down first, obviously, I’m not doing that in front of the one with the fringe—”

He pulled her down and stopped her mouth with his. She laughed into it. Then she didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay with her head on his shoulder. Dark room. His hand in her hair.

“To have married her. In August.”

“I meant it.”

“I know you meant it.” She lifted her head. “That’s why I choked.”

“You choked on soup.”

“I choked on my HUSBAND asking my FATHER for a blessing for THE REST OF IT, in front of Raiden, who will never ever let it go—”

“He said next Sunday.”

She went quiet.

“He did,” she said. “He did say that.”

chapters.title: An Yu Comes for Tea
chapters.desc: Elara finds out her silent sister got married before she did, and told nobody either. Then his brother flies down for one cup of tea, notices everything, and lets slip how rich the Wangs really are.
chapters.epigraph: “He rang me to ask whether love at first sight was in the literature.” — Wang An Yu
chapters.content:
Elowen never rang at eleven at night. On the Tuesday she did.

Elara was at the kitchen counter in her scrubs, eating peach yoghurt out of the pot after a late shift. She answered with the spoon in her mouth.

“Ev’s married.”

Elara took the spoon out.

“What?”

“Married. She’s been married since April. She told nobody.” Elowen’s voice was doing something strange. “The man from February. The one you—” She stopped. Who knew what? Nobody was saying it on a phone. “He went to see Baba on Saturday. In his office. There was a knife. Nobody’s hurt. Baba’s fine. Baba CRIED. And he told Baba that Ev was his wife, with Ev standing in the doorway.”

“Since APRIL?”

“Since April. A registry in a border town. And then they went to the market, the two of them, and he asked her at the orchid stall to marry him again, properly, in front of us. And it was yes. Out loud. In front of the orchid woman.”

Elara put the yoghurt down on the counter. Upside down.

“Yes. Out loud.”

“The orchid woman gave them a plant.”

Elara started to cry.

She stood at his counter with the phone against her ear and cried with her hand over her eyes. Elowen told her the rest. His name, Lee Jun Hyuk. Enormous. Talks all the time. Can’t cook.

“April,” Elara sobbed. “APRIL. I saw the ring! At Sunday lunch! I was half asleep over a dumpling and I saw it, and I didn’t—”

“Why didn’t you ask?”

“Because she never asked me about the phone calls! And she’d been MARRIED. She did it FIRST. She beat me by four months—”

“Elara. Elara, it’s good news.”

“I know it’s good news! That’s why!”

“And you’re one to talk.”

“I KNOW.”

Elowen laughed down the phone. Elowen almost never laughed.

When Elara put the phone down, Xing Yue was in the kitchen doorway in his reading glasses with a journal.

“Evangeline.”

“She’s married. Since April. To the man with the knife wound. He’s called Lee Jun Hyuk. He’s enormous. He can’t cook. And nobody KNEW, she just WENT and DID it, at a registry, like a—” She stopped. “Like me.”

“Yes.”

“Don’t say yes like that!” She wiped her face on her sleeve. “I’m fine. I’m happy. I’m crying because I’m happy.”

He came over and took the yoghurt pot out of her hand, because she’d picked it up again upside down.

“You cry at everything good.”

“Not everything.”

“Dogs on the news. The banana prize. My handkerchief. Mr. Yin’s card. Your father saying next Sunday.”

She opened her mouth. Couldn’t argue with a single one.

“…Two sisters. Two secret weddings in one year. Baba must be having a heart attack.”

“Three. Raiden.”

“Oh my GOD. Three.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His brother came on Sunday, between two flights.

Xing Yue told her on Friday, like a change to the rota. An Yu was flying south for a meeting, back north the same evening, and would come for tea at three. He said it while cleaning his glasses. He’d been working out how to say it for two days.

“Your brother. An Yu. The one who rings on Sundays. The one who earns more before breakfast than you do in your life.”

“Yes.”

“He’s coming HERE. To our flat. And you’ve told me on FRIDAY.”

“He told me on Thursday.”

“Does he know about me?”

“He knows.”

“Knows what? Knows I exist, or knows—” She waggled her left hand at him. The ring was on the chain, but the meaning was clear.

“I rang him in August. From the registry steps.”

“You rang your brother from our wedding and you didn’t tell me you rang your brother from our wedding?”

“You were laughing at Mr. Yin.”

She spent Saturday cleaning, which she never did. She moved her things into piles. He moved the piles into rows. She moved them back. She bought a cake from the good bakery, then panicked that it was the wrong sort of cake and bought another one.

“What’s he like?”

“Like An Yu.”

“What’s An Yu like?”

“Like An Yu.”

She asked four times. She got the same answer four times. She threw a cushion at him.

✦ ✦ ✦

An Yu came at three exactly.

Shorter than his brother and broader. The same serious face, but closed a different way. Like a door with a better lock. His coat probably cost as much as a small car. The suit under it cost as much as a bigger one.

“Elara.”

He shook her hand. Dry. Brief. He gave Xing Yue a cake of old Pu’er in a paper wrapper at the door, the way other people gave wine.

Xing Yue made it in the small brown pot. An Yu sat on the grey sofa with his cup and his back straight, and let her talk.

And she talked. She couldn’t help it. The two cakes, and why there were two. The ferry. The man on her ward who’d swallowed a key. Mr. Yin’s card. She heard herself doing it. She couldn’t stop.

An Yu said “Yes” once. He said “I see” once. That was it.

But his eyes moved. She watched them go round the room while she talked, the way Eliana’s went over a screen. Her shoes by the door, facing out. The study through the open door: the low oak desk, the suturing board, the long-armed lamp. The kitchen counter, where there was a little heap of taxi receipts from the week, because she always got a receipt and never knew what to do with it. Her lanyard on the stairs. The second toothbrush mug by the bathroom door. His brother’s left hand.

Then his brother.

Halfway through the man with the key, Xing Yue laughed. A short sound under his breath, at the bit where the man asked for the key back.

An Yu turned his head and looked at his brother laughing. His face didn’t change at all. He looked down into his tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

“He rang me.”

It was the first thing he’d said that wasn’t yes or I see. He said it to Elara. He put his cup down.

“Two summers ago. June. A Saturday night. He doesn’t ring me. I ring him, on Sundays, to tell him he works too hard. He rang me at eleven at night and asked whether love at first sight was in the literature.”

Elara’s mouth fell open.

“What literature? Medical, he says. Psychiatric. Neurological. Anything with a reference. He’d seen someone on a ward and hadn’t slept, and he wanted to know if there was a documented mechanism. Or if it was just tiredness.”

“Two SUMMERS ago?”

“I sent him three papers.” An Yu picked his cup up again. “One was about voles.”

“…Voles.”

“Pair-bonding in prairie voles. It’s a well-known paper. He read all three and rang back to say the voles were the only useful one.”

Elara turned round on the sofa.

Xing Yue had his glasses off. He was cleaning them on his handkerchief. Every corner of every lens. Very slowly. His ears had gone dark red.

She laughed so hard she had to put her tea down. She laughed until she was crying, which apparently she did at everything. An Yu watched her with his closed face, and the corner of his mouth moved once. Exactly like his brother’s.

✦ ✦ ✦

It came out sideways after that.

She asked him, to be polite, what his meeting had been about. He told her. She got about a third of it. The numbers she got fine. They had a great many noughts in them, and he said them like they were small.

“Xing Yue said your father has some hospitals.”

An Yu looked at his brother.

“Some.”

“In the north. Your grandfather built them.”

“Fourteen.” He set his cup down. “And the medical school that trains the doctors for them. And the land they stand on.”

“Oh.”

“And the port the equipment comes in through.”

“A port?”

“And the house in the hills, where our grandmother lives and writes him every month to come home and get married.” He looked at Elara. “Some.”

Nobody said anything.

Elara was a Lin. Money came in the back door of her house at night in envelopes and went out the front in her father’s coat. Men stood up when her father walked down the street. There’d been a car and a driver her whole life. She’d thought she knew what rich was.

This was a different size. She didn’t have a word for this size. What were you supposed to say to a port?

She looked at Xing Yue. He’d put his glasses back on. No sorry on his face. No worry either. He looked like he was waiting to see which way she’d go.

✦ ✦ ✦

An Yu left at a quarter to four.

He put his coat on in the hall. He shook her hand again, brief and dry.

“Thank you for the cake. Both of them.”

She went red. She’d thought he hadn’t noticed there were two.

“Sister-in-law.” A nod.

Was that a joke? Was that a WELCOME? From An Yu it was apparently both.

Then she was in the kitchen with the cups, and she heard them at the front door behind her. Low.

“Nainai will ask. At New Year. When you’re bringing your wife home.”

A short silence.

“I am home.”

She stood at the sink with a cup in each hand and didn’t move. The door shut. His footsteps came back across the big room. She turned the tap on fast, so he wouldn’t know she’d been standing there. He came into the kitchen, looked at the tap running into an empty sink, and knew anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

She waited until she’d dried the cups.

Then she started.

“Fourteen. Fourteen HOSPITALS. And a medical school. And a PORT. You told me in May your father had some hospitals and I thought you meant clinics! Three clinics and a pharmacy! I told Elowen your family was in healthcare. I said it like a dentist’s!”

“You never asked.”

“Don’t. Don’t you dare. You said that about your cousin. You can’t keep not telling me things and then going you never asked, like it’s my fault for not guessing you’ve got a medical school—”

“You’re right.”

She stopped. He never said you’re right in a fight. He said it on ward rounds, about scans.

“You’re right. I didn’t tell you because I didn’t want it to be the thing about me. It’s been the thing about me my whole life. I came here so it wouldn’t be. That’s not a good enough reason.”

He told her the rest standing in the kitchen. Plainly. Like a history. His grandfather’s trust, which came at twenty-five. The top of this building, bought in 2019. The rest of it put somewhere and not looked at since. A consultant’s salary he hardly spent. He would never run anything in the north. His father knew that and didn’t believe it. His grandmother knew it and was the only one who did.

“None of it changes where I live. Or who with.”

She’d stopped being angry somewhere in the middle. She hadn’t noticed. That annoyed her, so she started again.

“We’re MARRIED. I haven’t even said it out loud at Harbourside yet, I’m still wearing it on a chain like a SECRET AGENT, and I find out on a Sunday afternoon from your BROTHER that I’ve married a port—”

He looked at his watch.

She stopped.

“Are you timing me?”

“I’m giving you five more minutes. Then I’m kissing you.”

She stared at him. Then she went on, louder, because nobody was going to tell her when she’d finished. His coat, which probably cost more than her loupes. The second cake. Cleaning all Saturday for a man who’d read her taxi receipts. She was halfway through the receipts when she saw his eyes drop to the second hand.

“You’re EARLY. That’s four. I saw you look, that’s not five, that’s—”

He took her wrist. Turned it over, two fingers on the pulse, like he was going to count it against the second hand.

Then he kissed her in the middle of the word. Against the counter. Her back to the clean cups.

She made a furious noise into his mouth and grabbed his shirt in both fists and kissed him back. Still furious. Then less. Then not at all.

“That was four.” She could barely get it out.

“I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the card on Wednesday.

She was at the hospital kiosk in his coat, which she’d stolen that morning because hers was in the wash, and she opened her wallet to pay for a coffee. There it was. In the slot behind her ID, where it hadn’t been on Tuesday.

A plain dark grey card from the green-taxi company. LIN ELARA. An account number.

She rang him from the kiosk.

“What is this?”

“An account. In your name. Every taxi you take goes on it. Anywhere. Any time.”

“Who gets the bill?”

“I do.”

“So you’ll see every taxi. Where from. Where to. What time.” The coffee was going cold in her hand. “You’ll get a LIST of everywhere I go.”

“I already know where you go.”

She opened her mouth. Shut it.

He did. He’d had her on his phone since February, a little blue dot, and she’d watched him check it, and she’d never once told him to stop. She didn’t tell him now. She hung up on him instead, and was furious for an hour, the way you’re furious about something you know perfectly well you’re going to keep.

At two in the morning she came out of Harbourside after a shift that had run six hours over. Rain. No cash. No bus. Feet screaming.

There was a green taxi at the rank.

She got in and handed over the card. The driver swiped it.

“Banyan Terrace, Dr. Lin?”

It was already on the account. She sat in the back of the warm car with the rain on the windows and the harbour going past, and got her phone out.

Elara: Fine.

He was asleep. He answered anyway, inside a minute.

Xing Yue: Good.

chapters.title: He Is Bad at Holidays
chapters.desc: He works every holiday so other people can go home. On Lunar New Year’s Eve his wife brings dumplings to Ward 9B, and he breaks his own rule.
chapters.epigraph: “I said not in the hospital. I’m allowed to be wrong.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
In January Raiden’s wife came to dinner at the red door for the first time, and Xing Yue was in theatre. He was always on the rota for the Saturdays nobody wanted. Elara had stopped asking him to swap. She’d started to understand it, though he hadn’t explained yet. She went on her own, late, from Harbourside, in scrubs under her coat.

Late that night his phone rang in the pocket of his scrubs. He was standing at the end of a theatre table watching a registrar close. He let it ring twice. Then he nodded to Suyin, his scrub nurse, who took it out of his pocket, answered it and held it to his ear. Four years she’d done that. She knew who rang at this hour.

“She CAME.”

No hello.

“Jinx. She came inside!”

“Inside the house?”

“She’s been married to Raiden for over two years and she’s never once come through the door. Tonight she came. And Baba opened it HIMSELF.”

“I’m glad.”

“And Ev was there, and Ev just sat there and watched Jinx with her face doing nothing at all, and I could tell she was pleased.”

“And Ah Sim?”

“Ah Sim came out of the kitchen. Looked Jinx up and down. He’s fat. About Raiden! To Jinx’s FACE!”

“What did Jinx say?”

“He cooks. Just like that. And Ah Sim told her to sit down and eat because she was too thin as well.”

On the table, the registrar had put a stitch in the wrong place. The third one. He’d watched the first two and said nothing. The first two had been Zou’s to get wrong.

“And after dinner Baba and Jinx were in the kitchen on their own. Drying up. We were all upstairs arguing about Raiden’s drawings—”

“Mm.”

“—and Baba LAUGHED. The big one. It came all the way up the stairs and everybody stopped. Nobody knows what she said. Raiden doesn’t know. She won’t tell him—”

“Wait.”

She stopped. He never said wait to her. He turned his head an inch from the phone.

“Dr. Zou.”

The registrar’s hands stopped.

“Take that out. And the one before it.” His voice didn’t go up. It went down. “You’re closing skin. Not wrapping a parcel. If you close a wound like that on anyone of mine again, you can go and work in a shoe shop, where it won’t matter what the stitches look like. Again. Slowly.”

Dr. Zou took them out. Nobody in theatre breathed. The anaesthetist found something urgent on her machine. He turned back to the phone.

“Sorry. Go on. He laughed.”

A pause on the line. A long one. Was she angry? He waited to find out.

“You just told someone to go and work in a SHOE SHOP. In that voice.”

“He’ll do it properly now.”

Another pause. Then she laughed, low, in the back of a taxi somewhere on the harbour road.

“Poor man. I’ll bring him a sweet on Monday. Which one’s Zou? Is he the one with the eyebrows?”

“Yes.”

“I’ve heard Baba laugh like that about four times in my life. I NEED to know what she said.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that week she asked him why he always took the holidays. Not as a complaint. She was lying on the floor of the study with her feet up on the armchair and the phone on her chest. He was on call again, walking an empty ninth-floor corridor in the small hours. He could hear she’d already guessed half of it.

He stopped by the window at the end. The harbour was down there, black. A ship going across with all its lights on.

“The ones with children should go home. Fei has two. Rao has a little girl. If I’m here, they’re not. That’s most of it.”

He could have stopped there. He always had, with everyone.

“The rest is that I don’t like them. Holidays. At home they were dinners.”

“Dinners?”

“Thirty people at my grandfather’s long table. My father at the end of it, talking about the hospitals. How many beds. How many new ones. Which son would take over which.” He watched the ship. “An Yu used to hide under the table with a book. I used to sit and wait for the courses to end.”

“Oh.” Very small.

“I’d rather be here. Here something happens.”

“Is that why you’re always on? Every Christmas? Every New Year?”

“Yes.”

“You told me that without me asking.”

“Yes.”

“You’ve never done that. Not once. I always have to dare you, or drag it out of you with a BROOM.”

He thought about it. She was right.

“Don’t get used to it.”

She laughed so loudly on the floor of his study that he had to hold the phone away from his ear.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Lunar New Year’s Eve he was on call. He had been every year since he came south. She went to the Walled City at six in a red dress she’d bought for it, with mandarins for the table and green tea biscuits for Eliana. From half six his phone buzzed in his pocket on the ward and didn’t stop.

Elara: Ev’s husband brought a kumquat tree. A TREE. on his shoulder. up the alley.

Elara: raiden says he’s a wardrobe. 4 times so far

Elara: Aurelia Chen is here with her husband. she’s in red. she looks like she could buy the house and everyone in it. she keeps looking at Jun Hyuk

Elara: he’s been talking to me about wound packing for 25 mins. he knows a LOT about wound packing. I told him he had better technique than half my registrars and he went bright red. all of him. he’s enormous so it took a while

Elara: now he’s on to Jinx. engines. intakes?? she’s LETTING HIM

Elara: Baba and Jun Hyuk have been talking about tides by the window for an hour. standing up. hands in pockets. Ah Sim says if they don’t sit down she’s giving their soup to the dog. we don’t have a dog

Elara: eliana just threw a bag of dumplings over the wall to the boy next door. your cousin. I saw. she doesn’t know I saw

He read them at the nurses’ station between patients with his face perfectly straight. Sister Shao watched him read them and pretended not to. At ten he sent one back.

Xing Yue: Eat something.

Elara: I’ve eaten FOUR bowls. ah sim’s counting

✦ ✦ ✦

Late that evening he was at the 9B station writing up a man with a bowel obstruction when the lift doors opened at the end of the corridor. She came out of them.

Red dress, coat over it, hair coming out of its pins. A cardboard box tied with string, Ah Sim’s kind, in her arms. A string bag of oranges off her wrist. Cheeks pink from the cold. She came down the corridor past the dark bays where the patients were asleep, and every nurse on the ward looked up, and Sister Shao put down her pen.

“Happy New Year,” Elara whispered at the station. “I brought you dumplings. Ah Sim made them. Pork and cabbage.”

“Elara—”

“There’s a coin in one, she says, but she won’t say which, and if you get it you have to tell her. And oranges. For luck. You HAVE to have oranges.” She put the box down in front of him. “I got a taxi. On the card. I thought you’d want to know.”

He looked at her. At the box. The oranges. The red dress under the coat. He put his pen down.

“Sister Shao. I’ll be in the on-call room. Bleep me.”

Sister Shao looked at Elara. At him. At the dumplings.

“Of course, Dr. Wang. Happy New Year, Dr. Lin.” She picked her pen back up. Then, not looking up, very low: “Mrs. Wang.”

Elara made a noise like a stepped-on toy.

“Leave me two.” Sister Shao was already back in her notes.

✦ ✦ ✦

The surgical on-call room on nine was narrow. A bed. A chair. A desk. A sink. A window looking west over the hospital garden and the roofs, all the way to the Walled City. They ate off the bed with the box between them, with the chopsticks Ah Sim had tucked under the string. She talked with her mouth full.

“Aurelia leaned over and said something to Ev. Ev didn’t answer. And Aurelia sat back looking like she’d won anyway! How do you WIN when someone doesn’t answer?”

“Practice.”

“And Baba laughed at something Jun Hyuk said. With his whole face. Twice in one month! What’s happening to him?”

“Your family’s getting bigger.”

“It was SO loud. The loudest New Year we’ve ever had. Everybody was there.”

“I wasn’t.”

“I know. That’s why I came.” She put a dumpling in his mouth before he could answer. “It’s not everybody if you’re not.”

He bit down. His teeth hit something hard. He took it out. An old coin, wiped clean, warm from the dumpling.

She stared at it. Then she put both hands over her mouth and laughed into them until her eyes ran.

“You have to tell Ah Sim. You have to RING her. Tomorrow. She’ll be furious. She’ll say you cheated. She’ll say I gave it to you on purpose—I didn’t! I swear I didn’t!”

He put the coin in the pocket of his scrubs. He wasn’t giving it back to anyone.

✦ ✦ ✦

The fireworks went up over the Walled City at midnight. They stood at the window with the light off. Red, gold, green, a long way off, from the old piers and the roofs. Each bang came a second late through the glass. Below them the garden was dark. The big camphor tree was black against the paths. The old block’s first-floor windows were dark too.

She stood with her back against his chest. He had his arms round her and his chin on the top of her head.

“Happy New Year.”

“Happy New Year.”

The last of them went up. The sky went smoky and quiet. She turned round in his arms and looked up at him. He watched her decide to be wicked.

“Your rule.”

He’d made it in the autumn. The first time she came up to 9B with his lunch, a nurse had found them in his office with the door half open and gone away with her eyebrows in her hair. Not in the hospital. Not where his team were. Not where his patients were. Outside the doors was outside. Inside was work.

She backed away from him, slowly, until her shoulders hit the on-call room door. She leaned on it. Folded her arms. Eyebrows up. Hair half down.

“Not in the hospital. That’s what you said. I’m in the hospital. You’re in the hospital. It’s very strict. I’m only saying, I wouldn’t want you to BREAK it, you’d never forgive yourself, you’d have to go and work in a shoe shop—”

He crossed the room. He put his hand flat on the door beside her head, pushed it shut the last inch, and turned the lock.

“I said not in the hospital.”

“You did.”

“I’m allowed to be wrong.”

He took her chin, tipped her face up to the light from the window, and kissed her in the middle of whatever she’d been about to say next. No warning.

She made a sound of pure triumph into his mouth. Her arms came uncrossed and grabbed him. She tasted of oranges. Her coat went somewhere. Her hands were cold from the window, and she put them up under his scrubs, on his back, on purpose. He made a noise he’d never made in this building. She laughed.

He lifted her off her feet, carried her the two steps to the bed, and sat down with her in his lap. She kissed him like it was a holiday. Slow. Then not slow. Her hands in his hair. Her knees either side of him on the narrow bed. His hands on her back through the thin red dress. She was kissing his throat. His eyes were shut. Which building? What building?

His pager went off. Loud. On his waistband. Right between them. She jumped. He opened his eyes. She was a few centimetres away, flushed, pink-mouthed, furious.

He unclipped it and read it with her still in his lap. Then he reached for the phone on the wall and dialled.

“Wang.”

Her forehead dropped onto his shoulder. She was shaking with silent laughter into his neck.

“Yes. Coming.”

He put the phone down.

“Bed eight’s pressure is dropping.”

“Go.” Still laughing into his neck. “Go, go, GO, save bed eight. I’ll wait. I’ll eat your dumplings.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Bed eight took two hours. When he came back she was asleep on the narrow bed in her coat and her red dress, curled on her side with her shoes still on. Empty dumpling box on the floor. An orange in her hand.

He sat on the chair and watched her for a while. Then he took her shoes off and put them side by side under the bed. Facing the door.

At three in the morning he walked her down to the taxi rank at the main doors. Cold and clear. The air smelled of fireworks. She was shivering in her coat. He took off his jacket and put it on her over the top, and did up one button at her chest.

“Now I’m wearing a surgeon.”

“You’re wearing his jacket.”

“Same thing.”

A green taxi pulled in. She turned on the kerb and put something in his hand. A small red envelope with a gold character on the front, folded flat.

“I’m married,” he said. “Married people give red packets.”

“Ah Sim doesn’t believe in registry offices.” She closed his fingers over it. “Until there’s a banquet you still get a red packet. And anyone who works on New Year’s Eve gets one. That’s an old rule. She might have made it up.” She kept her hand over his. “Don’t open it till I’ve gone.”

She got in the taxi. In his jacket. He watched it go down the hill. Then he opened it. No money. A slip of paper folded in four, in her round quick handwriting. Anybody on earth could read it.

Come home for breakfast.

He stood on the kerb outside the main doors in his scrubs, in the cold, and read it twice. Then he put it in his pocket with Ah Sim’s coin and went back up to his ward.

Sister Shao looked up from the station.

“My two dumplings, Dr. Wang?”

He’d forgotten. There’d been an orange in Elara’s hand and nothing else in the box.

“…Tomorrow.”

“Mm-hm.” She went back to her notes. She was smiling at them.

chapters.title: Staples on a Kitchen Table
chapters.desc: Her sister shoots a man in a noodle shop, and Elara staples her brother-in-law’s scalp on the kitchen table. She gets home after midnight and shakes on the hall floor, and her husband asks for names.
chapters.epigraph: “Next time ring me first. I’ll drive. I’ll wait in the car.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
“Why can’t I have a third pudding?”

“Because you’ve had two.”

“I’m eighty-four.”

“And you’ve got a brand new hip, and I’d like you to keep it.”

At two in the afternoon Elara was on the surgical floor at Harbourside, eleven months into her intern year, losing an argument about pudding. She was good at this floor. She knew every nurse’s children’s names. She knew which porter came fast if you asked nicely and which one came fast if you didn’t. The old man was laughing now. He’d given up on the pudding. He’d moved on to what they all moved on to in the end.

“Are you married, doctor?”

Her hand went to her collar. To the chain under her scrubs.

“…Yes.”

“Since when?”

“Shh! Nobody here knows!”

He was delighted. He put a finger to his lips. She’d said it out loud at Harbourside for the first time, to a man with a new hip, and her ears were on fire.

Her phone rang. A number she didn’t know. She stepped into the corridor.

“Miss Elara. It’s Bao. I drive your sister. Evangeline.” Low and quick. Traffic behind him. “Nam’s Noodles, River Bridge Road. Somebody came for her. There’s been shooting.”

“Is she—”

“She’s not hurt. She’s NOT hurt. She shot one of them. There’s a boy hit, and the old lady, and Mr. Lee’s head is open. She said call you. Nobody else.”

She was already walking.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went through the ED at a fast walk in her scrubs, smiling at everyone. The way you walked when you didn’t want anybody to look twice. By the ambulance-bay door there was a shelf of green bags, the grab bags the paramedics took out to the big calls. She took one. Nobody saw. If they had, she’d have smiled and said she’d been sent.

Green taxi at the rank. She gave the driver the card.

“Quick. Please!”

He looked at her scrubs and was.

Her phone buzzed in her lap halfway over the bridge.

Xing Yue: ?

One question mark. He’d watched the dot leave Harbourside in the middle of a shift, cross the river and head east into the old market district, where she had no reason in the world to be. What was she supposed to say? Hi, darling, Ev shot someone, back for dinner? She didn’t answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came through the broken door of Nam’s Noodles at a quarter to three, hair falling out of its clip, green bag on her shoulder, and stopped. Broken glass. The duck cabinet with a hole in it. A calendar on the floor. A boy against the wall with a tea towel pressed into his shoulder, crying steadily, like rain. A man in a pale shirt face down by the window with one of Zhao’s men sitting on his back. An old woman in a purple jacket in a kitchen chair with her wrist on a cushion, swearing.

And her sister on the wet floor, in a pale blue dress, with her husband’s head in her lap.

“Oh, Ev.”

Then she was a doctor.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did the boy first, because he was bleeding most. In and out. Through the muscle at the top of the arm. Nowhere near the big vessels. Nowhere near the bone. She felt her voice go clear and pleasant.

“You’re going to be fine. It went through. It missed the bone. You’re very lucky the person who shot you is a terrible shot.”

The boy stared at her. She packed it and taped it. Bao was by the door with a face like a closed fist.

“He needs an ambulance in the next hour. Not before.”

Bao looked at the man on the floor by the window.

“I’ll see to it.”

She didn’t ask what that meant. She’d grown up in a house where you didn’t. She did the old woman second.

“I’m fine.”

“You’ve got a broken wrist and probably a concussion, and you’re going to the hospital whether you like it or not.”

The old woman gave her a long look, from her trainers to her hair.

“You’re the doctor one.”

And let her splint it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then she knelt beside her sister. Jun Hyuk. Her brother-in-law. Who’d talked wound packing at her for twenty-five minutes at New Year and gone red all over. He was lying on his side with his eyes open, watching the room slide about. Ev’s hand was in his hair. The floor beside him had been cleaned with a tea towel. Of course it had. She parted his hair with gloved fingers and looked.

“Six centimetres. Down to the bone. It needs closing. Has he been sick?”

“Once.”

“Did he lose consciousness?”

“About a minute. Maybe two.”

Elara looked down at him.

“Do you know where you are?”

“Nam’s. On the floor. In the soup.” His eyes found her. “Your sister shot a boy.”

“He’s oriented,” Elara told Ev. “Rude, but oriented.”

“I’m not rude, I’m concussed, it’s different, I’ve read about it—”

“He needs a scan. Head injury, loss of consciousness, vomiting. That’s the rule. That’s not me being careful. A bleed under the skull can look like nothing for six hours and then kill him.”

“No hospitals.”

“Then he dies on the floor of a noodle shop,” Elara said pleasantly, “and I’ll tell everyone it was his own fault.”

Ev looked at her.

“There’s a place on the hill. Above the old racecourse.”

“The Crestview? It’s the most expensive hospital in the city. It costs more for one night than I earn in a month. Rich men go there to have their knees done and not be in the newspaper.”

“They don’t ask questions of people who pay.”

Elara looked at her sister. Then at the giant with his head in her lap.

“Can he pay?”

“Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He refused to go anywhere with a hole in his head. He said so at length. Then he was sick again, without any fuss, into a bowl Ev was already holding.

“Right. Kitchen.”

There was a staple gun in the green bag, because there always was. She sat him on the edge of the table in the back kitchen, among the flour sacks and the pots, head bent forward, Ev holding both his hands. She cleaned it. Numbed it. Closed it. Staple after staple along the line through his hair. Fast and neat.

“Ow!”

“That wasn’t one.”

“I was getting ready.”

“You’ll feel the next one. That’s three. Four. Stop talking.”

“I can’t stop talking, it’s how I—ow—”

At twenty past three a tall policeman in a long coat came in through the broken door. She heard him stop in the shop, the way everyone did. She heard him say Evangeline, and her sister not answer, and then a long conversation about a passport. She didn’t look round. She had her hands in a man’s hair and a staple gun in her fist. If the police wanted to watch her close a wound on a kitchen table, they could watch. She’d been smiling at policemen her whole life.

She’d finished when he came through to the back. He looked at the big man on the edge of the table. He looked at her, in Harbourside scrubs, peeling off her gloves. He knew exactly who she was. Every policeman in the city knew her father’s face. Most knew his daughters’.

“Dr. Lin.”

“Inspector.”

She smiled at him. She dropped her gloves in the bin. She went and washed her hands at Nam’s sink and listened to none of what came next.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Crestview looked like a hotel. They scanned his head at six. No bleed. A concussion, a bad one, and a fine crack in the skull that would heal by itself if he didn’t do anything stupid for six weeks. The doctor on duty was a calm grey woman. She looked at the stapled wound under the light. Then she turned and looked at Elara, standing at the end of the bed in her scrubs with the green bag still on her shoulder.

“Nice work.”

Elara went pink to the ears. Nobody had ever said that to her about a kitchen table.

She stayed in the corridor on a chair nicer than her sofa. At some point she heard him through the door start on Ev about a sandwich, then stop mid-word and not start again. She smiled into her coffee. At a quarter past midnight they let him go with a list. She took a green taxi home on the card. She laughed at all the driver’s jokes.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got as far as inside the front door. She shut it. She hung her keys on the hook. She stood in the dark hall at Banyan Terrace in her scrubs with the green bag on her shoulder.

And started to shake.

From nowhere. It came up from her knees. She’d been fine at Nam’s. Fine at the Crestview. Fine in the taxi. Now her teeth went. Her hands went. The bag dropped. She put her back to the wall and slid down it, onto the floor by the shoe rack, her own shoes in front of her still pointing out, and sat there with her arms round her knees, rattling like a cup on a train. The light came on upstairs.

He didn’t say anything. He came down in his T-shirt and soft trousers, sat on the hall floor beside her, and pulled her against his side so her head was on his chest. Then he held on. She talked. Of course she talked.

“The door was broken. The ducks had a hole in them. There was a boy, he was crying like it was raining, I told him he was lucky, I told him the person who shot him was a terrible shot—”

“Elara.”

“—and the old lady with the purple jacket, and the policeman. And Ev’s husband’s head was OPEN! I stapled it on a TABLE. There were flour sacks—”

“Breathe.”

She breathed. It came out in pieces.

“My sister shot someone. Ev. Ev shot someone.” She was crying now as well as shaking. “She had a gun. She knew how to USE it!”

“I know.”

“Somebody came into a noodle shop to take her and she shot him, and then she sat on the floor holding Jun Hyuk’s head as calm as anything. I’ve known her my whole LIFE.” Her voice went. “I didn’t know she could.”

He went still against her. Not his thinking stillness. Colder. It went through him like ice through water. She lifted her head and looked at his face in the light from the stairs and didn’t know it.

“Who?”

“Who what?”

“Who came into the noodle shop.” Perfectly level. “Who’s on the floor with one of Zhao’s men sitting on him. Who sent them. I’d like the names.”

“No.”

He looked at her.

“No. I’m not giving you names. You’ll do something. I can SEE you’ll do something. You’ve got the face you had with Nie.” She grabbed his T-shirt in her fist. “And it’s not yours. It’s Ev’s. It’s Zhao’s. It’s Wei Long’s, he was there, he’s dealing with it.”

“Elara—”

“That world raised me. That’s my family. Things come in the back door at night and you help and you don’t ask. I’m not going to stop going when they ring. Don’t ask me to.”

He didn’t. She watched him take it in. The whole of it. She watched him put the names away somewhere, and the ice with them, and come back.

“I won’t. Next time ring me first.”

She stared at him.

“I’ll drive. I’ll wait in the car. I won’t come in. I won’t ask who.”

“You’d hate that.”

“Yes.” His voice was steady. Then it wasn’t. “But I’m not finding out from a dot on a map that you’re in the old market district in the middle of a shift. And then nothing. For ten hours.”

“I’m sorry—”

“I watched it all afternoon. Nam’s. Then the Crestview. I didn’t know what you were doing.” It cracked. “I didn’t know if it was you that was hurt.”

She hadn’t thought of that. She’d thought of everything else in the world and not that.

“Yes,” she whispered. “Yes. I’ll ring you first.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When she’d stopped shaking he stood up and pulled her up by both hands. She thought he was taking her upstairs. He put her against the wall of the hall with his hands either side of her face and kissed her.

No word first. Glasses still on. Hard. His whole body holding her to the wall, steady, not letting up. Like pressure on a bleed. Like he could stop something coming out of her if he pressed hard enough. She held on to the back of his T-shirt with both fists and kissed him back with her mouth still wet from crying. Under her hands his heart was going fast. Much faster than his face had let her see.

When he stopped he kept his forehead on hers.

“You’re having a bath.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He ran it. She sat on the edge in her scrubs and talked about staples.

“—and they come in different widths, and on a scalp you want the wide ones because of the hair, and once I saw a registrar try skin glue on a scalp and glue the man’s hair to his own glove, he had to be CUT free—”

She got in. She sank down to her chin and kept going. He knelt on the tiles beside the bath, elbows on the edge, in his T-shirt, and listened. He didn’t look away from her once.

“—and there’s a little dial on the side, you’re meant to check it, and NOBODY checks it—”

She stopped.

He was kneeling there. Dry. Glasses on. Serious face. Being sensible. She took the front of his T-shirt in one wet hand and pulled.

He came over the side before he knew it was happening. All his clothes on. Glasses and all. A wave went over the edge and across the floor. He landed half in and half out, one knee on the bottom of the bath and his elbow in the soap dish, and came up gasping, glasses crooked, water pouring off his hair.

She laughed so hard she slid under.

He hauled her back up by the arms. And he was laughing too. Out loud. The real one, the one she’d heard maybe six times in her life. In a bath. In his trousers. He threw his glasses out onto the bathmat. He tried to get his T-shirt off and got stuck in it. She helped, badly. They laughed until the water started going cold.

Then it wasn’t funny.

When had it changed? She was holding his face. He had both arms round her in the water like she might go somewhere. She kissed him slowly, for the first time all day without any hurry or fear in it. He kissed her back the same way. Under her hands he was shaking a little. Not from the cold. She held him tighter.

✦ ✦ ✦

He got them out in the end. He sat her on the closed toilet lid in a towel and dried her hair. The towel first, rough and thorough, the way he did everything. Then the dryer, on low, his fingers working through it section by section while she leaned her head against his stomach with her eyes shut.

“You’re very good at this.”

“I’ve watched you do it badly for a year.”

“Rude.”

“Oriented.”

She laughed into his T-shirt. He switched the dryer off. In bed she lay along his side with her damp head on his shoulder. His thumb found the inside of her wrist and stayed on her pulse. Counting it, probably. Was he? Of course he was.

When he moved, once, she grabbed his arm.

“Where are you going?”

“The light.”

“Leave it.”

He left it.

chapters.title: The Vow at Dawn
chapters.desc: On the morning she finishes her intern year he meets her in the old garden at City Hospital and asks his wife to marry him again, in front of everyone this time. She’s talking about fish, and says yes in the middle of a sentence.
chapters.epigraph: “Sorry, what? Say it again. I was talking.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
“Dr. Wang. Elara’s husband.”

Aurelia Chen came out from the back of the shop herself. Grey dress. Hair up. She looked at him from his shoes to his glasses, exactly the way she’d looked at him across Elowen’s shop in September. A stone she hadn’t decided whether to set.

He’d walked past this window for five years on his way to the ferry. A broken necklace on black velvet, every break mended in a thin line of gold. No price. No label. In the second week of June he went in.

“I’d like a ring made.”

“Of course you would.” She sat down on the other side of the glass counter and folded her hands. “You married her with a plain band from a shop on Harbour Road that isn’t mine.”

“Yes.”

“I saw the chain. At the wedding. Under her collar.”

“I know you did.”

“I’ve decided to forgive you.” She opened a drawer. “Go on, then.”

He told her. He’d had it in his head for a year. A star sapphire. Not large. The grey-blue kind, with the star that slides across it under a light. A narrow plain gold band. Nothing that could catch in a glove. Small enough for a surgeon’s hand.

“A star.”

“Yes.”

She waited for him to explain. He didn’t. He watched her work it out, the way Elara had at Old Bian’s, and the corner of her mouth went.

“Star and moon. Elara told Elowen what your name meant. Elowen told me. We both thought it was the most nauseating thing we’d ever heard.” She put a tray of stones in front of him. “Enzo will set it. He’s the best goldsmith in the city and he’ll make you wait three weeks.”

“I need it in one.”

Aurelia looked up from the tray.

“Then it’ll cost you double. For rushing a genius.”

She named a figure. He didn’t blink. He’d known she would, and he’d known she’d enjoy it. He took out his card.

“I won’t tell Elowen.” She ran the card. “Not because you asked. Because it’s the only time in ten years I’ll have known something about her family before she did, and I’m going to enjoy it for as long as it lasts.”

“Thank you.”

“And when you do it again, in front of everybody, I’m making the bands. Both of them. Don’t argue.”

He didn’t argue.

✦ ✦ ✦

He carried it for nine days.

A small box covered in grey silk, in the inside pocket of his jacket. On the ward. In his locker in theatre. In the car at night, picking her up from the ferry. He didn’t give it to her, because the day wasn’t right yet, and he knew which day was.

On the first of July she’d start as a surgical resident at City Hospital. Professor Liao’s team. Colorectal and general, on seven. Not his team. Not his unit. She’d applied knowing that. He’d sat on no panels and signed no papers. Liao had read her Harbourside reports. Her prize. Her logbook. He’d taken her in a week. Then he’d cornered Xing Yue in the lift, sucking a boiled sweet.

“I don’t want to hear one word from you about her, Wang. Not one. Good or bad.”

“You won’t.”

“I know I won’t. I’m telling you anyway.”

On the thirtieth of June she’d come off her last night at Harbourside. Her intern year would be over.

That was the day.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I want to see it when nobody’s there,” she’d said, a week before. “The old part of the hospital. The garden behind it. Two years I’ve been coming and going and I’ve never once been in, because I’ve always been running. I want to see it before it’s mine.”

“I’ll meet you.”

“You’re never off on a Sunday.”

“I’ll meet you.”

At five to seven on Sunday morning he stood at the garden gate behind the old block and watched her dot cross the bridge. Come up the harbour road. Turn up the hill. He put his phone away when the taxi turned into the lane.

It had rained in the night. Everything was grey and soft and dripping. Warm, the way late June always was. A camphor tree older than the hospital. A round fish pond under it, low stone edge, koi going round. Orange. White. Gold. Benches. Two floors of tall arched windows on the back of the old block, paint coming off the frames. The first-floor row looked straight down on the pond.

The taxi stopped. She got out.

Scrubs. A cardigan over them. Canvas bag on her shoulder. Hair falling out of its clip. Night-shift shadows under her eyes. She saw him at the gate and her whole face lit up.

“You CAME. You’re here at seven on a Sunday. You never—”

“I swapped.”

“You never swap!” She came through the gate and stopped dead. “Oh. Oh, it’s beautiful. Nobody TOLD me. Two years and nobody told me there was this. Look at the tree. Look at the FISH.”

She took one step and her trainer lace flicked out across the wet path.

“Your lace.”

“Leave it, it’s fine, I’ll—”

He was already down. He knelt on the wet path and tied it. Double knot. She stood there with her hand on his shoulder, laughing at him.

“You’re kneeling in a puddle to tie my shoe.”

“Yes.”

He stood up. She didn’t notice his knee was soaked through.

✦ ✦ ✦

She walked round the pond and talked.

Her last patient, an old woman who’d had her gallbladder out on Thursday and given her a knitted bookmark at four in the morning, with a crooked cat on it.

“It’s got three ears. I think it’s meant to have two. I love it more than anything I own.”

The whole year. The ferry, the floor, the porters, the third pudding. She’d miss it. Her voice went wobbly. Then tomorrow.

“I’m scared. Not of the work. Of Professor Liao.”

“Liao’s harmless.”

“Everyone SAYS he’s lovely! He eats sweets on the round. He can tell from how you hold a pen whether you’ll be any good.” She turned round. “What if I hold a pen wrong? What if I’ve been holding pens wrong my whole LIFE and nobody’s ever told me?”

“You don’t.”

“You don’t know that!”

“I’ve watched you hold a pen for two years.”

She knelt on the stone edge of the pond and looked down at the koi.

“Do koi sleep? I don’t think I’ve ever known. They can’t shut their eyes, can they? They haven’t got eyelids. So how do you even know? Maybe they’re all asleep now and just moving out of habit. That one, the big gold one, I think that one’s asleep, it’s—”

“Marry me again.”

“—it’s sort of drifting, look, by the stone, and they live for AGES, don’t they, I read somewhere they live longer than people, there was one in a pond somewhere that was two hundred—”

She stopped.

She turned her head and looked at him over her shoulder.

He was on one knee on the wet path behind her. The same knee. He hadn’t planned that. His glasses had fogged at the edges in the warm wet air and he could only see her through the middle of them, kneeling on the pond’s edge in her scrubs with her mouth open. He held out the grey silk box. Open.

“Sorry, what? Say it again. I was talking.”

“Marry me again. In front of everyone.”

“We’re ALREADY married!”

“In front of everyone.”

She stared at the ring. She stared at him.

“Yes,” she said. “Yes, but I was saying about the koi, there was one in a pond in—oh my God. OH MY GOD. Yes. I said yes in the middle of the fish. Wait. That doesn’t count, I want to say it properly, I want—”

He stood up and put his wet hand to the side of her throat, two fingers where her pulse was going like a bird’s. Then he stopped the rest of it with his mouth.

She made a sound that was half a laugh and half a sob. She grabbed his shirt. She stood up on the stone edge to reach him better and nearly went in. He held her. She kissed him back with both hands in his collar, the camphor tree dripping on them, the fish going round underneath.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she let go she said it again. Properly. Standing on the stone edge so her eyes were level with his, both hands flat on his chest.

“Yes. I’m saying it properly now. Yes.”

Then she cried. All at once. With her whole face.

She was still doing it when she pulled the chain out from her collar. She undid the clasp with shaking fingers and slid her plain gold band off it, and put it on her own finger. Then she held her hand out to him.

He put the star on above it. It fitted. Of course it fitted. He’d measured her finger with a piece of thread in April, while she was asleep.

She held her hand up to the grey light. Two rings. The plain one, and the star. When she turned it, six thin lines of light slid across the blue-grey stone.

“It’s a star.”

“Yes.”

“You put a star on me.” She laughed through it. “Star and moon. That’s SO embarrassing. That’s the most embarrassing thing anyone’s ever done. Did Aurelia make this? This is Aurelia’s, I can tell, look at the setting, that’s Enzo—”

“She charged me double.”

“Of course she did. Has she told Elowen?”

“She says she’s going to enjoy not telling her.”

Elara laughed so hard she had to sit down on the bench under the tree. He sat beside her, wet at the knee. She held her hand out in front of them both and turned it so the star moved. Over and over.

✦ ✦ ✦

“They come off for theatre.” She was frowning at them. “Both of them. Every day!”

“Yes.”

“Where do I put them? I’ll lose them. I lose everything. I’ll put them in a pocket and the pocket will go in the wash and some poor woman in the laundry will find a star sapphire in a pair of scrubs—”

“There’s a hook.”

She looked at him.

“In your locker. The residents’ changing room on seven. Third from the end on the left. There’s a small gold hook inside the door, at the top, where you’ll see it. For the rings.” He looked at the koi. “I asked the porters on Friday.”

She was quiet for one second. Friday? FRIDAY?

“On Friday. Before you’d asked me. You had a hook put in my LOCKER.”

“Yes.”

“What if I’d said no?”

He turned his head and looked at her.

“You didn’t.”

She hit him with her bag.

Quite hard, on the arm. Knitted bookmark, stethoscope, three phone chargers. He let her. She hit him again. Then she put the bag down and put her face in his shoulder and laughed until she was crying again.

She kept the hook.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went home and slept till three.

She fell asleep in the car before they were out of the lane, her left hand held up in front of her face, looking at it, sinking slowly into her lap. He carried her up the stairs. She woke on the landing.

“Did I say yes?”

“Twice. Once in the middle of a fish.”

“Good.”

She went back to sleep on his shoulder.

He woke at three to stripes of sun through the blinds. She was awake beside him, propped on one elbow, looking at her hand in the light. She saw him wake. She put her hand flat on his chest, rings and all, and looked at it there.

“I want to tell you something. Before anybody else gets to say anything about it.”

He waited.

“I love you. That’s all. I wanted to say it first today. Before Raiden makes a joke.”

He took her hand off his chest. He turned it over and kissed the inside of her wrist. Then her palm. Then the rings.

Then he sat up and took her face in both hands and just looked at her.

“What?” she whispered.

“Nothing.”

“You’re LOOKING.”

“Yes.”

She went pink from her collarbones up. He didn’t stop looking.

It was slow. The whole afternoon was slow. Nowhere to be. Nobody to ring. Nothing tomorrow that mattered as much as this. She lay back in the striped light and let him take his time, and for once she didn’t talk. Then she did. His name, and yes, over and over, like now she’d started she couldn’t stop. He kissed every bit of her he could reach. When she pulled him down, the rings on her hand were cool on the back of his neck. He felt them there the whole time.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay on her front with her chin on his chest and her hand beside her face.

“I’m going to be SO annoying about this.”

“I know.”

That evening she told the family chat. A photo of her hand on his knee, rings on it. No words. She sent it, put the phone face down on the cushion and put both hands over her face.

It buzzed. And buzzed. And didn’t stop.

She turned it over and read them to him one at a time.

Elowen: ELARA

Elowen: Why didn’t Aurelia tell me

Eliana: Spreadsheet updated.

Raiden: First try? Show-off.

Raiden: I needed thirty-one. Some of us had to work for it.

Evangeline: Good.

Then her phone buzzed once more. Not the chat. A number that never texted anyone.

Baba: Bring him on Sunday.

She read it twice.

“He comes every Sunday anyway. Baba KNOWS he comes every Sunday. Why’s he saying bring him?”

“Because he wanted to say something.”

She looked at him. She looked at the phone. Then she put her face in his shoulder and cried again, at another good thing.

chapters.title: The Seventh Guest
chapters.desc: Elara kneels by a river after midnight with her green bag while her husband waits in the car, then runs late up a lane in scrubs to her sister’s garden wedding. That night she says she doesn’t know who her own mother was.
chapters.epigraph: “Ev knows who her mother was now.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
“You hold your pen like a scalpel.”

Elara froze with the pen in mid-air. Second day on Professor Liao’s team. The whole round turned to look.

“Is that—bad?”

“It’s correct.” Liao held out a boiled sweet. “Lemon or ginger?”

So he could tell. Everyone had been right.

The rest of the autumn went past her in pieces. One Sunday in October the whole family drove up to Ev’s new house on Fig Tree Lane in three cars, the first time all of them had gone up the lane at once. Ev’s neighbours watched over the wall. In November Jinx opened her own shop three doors down from the garage near the Docks. Elara came straight from a night shift in her scrubs and stood at the back eating a pastry and crying, because it was a good thing. He wasn’t at either. On call for one. In theatre for the other.

“Tell me,” he said on the phone, both times.

She told him all of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first Saturday in December, late, her phone buzzed on the arm of the sofa.

Evangeline: The bridge at the border. Boat. About thirty people. Some hurt. Old. Cold. Police coming. Bring your bag.

She read it twice. Then she looked up. He was at the other end of the sofa with a journal and her feet in his lap. He’d looked up when the phone went. He’d seen her face change.

“Ev?”

“Ev.”

She held the phone up so he could see. Then she took it back and rang him. He was sitting a metre away. His phone went off in his pocket.

He looked at it. He looked at her.

“You said ring you first. I’m ringing you first.”

He answered.

“I’ll drive.” Into his phone, looking at her down the length of the sofa. “Get your bag.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The green bag lived in the hall cupboard now. She’d never given it back to Harbourside. She restocked it herself, a bit at a time, from places she didn’t think about too hard. He’d been through it. She knew he had. One night in October she’d packed it in a hurry with the scissors on top, and in the morning they were in the side pocket where they belonged. The out-of-date saline she’d been meaning to bin was gone. She’d never said a word about it. Nor had he.

In the hall he took her coat off the hook and held it out. She put her arms in. He zipped it up to her chin, all the way, like she was six.

“I can zip my own coat.”

“It’s cold at the river.”

“How do you know it’s cold at the river?”

“It’s December. It’s a river.”

She opened her mouth. Shut it. Went down the stairs with her chin buried in her collar.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nearly two hours north. The expressway, then the old road through the flat country. Fish ponds black on both sides. The border towns orange on the low cloud. She talked for the first hour about nothing, because she was frightened and didn’t know of what. Ev’s house. The fig tree, the stream, the green door with the menu taped inside it.

“And there’s a cat. It’s not hers. It just comes. She feeds it, which means it’s hers.”

She opened the glovebox for a tissue. Green tea biscuits. Three packets. The ones from the ferry shop.

“…When did these get here?”

“October.”

“I’ve been in this car fifty times since October!”

“You never open the glovebox.”

She ate one. She stopped talking. The second hour she held her bag on her knees and didn’t say anything at all.

There was a checkpoint before the bridge. Police cars across the road with their lights going. An ambulance. People in blankets being brought up a track from the river one at a time. He pulled onto the verge and turned the engine off.

“I’ll be here.”

“You can’t sit in the car all night.”

“I said I’d wait in the car.”

She looked at him. He’d said it on the floor of the hall in June. He was going to do exactly that. Nothing she said would get him out of the car and down that track, because she’d told him it wasn’t his, and he’d listened.

She leaned over and kissed him. Hard. Once. Then she got out with her bag and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

A tall policeman in a long coat stood by his car at the checkpoint, watching people in blankets come up from the jetty. Inspector Song. Nam’s kitchen table. A long look. He nodded at her as she came past. Like he’d expected her.

Then she saw his eyes go past her to the dark blue car on the verge. To the man sitting in it with his hands on the wheel. Wei Long lifted one hand off the roof of his car. In the car on the verge, Xing Yue lifted his off the wheel.

She stopped.

“You know him?”

“He’s Yu Chen’s cousin. The other side of the family. Yu Chen talks about him.” Wei Long looked at her. “The old ones are at the bottom of the track. One of them’s bad.”

She went down.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bad one was a woman called Auntie Lian. She’d been at the front of the deck. She was sitting on the track in a foil blanket with her lips blue and her breath coming short and her hand on her chest.

Elara knelt on the wet stones and opened the bag. She didn’t think. She never did, once she’d started. Warm. Cheerful. Clear.

“I’m Elara. I’m a doctor. What’s your name?”

“…Lian.”

“Auntie Lian. I’m going to listen to your chest. My hands are cold, sorry, sorry—”

“Cold,” the old woman agreed. “Very cold.”

“I know! Mine are worse than yours. We’ll warm each other up.”

She counted the breathing. She wrapped her in a second blanket under the first. She held the old woman’s cold hands in her own until they started to warm.

At the top of the track an old woman in a purple jacket, wrist still in the splint Elara had put on it in June, was directing police officers to her back room like they were her staff.

“You!” Old Nam had spotted her. “Doctor one! The old ones first!”

“I KNOW!” Somebody was crying further down. The river went past under the bridge, black and slow.

Then the next one, and the next. A man with a cut leg from the deck. A girl of about fifteen who wouldn’t let go of her own hands. A boy with his ankle up like a balloon. An old man who was only cold and frightened and wanted to tell her where he’d come from.

“Tell me, then. Go on. Where?”

He told her. A village. A river much smaller than this one. A brother.

“Is he here?”

“No.”

She wrapped him up and held his hand a minute longer than she had to.

At some point she looked up and saw Ev’s husband by Wei Long’s car, enormous in the checkpoint lights, handing something over. A long case. Wei Long looked at it. At him. Took it. What did that mean? She didn’t know. She knew it meant something. She went back to Auntie Lian.

✦ ✦ ✦

They drove home at four. She talked at first. The thirty. The boat. The cold. The girl with her hands. Auntie Lian, whose breathing had come back to normal by three, and who’d held Elara’s face in both hands and said something in a dialect Elara didn’t know. All in pieces. Too fast. Then she stopped. She sat beside him in the dark with the fish ponds going past and said nothing at all. He looked across at her. She knew he was looking. When had she ever been quiet in his car? Never. Not once. Not for more than a minute, in two years.

A long way further on, she spoke.

“Ev’s husband gave away his rifle. To Wei Long. At the bridge. I saw him.”

“Yes.”

“You saw too?”

“From the car.”

“I don’t know what that means.”

She reached over in the dark and took his left hand off the gearstick. She held it in both of hers in her lap. Then she lifted it and pressed her mouth into the middle of his palm, and held it there against her face with her eyes shut, for a long way down the old road. He drove one-handed all the way to the expressway, and didn’t ask for it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ev had her wedding two weeks later, on the longest night of the year, in the garden at Fig Tree Lane, with six guests, twenty months after a registry office in a border town that only Old Nam had seen. Elara was supposed to be the seventh.

She was on a twelve-hour night at City Hospital. She couldn’t swap. She’d begged. Nobody would. At four in the morning she sent the family a message from the doctors’ room.

Elara: On a twelve-hour. Two crash calls already. Will come when I can. Start without me. DON’T START WITHOUT ME.

Raiden: we will NOT start without you

Raiden: (we will)

She came off at eight, and then didn’t. A man she was handing over wouldn’t stop bleeding, and she stayed with him until he did. That was eleven. At noon she got a taxi on the card from the main doors, scrubs, lanyard still round her neck, and fell asleep in the back.

“Fig Tree Lane, Dr. Lin?”

She woke on the reservoir road with the hills going past.

“Stop here! Stop at the bottom, I’ll run, it’ll be quicker—”

It wasn’t quicker. Her hair came out of its clip halfway up. She was shouting before she reached the gate.

“I said don’t start without me!”

She came in through the green door at a quarter to two. They were all at the long dark table in the front room with the windows open, eating long noodles nobody was allowed to cut. A viola case on the window seat. White silk round the neck of a jar on the table. Everyone looked up at her in the doorway. Her sister was at the head of the table, in white. White, with a bent silver pin in her hair. And laughing. Not the little movement at the corner of her mouth that was all Elara had ever seen. Laughing out loud, at something Jinx had said. Head back. Whole face. In front of everyone.

Elara burst into tears.

“Seventh guest!” Raiden pulled out a chair.

“You STARTED.”

Elowen didn’t even look guilty. “We waited till one.”

“One isn’t waiting, one is LUNCH—”

“Sit down.” That was Jinx. “Eat. She’s been laughing for an hour. You missed the start of it.”

“Don’t tell me that!”

Ev looked down the table at her, still smiling.

“Sit.”

Elara sat.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got home at seven with a jar of salted lemons Ev had pushed into her hands at the green door, a container of noodles from Ah Sim, and her eyes swollen shut. He was home. A whole weekend off, the first in months. He took the jar and the noodles and put them on the counter. She sat on the stool and told him.

“There was frost on the garden. She carried herbs. From her own glasshouse. Not flowers! Tied with white silk. And the neighbours sat on two chairs over the wall with a ginger cat between them, like a FRONT ROW—”

“And the viola?”

“Her mother’s.” She was turning the jar of lemons round on the counter. Round and round. “Ev’s real mother. She played the viola.”

“Ev found out?”

“This year. A man who knew her told Ev she talks just like her. And she had it sent, and she’s LEARNING. And the pin in her hair. That was her mother’s too.”

Round and round.

“Ev knows who her mother was now.”

He waited.

“I don’t know who mine was.”

She heard herself say it. She’d never said it. Not to Baba. Not to her sisters. Not even out loud in an empty room.

“I don’t even know her name.”

“Elara—”

“I don’t know what she looked like. If she was alive when they took me to the children’s home. If she gave me away. If somebody took me.” The jar stopped. “What if she talked? What if I talk because SHE did? That’s so stupid. That’s the stupidest—”

He came round the counter and took the jar off her before she dropped it.

“I never wanted to know. I always thought, I’ve got the Lins. I’ve got Baba. That’s enough. It’s greedy to want another one.” Her eyes filled again. “And then I watched Ev laugh at her own wedding with her mother’s pin in her hair, and I wanted it so much I couldn’t breathe.”

“What do you know?”

“Nothing! That’s what I’m SAYING. Baba brought me home from a children’s home when I was three. That’s it. That’s all there’s ever been.”

He didn’t say anything to that. He put his arms round her on the stool, and she put her face in his shirt and cried. For Ev. For herself. For a woman she couldn’t picture. Until she was hiccupping.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine she said she was going to sleep for a week. Thirty-six hours awake. A night shift, a bleeding man, a taxi, a lane, a wedding, and crying for most of the day. She lay down on the long grey sofa with her head in his lap. He pulled the blanket off the back and put it over her side, tucked it under her feet.

He was stroking her hair. He’d been doing it since she lay down. His hand stopped.

“Please.”

She opened her eyes.

He never said please. Maybe once in two years, to a porter, under extreme circumstances. He was looking down at her in the lamplight, glasses on, serious, and he didn’t say anything else. He’d sat beside her all evening while she cried for something he couldn’t give her.

She gave in at once. She hadn’t been going to hold out anyway. She sat up. She took his glasses off and put them on the arm of the sofa. Then she kissed him.

Slow. Sleepy. Warm. They didn’t get as far as the stairs. They didn’t try. She was so tired she was clumsy, and she laughed at herself, and he didn’t laugh. He just held on to her. Like she was the thing he’d asked for, and he wasn’t wasting a second of it. His hands slow on her back under the scrubs top she’d never changed out of. His mouth slow at her throat.

“I’m too tired to be any good,” she mumbled.

“Then don’t be.”

She pulled him down onto the cushions and wound herself round him. Everything soft and heavy and close. The lamp low. The frangipani tapping at the study window. His breath on her neck and his name in her mouth. She felt like she was being held together. She let him do it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay on top of him under the blanket, ear on his chest. Not sleepy at all.

“I want ours outdoors.”

His hand moved on her back.

“The garden one. When we do it in front of everyone.”

“Outdoors.”

“Ev’s was in a garden, in the frost. It was the best one I’ve ever been to. Elowen’s was beautiful too. But I want ours outside. Early. When the light’s coming. Somewhere with trees.” A pause. “Somewhere nobody’s ever bled.”

“All right.”

“You’re not allowed to organise it.”

“All right.”

“You are, a bit,” she said, and fell asleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning she came downstairs at seven. He was at the counter already, dressed, with a cup of tea and his prescription pad. Writing something. When she came in he tore the sheet off, folded it, and put it in his shirt pocket.

“Patient?” She yawned.

“Something I need to look up.”

“On a Sunday?”

“It’ll keep.”

He made her tea. She sat on the stool in his T-shirt eating a slice of Ev’s salted lemon with honey.

“Eggs?”

“I hate eggs.”

“Pancakes.”

“Spring onion ones. With the hot sauce.”

He made them. She didn’t think about the sheet of paper again. Why would she? It was a year before she saw it, in an envelope.

Her birthday. Children’s home? And under it, underlined twice, in handwriting only she could read:

Find her.

chapters.title: A Name in a Ledger
chapters.desc: He finds the old matron of the children’s home and the birth name his wife has never heard. He decides to keep it for their garden day, and she catches him hiding something.
chapters.epigraph: “They called her the bell girl. She never stopped.” — Matron Sima
chapters.content:
A birthday. The words children’s home. The age of three. That was what he had. That, and a tall house behind a red door, and a man who had his postman checked every New Year. He kept the sheet from the prescription pad in his wallet behind his driving licence. On nights when she was on call and he wasn’t, he sat at the kitchen counter with his laptop and looked.

He rang the children’s homes that were still open, from his office between clinics. The women who answered were kind.

“I’m sorry, doctor. Records of a child placed with a family are closed. To anyone but the child.”

“I understand.”

“Is it for a patient?”

“No.”

The ones that had shut had sent their files to the welfare archive behind the courts. He went on a Saturday in January. A grey building. An index card for Plum Steps Children’s Home, closed 2011. Boxes of files he wasn’t allowed to open.

What he found, in the end, was a newspaper. A short piece from the week the home closed. A small woman in a cardigan at an iron gate with a bag of keys, looking at the camera like she didn’t think much of it. Matron Sima Huijun, who has run Plum Steps for thirty-one years. He found her through the church on the steps below the old home, where she still did the flowers. It took three weeks for her to agree to see him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took a Friday off in March. He never took Fridays off.

“Dentist,” he told Elara.

“Open.”

“What?”

“Open your mouth.”

She looked at his teeth. All of them. With a torch.

“…Very clean.”

“Thank you.”

Fourth floor. No lift. Two rooms that smelled of camphor and cooking oil. Her husband’s photograph on the wall in a black frame, a dish of oranges in front of it. She was eighty-one and tiny. She made him take his shoes off and sit on a stool too low for him. She poured his tea and not hers.

“You’re a doctor.”

“A surgeon. City Hospital.”
