“And you want a child.”

“I want to know about one. She doesn’t know I’m here.” He put the cup down. “She came to you in October 2002. Nearly three. She went to a family in November. Her birthday’s the second of November.”

“Lots of children.”

“She talks.”

Matron Sima looked at him with small hard eyes.

“Why should I tell you anything?”

He had a story ready. He didn’t use it.

“She told me she doesn’t know who her mother was.”

“Plenty don’t.”

“She’s never said it to anyone else. She said she wanted it so much she couldn’t breathe.” He kept his hands flat on his knees. “I’m her husband. I’m going to marry her again, in front of everyone. I’d like to be able to give it to her.”

The old woman didn’t answer.

She got up. She went into the other room. A cupboard opened. A lot of things got moved. Something heavy went down. She came back with a ledger bound in red cloth, the corners worn through, and put it on the table between them. She sat. She didn’t open it.

“The bell girl.”

He waited.

“That’s what we called her. The girls in the kitchen named her. She talked from the minute she woke up to the minute she went to sleep.”

“She still does.”

“In her sleep too?”

“Yes.”

“Followed you round all day like a bell on a cat. You always knew where she was!” Something like a smile went over the old face. “She asked the boy fixing the roof if his ladder had a name.”

“Did it?”

“She gave it one.” The smile went. “She never cried. All those weeks. The other ones from fires cried at night, or wouldn’t eat. That one talked. She sat on the end of my bed and told me about the boats.”

“Boats.”

“Her father’s boats. The little ones that go out to the ships.”

She opened the ledger.

✦ ✦ ✦

He read it upside down at first. Then she turned it round for him. Every child who’d come through the iron gate in thirty-one years. The same small upright hand, in blue ink.

“The official files went to the archive. The government can keep them. This one’s mine. I wrote in it every night.”

October 2002. A line near the bottom of the page.

Qu Xiaoyue. Little moon. Born 2 Nov 1999. Brought by police, 12 Oct, from the fire at Qu Lighterage, Walled City piers. Found in a laundry basket under wet towels. Father Qu Mingde, lighterage, deceased. Mother Shi Yuning, nurse, deceased. No relatives found.

Under it, same hand, different ink. 16 Nov. Gone to a family. Papers came back with another name. He read it three times.

“The papers came back with another name. So I wrote the first one down.” She tapped the line. “I always did. If somebody’s going to take a child’s name away, somebody should keep it.”

“Who took her?”

“A man came in a black car. He paid for the roof.”

“The roof.”

“Six years it leaked! The government never paid. He paid for all of it. Cash. And the next week he came back for her.” Her mouth shut tight on whatever else she knew. “I don’t know his name. I never asked. You didn’t, then.”

“No.”

“She went down the steps holding his hand and talking. He didn’t say a word. He looked like he’d been hit.”

He didn’t say anything.

“Can I photograph the page?”

“No.”

“Can I copy it out?”

She looked at him a long time. Then she fetched a pencil and a sheet of paper from a drawer. He copied it at her table on the low stool. Every word. In square block capitals, so anybody could read it.

At the door she held on to his sleeve.

“Does she still talk?”

“All the time.”

The old woman nodded and let him go.

✦ ✦ ✦

The clipping turned up that afternoon in the newspaper room at the central library, on a machine with a screen that flickered. Saturday, 12 October 2002. Page nine.

Fire at Walled City lighter office kills two.

Four short paragraphs. A small lighterage company by the old piers, and the flat above it. The owner and his wife found dead by firemen. The boats undamaged. Police suspected the fire was set. No one charged. No child in it. Nobody had told the paper about a basket. No other names. Nothing pointing anywhere at all.

He paid the man at the desk for a printout and sat in his car outside the library with it on the passenger seat, beside the pencilled page. He didn’t start the engine. Her mother had been a nurse. Her father ran boats out to the ships. Somebody had put a child in a laundry basket under wet towels while the building burned. It had worked. Six weeks later somebody looked at a girl called little moon and named her Elara, because Elara was a moon too. So she’d keep a piece of it without knowing.

My mother chose it, she’d told him, at Old Bian’s, delighted. My father says she liked the sound.

He put the papers in a brown envelope in the glovebox. Next to her hair clip. He’d give it to her on their garden day. In the morning. Before anybody else was up. Her mother’s name in her hands on the day she married him again, and nobody else’s voice in the room when she read it.

Did he have the right to choose the day? He didn’t ask himself. Not then.

✦ ✦ ✦

That week they set the date. On the Wednesday she came in from a long day on Liao’s list, sat at the counter with a bowl of his noodles, and announced it.

“The hospital garden.”

“The hospital garden.”

“Where you asked me. Under the tree. By the fish. It’s the only place I can think of that’s outdoors and has trees and where nobody’s ever bled. I checked! I asked Sister Shao.”

“What did she say?”

“Thirty years, and nobody’s ever bled in the garden. Except a porter who fell off a bench. And that was his nose, and it doesn’t count.”

“You’ll have the windows full of patients.”

“Good. They can wave.”

He reached over and took a mouthful of noodles off her fork while she was talking. She stared at the empty fork.

“THIEF.”

“They’re my noodles.”

“They’re my FORK!”

She wanted May, after her first surgical exams, because she’d cry at both and couldn’t be expected to cry that much in one month. She held her phone up across the counter and scrolled. He watched her finger go through the rest of 2025 and into 2026 and stop.

“The ninth of May. A Saturday. Next year. That’s fourteen months. Is fourteen months too long?”

He thought of the envelope in the glovebox.

“No. It’s good.”

She put it in her calendar. Then in his, by taking his phone out of his pocket while he ate. She typed GARDEN WEDDING in capitals. Under it: DON’T BOOK ANY LISTS.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the second week of March he came out of theatre between cases and heard her before he saw her. She was in the corridor outside the women’s changing room in scrubs and a paper hat, phone to her ear, laughing.

“Raiden, you’re being an idiot. You’re being an idiot with great conviction, and I’m proud of you. But a KING signed it. You can’t win against a king! I’ve got a gallbladder, I’m going back in—”

She saw him and waved her coffee at him.

He kept walking. It was about Evangeline’s birthday. He knew that much. He didn’t ask what a king had to do with it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The driver came in on a Thursday night at the end of March. Xing Yue was the consultant on call. He’d been down to resus for an old man with a twisted bowel and was writing up the notes at the station when he saw her across the department. Cubicle eleven. Curtain half open. She was the surgical resident on call, sent down to see a hand.

He knew the man. Not his name. His face. A face you’d seen at the bottom of a hill road at four in the morning. One of Zhao’s drivers. A thick quiet man who’d brought the car down from the house to the bus shelter some mornings and looked at nothing. He was on the trolley now with his left hand on a pillow in a towel that had been white. His face was the same colour as the towel.

A police constable stood at the curtain. Young. Notebook. Elara was talking to him. The way she talked to everybody. Warm. Cheerful. A boiled sweet in her cheek. She unwrapped the towel and looked at the hand.

For one second there was nothing on her face at all. Nothing warm. Nothing cheerful. A cold, clear, flat attention. The wound. The man’s face. The constable’s notebook. Back.

Then it was gone. She said something to the constable that made him laugh. She closed it at the trolley. Fast. She talked the constable through every bit of it, tendons, luck, a man she’d once seen fire a nail through his own boot.

“Through his BOOT! Can you imagine? He wanted to keep the boot!”

The constable had stopped writing. Xing Yue signed off the old man’s notes and went up to theatre. In the morning, before the round, he read hers.

Nail-gun injury, building site. Through and through, left hand, between second and third metacarpals. Tendons intact. Washed out and closed. PC present at assessment. Patient declined to give a statement.

He wrote under it, as consultant on call: Seen and agreed. He signed it.

At the round Dr. Zou leaned over his shoulder at the screen.

“Funny kind of nail gun. That’s a big hole for a nail.”

Xing Yue didn’t look up.

“Did you see him?”

“No, I was—”

“Then you don’t know what size the hole was. Bed four’s drain chart has nothing on it since midnight. Go and find out why. When you’ve found out, find out why you didn’t know at six.”

Dr. Zou went. The nurse with the drug trolley looked at the floor.

That night Elara was asleep on the sofa when he came in, one foot hanging off the edge. He stood and looked at her for a while. He thought about her face in cubicle eleven. Did he want her any different? Not one bit.

✦ ✦ ✦

She caught him on the first Sunday in April. He’d never been good at hiding things. The Friday at the “dentist”. The Saturdays. He cleaned his glasses every time she asked where he’d been, and she’d started asking just to watch him do it.

That evening she sat on the sofa beside him. Then on the arm of it. Then she took the journal out of his hands, dropped it on the floor, and climbed on him.

“You’re hiding something.”

She sat across his lap with her hands on his shoulders and looked down at him like a chart she didn’t trust.

“Since Christmas. Saturdays. A Friday off. An envelope in the car next to my hair clip, which I’ve known about for TWO YEARS, by the way—”

He reached for his glasses. She got there first. She took them off his face and held them up out of reach.

“No. No cleaning. So. One. Is it bad?”

“It’s not bad.”

“Two. Is it about the hospital? Three—”

“Elara.”

“Three is the important one. Three is, is it about ME? Because if it’s about me—”

He put his hand flat on her back, between her shoulder blades, under her jumper. He pulled her down and stopped her mouth with his.

She made a noise of pure outrage against his lips. She kept hold of his glasses. She kept kissing him too. One hand on his shoulder, his glasses in the other, kissing him back hard. Like she was still arguing and had found a better way to do it.

When she pulled back she was pink to the ears.

“That’s cheating. That’s what you do. You do that to stop me talking.”

“It works.”

“It works because I LET it.” She sat back on his knees. “Is it about me?”

“It’s a wedding present.”

She went still on his lap.

“You can have it on the day. In the garden. In the morning, before anybody else is up.”

He watched her want it. She opened birthday presents on the bus home. She’d once read the end of a crime novel in a bookshop and put it back on the shelf. Then he watched her get annoyed. Properly. That was harder.

“You’ve decided. You’ve decided when I get to know something.”

He didn’t answer.

“It’s mine, isn’t it? Whatever it is. It’s mine, and you’ve got it, and you’ve picked a day for me to have it.”

He had no good answer. He didn’t want to give her a bad one.

“I hate that.”

“I know.”

She sat on him frowning, his glasses in her hand. Then she folded them and put them on the table, the way he did. She took his face in both hands.

“Fine. Keep it. But it had better be GOOD.”

“It is.”

“Better than the loupes. The loupes were the best present anyone’s ever given me, so you’ve made it really hard for yourself!” She kissed his forehead. “And I’m writing down that I hate it. So that on the day, when I cry, you’ll remember I was cross first.”

She got up and wrote it on the fridge list. Under peach yoghurt. Above sesame paste. XY’S SECRET — CROSS ABOUT IT.

Then she came back and sat in his lap and kissed him until he’d forgotten the envelope was anywhere at all. It stayed on the fridge for months. He read it every morning while the tea brewed.

chapters.title: Again?
chapters.desc: At five in the morning her brother and his wife come in from a fire with burned hands. For six weeks she spends her days off fixing switches in the rebuilt shop, humming, and her husband catches her on a ladder.
chapters.epigraph: “You’ve got good hands. Steady. I’d hire you.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
“Dr. Lin? It’s the ED. Your brother’s down here.”

Elara had the biscuit halfway to her mouth. First time she’d sat down since midnight. Nights, covering the surgical floors. She’d been saving that biscuit for three hours.

“Raiden?”

“And his wife. Smoke, and burns. They’re both all right.” The nurse had known her since she was a student. She knew whose sister she was. “I thought you’d want to know before somebody else told you.”

Elara put the biscuit down.

She didn’t remember the stairs. She remembered the doors at the bottom. The corridor. Two trolleys side by side in the end bay with the curtain pulled back. Raiden on one, oxygen mask on his face, both hands wrapped in white and held up on his chest like two clouds. Jinx on the other, mask too, a dressing on her left forearm, black still in her hair and in the lines round her eyes. Staring at the ceiling. Raiden’s head was turned towards her. Jinx’s hand was on his wrist, above the bandage. Four years ago he’d been on the sixth floor of this building after a van.

“Again?”

It went right up the corridor. A porter looked round. Raiden turned his head and looked at her over the mask. His eyes creased. Idiot was grinning.

✦ ✦ ✦

She checked everything. She couldn’t not. She read their notes. She lifted the edge of Raiden’s dressings and looked at his palms and put them back. She didn’t say anything about the blisters, because he was watching her face, so she kept it nice. She listened to both their chests.

“What were his sats when he came in?”

The nurse told her.

“And now?”

The nurse told her.

“Sorry. And now?”

“Same as I just said, Dr. Lin.”

“Right. Yes. Good.”

“The shutter,” Raiden said through the mask, muffled. “I put my hands on it. I didn’t know where she was.”

“You put your HANDS on a HOT SHUTTER?”

“I didn’t know where she was.”

She had nothing to say to that. She did Jinx.

Jinx let her. She lay there and let Elara turn her arm over and look at the burn on the inside of it, right across the edge of a tattooed carp. She didn’t say a word. Elara had worked out that this was how Jinx said thank you. “You’ll want silicone gel on that. When it’s healed over. Not before. It stops it going thick and red.” Elara frowned at the arm. “I told you that at Elowen’s wedding about your exhaust burns, and you didn’t do it, I can SEE you didn’t do it, they’re still there—”

“You told me.”

“Well, I’m telling you again. And this time you’ll do it, because it’s on the same arm as the fish, and you want the fish to stay a nice shape.”

Jinx looked at her. One corner of her mouth went up. Nearly.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six her husband came in for his day. He walked to work every morning. Main doors, not the ambulance bay. He had no reason in the world to come through the ED. He came through it. She was against the wall outside the bay. He came down the corridor in his coat, bag on his shoulder, two teas from the bakery. He stopped beside her and held one out.

She took it in both hands. Just held it. He didn’t ask if they were all right. He’d have read the board on the way past. He stood next to her against the wall with his own tea and looked at the trolleys. His shoulder was against hers. After a while she leaned her head on his arm.

“His hands. He draws with his hands. That’s all he does.”

“Second degree. Partial thickness. I looked.”

“You LOOKED? On your way PAST?”

“They’ll heal.”

“I KNOW they’ll heal. I know that. I’m a doctor.” Her voice went up. “It’s just—it’s the second time. The second time I’ve come down a corridor in this building and found him on a trolley.”

He put his hand on the back of her neck, under her hair. He left it there. In the corridor. In front of the whole department.

“Drink the tea.”

“I’m not—”

“Then eat something. Then go back up. You’ve got two hours left and somebody on nine is going to need you. You’re no use to them on one biscuit.”

“I didn’t even EAT the biscuit.”

“Then two hours on no biscuit.”

She wanted to argue. She drank the tea instead. He’d put sugar in it. He never put sugar in anything.

Behind the curtain she heard Raiden on the phone to Elowen, muffled through the mask.

“—no, she’s here, Elara’s here. Is on nights. She’ll come on her days off. She’s very good at small things.”

“I’m not very good at small things,” Elara muttered into her tea.

“You are.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They rebuilt the shop in six weeks. She came on her days off. She’d told Elowen she would and then lay awake wondering what use she’d be. Men with scaffolding. Aurelia’s glazier. Eliana on the floor with a laptop and a nest of wires. Jun Hyuk carrying steel and talking.

On the first day she found out. Nobody wanted the small jobs. Switch plates. Light fittings. Little brackets for the shelves. Hooks for the tools. The hundred fiddly things that went back on the walls once the paint was dry.

She did them all. She liked it. Who knew? Stepladder, screwdriver in her teeth, a bag of fixings in her pocket. One bracket after another. Her hands knew what to do the way they did with a suture. Small and quick and exact. She hummed. She didn’t know she was doing it.

On the second Saturday Jinx came and stood at the bottom of the ladder. She’d been on the floor all morning under a broken machine. Overalls. Black on her hands. Bandaged arm. She watched Elara do a bracket. Then another. She said nothing. Elara had stopped expecting her to. They’d been sisters-in-law since a flower shop and spoken maybe forty sentences, most of them about burns.

“You’ve got good hands. Steady. I’d hire you.”

Elara stopped with the screwdriver in the air.

“I’m a surgeon.”

“I know. I’d still hire you.” Jinx looked up at the bracket. “That’s level. Nobody does them level. Eliana’s are all a degree off and she says it’s the wall.”

“It’s not the wall.”

“No.”

That was the first real conversation. It went on, off and on, all afternoon. Jinx told her what the brackets were for. Elara told her about bananas.

“BANANAS?”

“For suturing. They’re the closest thing to skin for the price.”

Jinx thought about that.

“Do they complain?”

“Bananas? No.”

“Better than people.”

“I stitched my own hand once.”

“You WHAT?”

“Nineteen. Under the flyover. Fishing line.”

Elara came down the ladder to look at the scar and was so appalled that Jinx laughed out loud. The short rough laugh Elara had only ever heard her give Raiden.

“Does your husband know you’re up ladders all day?”

“My husband doesn’t get a vote.” Elara had all the dignity of a woman on a ladder.

“Your husband’s going to find out.”

“He finds out everything. He doesn’t get a vote on that either.”

They ate noodles sitting on a crate. Jinx said nothing else nice all day. It was plenty.

✦ ✦ ✦

One Thursday in July Baba came. The black car. Uncle Mok. His good coat. He stood in the middle of the shop floor and looked at the walls going white and the new window going in. Jinx’s father was there. He was there every week. An old man with a broom, sleeves rolled up, sweeping round the benches. Baba watched him for a while. Then he took off his coat. He folded it over the back of a chair. He took the other broom from against the wall and started sweeping on the far side.

Elara was on the mezzanine stairs with a box of switch plates. She stopped dead. Two old men swept that floor for two hours. They didn’t talk. They didn’t look at each other. Long slow lines, one on each side, passing in the middle and going on. The dust ended up in two neat piles by the door. Somewhere up on the mezzanine, she knew, Jinx was watching too.

“Elara?” Eliana’s voice, from under the wires. “Where are you going?”

“Air. I need some AIR.”

Elara put the box down on the step and went out to the street.

She stood on the cobbles with her back to the shop and her hands over her face. What had happened between those two men? Years ago. Under a flyover. She didn’t know. Something had. And her father had taken off his coat.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the tenth of July, Yu Chen and Eliana graduated on the same afternoon in the Great Hall, in two different gowns. Xing Yue sat with her near the front in his dark grey suit, back straight. He was Yu Chen’s mentor. Had been for four years. He’d been asked to come. When Yu Chen went up, Xing Yue clapped exactly as hard as everyone else. Elara looked at him sideways. His jaw was tight.

“You’re proud,” she whispered.

“I’m clapping.”

“You’re PROUD.”

“Elara.”

Afterwards, on the steps, Eliana kissed Yu Chen in front of everyone. Everyone saw it. Elara burst into tears, then went and hugged her little sister so hard her cap fell off and rolled down two steps.

“Okay. Okay. You can stop now.” Eliana stood there stiffly with her arms out. “Elara. You can STOP.”

Yu Chen came over with his ears red and shook his cousin’s hand.

“Emergency. You’ll be good at it. You don’t panic and you don’t like being thanked.”

Yu Chen looked at him like he’d been handed something heavy and didn’t know where to put it down.

“…Thank you.”

“That’s what I mean.”

On the way down the steps Elara put her arm through her husband’s and didn’t say a single thing about his jaw.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ladder was on a Tuesday afternoon in the last week of the rebuild. She was off. He’d had a clinic in the morning and nothing after, which happened about twice a year, and he came down to the shop. He wanted, he said, to see what she’d been doing with her days off for a month.

She was at the top of the tall ladder by the back wall, putting up the last of the tool hooks. Hair tied up in one of Jinx’s scarves. Screwdriver in her hand. The ladder went still under her. She looked down. He was at the bottom in his work shirt with the sleeves rolled up, one hand on the ladder and the other round her ankle.

“Let go. I’m FINE. I’ve done about two hundred of these.”

“You’re humming.”

“I always hum!”

“You’re humming and leaning out to the left. And the left foot of the ladder’s on a drain cover.”

She looked. It was.

She went red and finished the hook anyway. He didn’t let go of her ankle the whole time. His hand warm round it above her trainer. His thumb on the bone. She felt it all the way up.

When she came down he didn’t move out of the way. Rung by rung until she was nearly level with him. On the rung above the bottom she caught the back of her thumb on the edge of the last bracket and said a word Ah Sim would have washed out of her mouth. He took her hand. He turned it over and held it up to the light from the new window. A cut in clinic. A thin red line across the back of her thumb. He looked at it closely, frowning.

“Bracket?”

“Bracket.”

“Clean?”

“It’s a NEW bracket, Xing Yue.”

“It’s NOTHING. It’s a scratch. Don’t you dare put a plaster on it, I’ll never hear the end of it from Jinx—”

He kissed it. The back of her thumb. Then, before she’d finished telling him it was nothing, her mouth.

She came off the last rung into his arms. The screwdriver hit the floor. She got her arms round his neck and kissed him back in the middle of the half-built shop, sawdust in the air, new paint. He held her up against him with her feet off the floor. She laughed into his mouth and didn’t stop kissing him to do it.

Somebody coughed. Raiden, in the arched doorway, with a tray of coffees in his healing hands and a face of enormous innocence.

“I’ll come back. In about ten minutes. Or tomorrow.” He started backing away. “Jinx says the hooks are level!”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she had plaster dust in her hair. In her eyebrows. Down the back of her neck. She sat on the bathroom counter in her vest while the shower ran hot and picked dust out of her own fringe and talked. Switch plates. Jinx’s fishing line. Two old men with brooms.

He stood in the doorway with his arms folded. Clean shirt. Being sensible. At the end of a day when he’d held her ankle on a ladder and she’d felt it all afternoon.

She hooked two fingers into his belt and pulled him in between her knees.

“You’ve got dust on you. From me. On your shirt. And in your eyebrows. Both of them.”

“I haven’t.”

“You have! Look.”

She turned him by the belt to face the mirror. A grey streak through one eyebrow, from where her hands had been in his hair at the shop. She laughed so hard she nearly fell off the counter. He caught her. She was still laughing when she started on his buttons.

It was mostly laughing after that. The dust wouldn’t come out of her hair, so she made him wash it under the shower, standing behind her. He got shampoo in her eyes. She swore at him. He laughed against her shoulder. She soaped his face with enormous care, like she was cleaning a wound.

“Keep still.”

He didn’t.

They knocked the shampoo off the shelf. The water ran grey, then clear. He kissed her with it running down both their faces, and for a while she stopped laughing.

Later, in bed, she lay across him with her wet hair all over his chest.

“You held my ankle ALL AFTERNOON.”

“Ten minutes.”

“It felt like all afternoon.” She lifted her head. “Don’t do that on a ladder again. I couldn’t think. I nearly put a hook in upside down.”

He reached down under the sheet and put his hand round her ankle. Same one. Thumb on the bone. She put her face back on his chest and gave up.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Friday before they reopened, she put up the last bracket. A small brass one by the new stair door, for a fire blanket. Jinx had saved it for her. Everyone else had gone. Eliana’s cameras blinked in the corners of the ceiling. Raiden was upstairs at his desk behind the new glass, his hands unwrapped at last, drawing.

Elara stood on the low step and put in the screws. One. Two. Three. Four. She tested it with her hand. It didn’t move. She turned round. Her father was at the bottom of the step. She hadn’t heard him come in. Good coat. He was looking at her hands.

“You have your mother’s hands.”

Elara laughed. She came down off the step and put the screwdriver in her pocket.

“Mama’s? Ah Sim always says Mama couldn’t sew a button! She says Mama burned rice. She says she was the worst cook in the Walled City and you married her anyway.”

Baba didn’t say anything. He was still looking at her hands. His face had gone the grey it went sometimes when somebody brought up the old days at the table.

“She did burn rice.”

That was all. He put his hand on her shoulder, heavy and brief, which he almost never did. Then he went out to the black car where Mok was waiting.

She watched him go. He looked tired. She’d tell Elowen he looked tired.

“What did he say to you?” Jinx was leaning over the mezzanine rail.

“Mama burned rice.”

“…Okay.”

“COFFEE!” Jinx yelled down from the mezzanine.

She forgot.

chapters.title: The Knife at the Red Door
chapters.desc: After Sunday lunch a man in a seaman’s jacket comes for her father with a knife. Elara gets in the way, and her husband keeps her alive on the stones of the alley, then stands in the corner of theatre with empty hands.
chapters.epigraph: “Stop diagnosing yourself. I know what’s cut.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
Sunday lunch was soup.

The pork bone one with lotus root that took Ah Sim two days. It was November, the first cold week, and Elara had turned twenty-six a fortnight ago, and Ah Sim still thought she was too thin.

“Eat.”

“I’m eating!”

“Eat MORE.”

Seven at the long table. Elowen and Zhao had come for the soup and gone again by two. Raiden and Jinx were at one end arguing about a carburettor. Evangeline sat beside Jun Hyuk, who was explaining lotus root to Lin Jian. Lin Jian had been eating lotus root his whole life.

“—it’s the holes, you see, the holes are for air, it grows in mud, it has to breathe somehow—”

“Yes.” Lin Jian went on eating.

Elara talked about the garden. Six months away. She had a dress now. Nobody was allowed to see it.

“Not even you.” She pointed her spoon at Xing Yue. “Especially not you. You’d measure it.”

“I’d—”

“You’d MEASURE it.”

He would have. He let it go.

“I asked Sister Shao if the koi would mind. She said the koi have seen worse. And his grandmother’s coming from the north. With a stick. She points it at people.”

“I’d like to see her try it on Baba!” Raiden was delighted.

Lin Jian laughed. The big rusty one, straight into his soup. Xing Yue watched his wife laugh at her father laughing, and put another piece of pork in her bowl while she wasn’t looking.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three everyone got their coats.

“We’ll get a taxi.”

“No.” Lin Jian was already at the hook by the stairs for his good coat. “Mok has the car at the bottom. I’ll walk you down.”

Ah Sim pushed a box into Xing Yue’s hands. Leftover soup. Three dumplings on top.

“Make her eat them.”

“I will.”

“You say that. Make her.”

Elara was on the step buttoning her coat with one hand, talking with the other. She missed the top button. She always missed the top button. He reached over and did it up for her.

“I CAN do my own—”

“You can’t.”

She made a face at him.

“Bye, Ah Sim! I’ll eat them, I PROMISE—”

Lin Jian opened the red door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Grey alley. Cold. The light already going. The noodle stall at the mouth had its shutters half down. Beyond it, the black car at the kerb, Mok at the wheel. A man was standing by the stall.

Xing Yue noticed him because there was nobody else. Sixty, about. Thin. Weathered. An old navy jacket with a high collar, the kind men wore on deck. Hands in his pockets. Looking at the red door. When it opened, he took his hands out.

“Lin Jian. Do you remember the Qu boats?”

Lin Jian stopped on the step. His face went grey. All at once. The way a patient’s did when the pressure went. And something in Xing Yue’s head caught on the name. Like a foot on a step in the dark.

Qu. Then there was a knife, and the man was coming up the alley.

He didn’t run. He walked fast, straight at the old man on the step, knife held low. His face was calm. And Lin Jian didn’t move. He stood in his own doorway in his good coat and watched him come and didn’t lift a hand. Like he’d been waiting twenty years for this and had decided long ago that he wouldn’t.

Elara was closest. On the step below her father. She didn’t think. He saw her not think. She put up her right arm and grabbed at the man’s wrist. Like putting a hand out for something falling.

The blade went across the inside of her wrist.

✦ ✦ ✦

He dropped the box. He heard it hit the stones and the soup go everywhere, and he was already there. His hands were round her forearm before she’d started to fall. Both hands. Hard. The blood came through his fingers anyway. Bright. Too bright. In spurts that went with her heartbeat.

He knew exactly what that meant. He put it away.

“Lie down. Elara, lie back for me. Keep it up.”

He got her down on the stones with her back against the step and her arm straight up over her head, his hands locked round it above the wrist. She was looking at it. At her own hand. With great interest. Like it belonged to a patient.

Behind him somebody shouted. He didn’t look. A body hit the ground. Mok’s voice, Mok who never said anything, saying something low and terrible. The red door banged open behind him and there was a noise like a wardrobe falling over. He glanced up for half a second. The man in the seaman’s jacket was face down on the stones with Mok’s knee in his back and Jun Hyuk sitting on top of both of them, enormous, holding the man’s arms. The knife was skittering into the gutter.

Blood on Lin Jian’s coat. None of it his.

“Belt! I need a belt! Someone hold her arm!”

Feet at a run. Out of the gate of the house next door. Tall, thin, grey jumper. Yu Chen. He knelt on the stones and didn’t ask anything. He put his big careful hands round her forearm exactly where Xing Yue showed him, and held it up, and held it hard. Xing Yue pulled his own belt out of his trousers in one movement.

High on her upper arm, near the shoulder. As tight as it would go. He held it. The spurting slowed. Then it stopped. He looked at his watch and said the time out loud, so Yu Chen would remember it if he didn’t.

“Car. Get the car into the alley.”

“I’ll clear it.”

Eliana. In a hoodie at the gate next door. Already walking up to the mouth of the alley, where people had started coming out of their doors to stare. She said something to them. They went back in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara was talking. Of course she was. White to the lips. Coat soaked down one side. Sitting on the cold stones of her father’s alley with her arm in the air, held by two men. Talking.

“It’s the ulnar. The artery. That’s why it’s spurting like that. You’ve stopped it. Good. That’s good.”

“Elara—”

“And the tendons. It went deep. I felt it go deep.”

“Keep it up.”

“It’s the flexors, three at least, I can’t bend my fingers—” She tried. He watched her see it. “And I can’t feel my little finger. Or half the next one. That’s the ulnar nerve. It’s CUT. And the thumb’s wrong too, the thumb’s numb, so that’s the median, it’s both of them, Xing Yue, it’s BOTH—”

“Stop diagnosing yourself. I know what’s cut.”

She stopped. His voice was calm. He heard it. Calmer than he’d ever heard it in his life. Slow. Level. It came from somewhere a long way below his chest where nothing at all was happening.

“I’ve got you. I know what’s cut. Keep your arm up. Look at me.”

She looked at him. Her pupils were huge. There was blood on her chin. Her mouth shook once. Then she pressed it shut and nodded.

“ELARA!” Raiden came out of the red door.

No joke. Not one. He looked at his sister on the stones and went white. Then he bent down and lifted her, all of her, soaked coat and all, like she weighed nothing, while Xing Yue held the arm up and Yu Chen let go. Raiden carried her down the alley at a fast walk with her head on his shoulder. Past the noodle stall. Past the doors Eliana had shut. To the black car, engine running, back door open.

Xing Yue got in first. Raiden put her across his lap. He held her arm up against the roof with one hand and the belt with the other. Mok got behind the wheel. Where had he come from? His trousers were torn at the knee. Somebody else’s blood on his hands. He said nothing. He drove.

He went through every light between the Walled City and the hill, red or not, and never once touched the horn. The old car got to the ambulance bay faster than any ambulance.

She talked the whole way. About the soup. About Ah Sim, who’d be furious about the box.

“She’ll say I did it on PURPOSE—”

“She won’t.”

“She’ll say I didn’t want the dumplings—”

“I’ll tell her you wanted them.”

He’d never talked back to her like this. About nothing. A box. Some soup. He kept doing it. Her voice was getting slower, and as long as he talked, she’d go on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Resus at City Hospital on a Sunday afternoon was Dr. Toh’s. They ran her in on a trolley with his hands on her arm. The registrar on duty met them at bay two. A young man. Competent. Xing Yue had watched him run an arrest and been satisfied.

The registrar looked down at the trolley and saw who it was, and stopped. Gloved hands up. Staring. Dr. Lin from the surgical floor, who brought sweets to the department at New Year and always asked after the registrar’s girlfriend by name. White on a trolley with her coat soaked through. He looked two seconds too long.

“Get out of my resus.”

“It’s not your—”

“Get out. Get me two large lines. Blood for cross-match, six units. Get Dr. Meng from plastics on the phone. If she’s at home, get her out of it.” He didn’t look up. “Then go and stand somewhere I can’t see you.”

“Now!”

The registrar went. A nurse had a line in Elara’s left arm before he’d finished. She glanced at the left hand.

“Rings.”

He took them off himself. The plain gold band. The star. He slid them off his wife’s finger and onto his own little finger, beside his ring, and didn’t take his other hand off her arm.

Dr. Toh came in from the next bay. Small. Brisk. She looked at the trolley. At him.

“Wang. This is my department.”

“Then you can tell me if I’ve missed anything.”

She looked at him. Then she went round the other side of the trolley and checked everything he’d done, from the top, and didn’t send him out. Professor Liao came before four. Somebody had rung him at home. He came into the bay in a cardigan with his car keys still in his hand and looked at Elara, and his face went still.

“Step back, Wang.”

Xing Yue didn’t move.

“You can’t treat her. You know you can’t. She’s your wife. Step back and let the department do it.”

“When Meng’s here.”

Liao looked at him across the trolley. He didn’t say it again. Dr. Meng Shuhua came a few minutes after four in a tracksuit with her hair still wet. She pushed through the curtain and looked at the wrist, all of it, fast, turning it in her hands.

“Theatre. Now. I’ll take it.”

He took his hands away. He took them off her arm and stood back from the trolley and held them up in front of him. They shook. They hadn’t shaken in the alley. Or the car. Or the bay. Now they shook so hard he had to jam them in his armpits and stand there, while the trolley went out past him and down the corridor to the lifts.

✦ ✦ ✦

The repair took five hours. He shouldn’t have been in the room. Everybody in it knew that. He was her husband, and he was a surgeon, and there were rules about both. Meng looked at him when he came in scrubbed and gowned and gloved.

“I won’t touch anything.”

She looked a moment longer. Then she nodded at the corner by the anaesthetic machine and went back to her microscope. He stood in the corner with his empty gloved hands held up in front of his chest. He watched.

Meng did the tendons first. One by one. Then the artery, and the hand went pink. Then the microscope came down for the nerves, and she spent most of three hours on them. Stitches finer than a hair. So slow the scrub nurse shifted her feet. Nobody spoke. The theatre was cold. On the board on the other side he could see Elara’s left hand, small and pale and still, with nothing on it now. Her rings were on his finger under his glove.

Nobody hummed.

After nine Meng sat back. She took her loupes off and rubbed her eyes. Then she came over to the corner, stripping her gloves.

“The repair’s good. As good as I can make it. It was a clean cut, she’s young, and you got her here fast.” She looked at him. “She’ll keep the hand. Whether she keeps the surgeon’s hand, nobody can tell you for a year.”

He nodded.

“Thank you.”

“Go and sit with her. She’ll want you when she wakes.”

He’d known it all on the stones. He nodded again, because he didn’t trust his voice. Meng put her hand on his arm, briefly, like you would with a relative, and went out.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke in recovery at ten. He was beside the trolley on a stool. Her right arm was in a thick splint to the elbow, raised on pillows. He’d been watching her face for forty minutes.

Her eyes opened. They wandered over the ceiling and the monitor and found him.

“Oh. It’s you.”

Thick. Slow. She frowned at him.

“You look terrible. Has somebody died? You’ve got your—your bad face. The one for registrars.” Her eyes went half shut and opened again. “Is it me? Did I die? I don’t think I died. If I’d died I’d be cross about the soup.”

“You didn’t die.”

“Good.” She tried to lift her right hand. The splint wouldn’t let her. She looked at it. He watched her remember. Her face went still.

Then she looked back at him and made her mouth smile. Crooked. The drugs in it.

“Well. At least it wasn’t my talking hand.”

He couldn’t answer that. She saw that he couldn’t. Her eyes were swimming.

“Xing Yue.”

Just his name.

He stood and bent over the trolley and kissed her forehead. He kept his mouth there, on her cold skin under the edge of the paper cap, as long as he could. Then he took her left hand. He worked the rings off his little finger and put them back on hers. The band. Then the star. It took him two tries. His hands still weren’t right. He turned the hand over and kissed the inside of her wrist where the pulse was. Slow. Steady. There.

“I’m here.”

She was already asleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wei Long came up to the ward at midnight. Xing Yue was in the chair beside her bed in a side room on the plastics floor. Lin Jian was in the corridor outside on a plastic chair, where he’d been since six. Blood dried on his coat. He wouldn’t go home. He wouldn’t come in. Raiden had taken Jinx home. Ev and Jun Hyuk were in the relatives’ room. Every hour Jun Hyuk put his head round the door.

“Anything?”

“Asleep.”

“Good. Good. Ev says good.” He went away again.

Wei Long stood in the doorway in his long coat. He looked at the splint. Then at Xing Yue. He tipped his head at the window at the end of the corridor. Away from her father.

“He’s not saying much. He’s not denying anything either. He came for Lin Jian. He says he didn’t mean to touch anyone else.” Wei Long’s long face didn’t move. “He keeps asking if she’s all right.”

“Who is he?”

“Qu Wenjun. Fifty-seven. A seaman. Merchant ships, thirty years. A prison term in the middle for a fight.”

“And?”

“He says Lin Jian burned his brother’s boats in 2002. Killed his brother and his brother’s wife.” Wei Long was watching his face. “He says Lin Jian killed the child too. He says the whole family died.”

Xing Yue looked out at the dark car park. Qu.

Qu Lighterage. Walled City piers. Qu Mingde. Shi Yuning, nurse. A child in a laundry basket under wet towels. A man in a black car who paid for a roof in cash, came back the next week, and went down the steps without a word, looking like he’d been hit. No relatives found.

He went cold. It started in his hands, where her blood had been. It went up his arms and into his chest. He stood at the window and let it.

“Xing Yue.”

“I’m all right.”

“You don’t look it.”

“I need to go back in. She wakes up and talks. I don’t want her to wake up and find nobody there.”

He went back down the corridor. Past Lin Jian on his plastic chair. The old man lifted his head and looked at him. Xing Yue looked back.

He’d guessed. Did the old man know he’d guessed? Not yet. He went in and sat down by her bed. He took her left hand, rings and all, and put his thumb on her pulse.

He kept it there until the window went grey.
